children.title: Algebraic Core Notions
children.top_down_role: Direction-based interior substitutes independent of a strong topology.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Core Failure in a Deficient Affine Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set in a proper affine subspace has empty ambient algebraic core; using intrinsic directions removes that obstruction but does not universally guarantee nonemptiness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{aff}C\neq X\), then \(\operatorname{core}C=\varnothing\). Passing to the intrinsic direction space \(\operatorname{span}(C-C)\) removes this particular obstruction, although without finite-dimensional or additional algebraic regularity assumptions the intrinsic core can still be empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact obstruction created by testing all ambient algebraic directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional-Cone Characterization of Algebraic Core
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point belongs to the ambient or intrinsic algebraic core exactly when its feasible-direction cone fills the corresponding direction space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subseteq X\) and \(x\in C\), \[x\in\operatorname{core}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=X.\] If the core is computed intrinsically in the direction space \(\operatorname{span}(C-C)\), then \[x\in\operatorname{icr}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\operatorname{span}(C-C).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent feasible-direction characterization of ambient and intrinsic algebraic cores.

notation.meaning: Conic hull of the translated feasible set.
Intrinsic algebraic core, computed in directions parallel to the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Core Notions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point belongs to the algebraic core when every ambient direction permits a sufficiently short two-sided line segment through that point remaining in the convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algebraic core of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{core}C=\{x\in C:\text{for every }v\in X\text{ there exists }\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }x+tv\in C\text{ whenever }|t|<\varepsilon\}.\] The radius \(\varepsilon\) may depend on \(v\). This predicate uses only vector-space operations and quantification over directions, so it does not require a topology. Replacing \(X\) by \(\operatorname{span}(C-C)\) gives the corresponding intrinsic algebraic core relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{core}C=\{x\in C:\forall v\in X\ \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall t\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon),\ x+tv\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient algebraic core, defined without choosing a topology.

notation.meaning: Algebraic interior, or core, relative to all ambient directions.
An arbitrary algebraic direction in the ambient vector space.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.2 Generalized Interiors p. 114

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Generating Cone with Empty Algebraic Core
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of generatingness to guarantee nonempty ambient algebraic core in infinite algebraic dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) be the vector space of all real sequences and let \[K=\{x=(x_n)_{n\geq1}:x_n\geq0\text{ for every }n\}.\] Then \(K-K=X\), so \(K\) is generating, but \(\operatorname{core}K=\varnothing\). Thus full algebraic span is necessary but not sufficient for a convex cone to have nonempty ambient core in infinite algebraic dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinatewise nonnegative cone of all real sequences generates the whole sequence space but has empty algebraic core.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) is treated as a real vector space without topology.

notation.meaning: Vector space of all real sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: A Generating Cone with Empty Algebraic Core

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic stability properties of the ambient core of a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a real vector space. Then \(\operatorname{core}K\) is convex and, whenever it is nonempty, \[K+\operatorname{core}K\subseteq\operatorname{core}K,\qquad \lambda\operatorname{core}K=\operatorname{core}K\quad(\lambda>0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algebraic core of a convex cone is convex, stable under addition of cone elements, and invariant under positive scaling.

notation.meaning: Ambient algebraic core of the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic-Core Calculus for Convex Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absorbing-Translate Characterization of the Algebraic Core
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent topology-free formulation of algebraic-core membership for a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space \(X\), and let \(x\in C\). Then \[x\in\operatorname{core}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C-x\text{ is absorbing in }X\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=X.\] Equivalently, every ambient direction belongs to the cone of feasible displacements from \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is in the algebraic core exactly when its translated feasible set absorbs every direction, equivalently when its conic hull is the whole ambient vector space.

notation.meaning: Set of feasible displacements from x.
Conic hull of the feasible displacements.

knowledge_statements.title: Absorbing-Translate Characterization of the Algebraic Core

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic interior computed only in directions parallel to the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq X\), its intrinsic algebraic core is \[\operatorname{icr}C:=\left\{x\in C:\forall v\in\operatorname{span}(C-C)\ \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall |t|<\varepsilon,\ x+tv\in C\right\}.\] It is the ambient algebraic core of \(C\) when \(C\) is regarded as a subset of \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic algebraic core tests two-sided feasibility only along directions parallel to the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Algebraic Core

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient Core and Deficient Affine Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic obstruction caused by using all ambient directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\neq\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{aff}C\neq X\), then \(\operatorname{core}C=\varnothing\). The intrinsic core need not be empty for this reason, because it tests only directions in \(\operatorname{span}(C-C)\); however, in infinite-dimensional algebraic settings even \(\operatorname{icr}C\) can be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set in a proper affine subspace has empty ambient core, while passing to intrinsic directions removes that particular obstruction but does not guarantee nonemptiness in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Core and Deficient Affine Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent algebraic characterization for convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subseteq X\) and \(x\in C\), \[x\in\operatorname{core}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=X.\] Likewise, \[x\in\operatorname{icr}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\operatorname{span}(C-C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is in the ambient or intrinsic core exactly when its feasible-direction cone fills the corresponding ambient direction space.

notation.meaning: Conic hull of the translated feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional-Cone Characterization of the Core

children.title: Quasi-Relative Interior
children.top_down_role: Generalized interior structure used in infinite-dimensional convex analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: An Infinite-Dimensional Cone with Empty Quasi-Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone in l2 over an uncountable index set has empty quasi-relative interior because every point has a zero coordinate that leaves a one-sided feasible-direction constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be uncountable and let \(C=\ell^2_+(I)\). Every \(x\in C\) has countable support, so some coordinate \(i\in I\) satisfies \(x_i=0\). Every vector in \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}\) then has nonnegative \(i\)-th coordinate, while the cone contains a vector with positive \(i\)-th coordinate. Hence this closed feasible-direction cone is not a linear subspace for any \(x\in C\), and \[\operatorname{qri}C=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit infinite-dimensional failure of quasi-relative-interior nonemptiness.

notation.meaning: Hilbert space of square-summable real families indexed by I.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Characterization of Quasi-Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-set point is quasi-relatively interior exactly when its continuous normal cone is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[N_C(x):=\{x^*\in X^*:\langle x^*,y-x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}.\] Then \[x\in\operatorname{qri}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N_C(x)\text{ is a linear subspace of }X^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{qri}C\iff N_C(x)\text{ is a linear subspace of }X^*.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-dual characterization in a Hausdorff locally convex space.

notation.meaning: Continuous normal cone to C at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Collapse to Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior is contained in quasi-relative interior, and the two coincide in finite dimensions; quasi-relative interior can still be empty in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is nonempty, \[\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq\operatorname{qri}C.\] If \(X\) is finite-dimensional, then \[\operatorname{qri}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\] In infinite-dimensional locally convex spaces, equality and nonemptiness of the quasi-relative interior can fail.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space.
Equality is asserted when \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical relative interior as a sufficient condition and the exact finite-dimensional specialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is in the quasi-relative interior when the closure of the cone of feasible directions from it is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quasi-relative interior of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{qri}C=\{x\in C:\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}\text{ is a linear subspace of }X\}.\] Here the closure is taken in the given topology of \(X\). Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{qri}C\) precisely when the closed cone of feasible directions from \(x\) is symmetric under multiplication by \(-1\). The closure permits this set to remain useful when ordinary or relative interiors are empty in infinite-dimensional spaces.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard locally convex-space definition via the closed cone of feasible directions.

notation.meaning: Quasi-relative interior of the convex set.
Topological closure in the ambient space.
Conic hull of the translated set.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.2 Generalized Interiors p. 114

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Cone in Hilbert Sequence Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical infinite-dimensional separation of ordinary, relative, and quasi-relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[K=\ell^2_+=\{x\in\ell^2:x_n\ge0\ \forall n\}.\] Then \(\operatorname{span}K=\ell^2\), but \[\operatorname{int}K=\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{qri}K=\{x\in\ell^2:x_n>0\ \forall n\}\ne\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone of l2 has empty ordinary and relative interiors but nonempty quasi-relative interior consisting of coordinatewise positive sequences.

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise nonnegative cone in the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Cone in Hilbert Sequence Space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Segment Stability and Density of Quasi-Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core stability property when quasi-relative interior is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{qri}C\), \(y\in C\), and \(0\le t<1\), then \[(1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{qri}C.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{qri}C\) is convex and, whenever it is nonempty, \[\overline{\operatorname{qri}C}=\overline C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-relative-interior point remains quasi-relatively interior along every segment toward a point of the set, except possibly at the other endpoint; hence nonempty qri is convex and dense up to closure.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{qri}C\) for \(y\in C\) and \(0\le t<1\); if \(\operatorname{qri}C\ne\varnothing\), then \(\overline{\operatorname{qri}C}=\overline C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Segment Stability and Density of Quasi-Relative Interior

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic relation between quasi-relative and ordinary relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex \(C\), \[\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq\operatorname{qri}C\subseteq C.\] If \(X\) is finite-dimensional, then \[\operatorname{qri}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\] In infinite dimensions the first inclusion can be strict, and quasi-relative interior need not be nonempty without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior is contained in quasi-relative interior, and the notions coincide in finite dimensions but can differ in infinite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Inclusion and Finite-Dimensional Collapse

children.title: Cone Regularity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Regularity classes governing lineality, interior, closure, and nondegenerate order structure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(E\) is a real topological vector space, \(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone, and \(\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\). When properness is invoked, \(E\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The taxonomy records independent algebraic and topological properties. The conventional finite-dimensional term “proper cone” combines four of them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(K\) is pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\), solid when \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), closed when \(K=\overline K\), and generating when \(K-K=E\), equivalently \(\operatorname{span}K=E\). In finite dimensions, \(K\) is proper when it is simultaneously convex, closed, pointed, and solid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularity taxonomy classifies a convex cone by lineality, ambient interior, closure, and span. Pointed cones have no nonzero lineality, solid cones have nonempty ambient interior, closed cones contain their limits, and generating cones span the ambient space. A finite-dimensional proper cone is convex, closed, pointed, and solid.
assumptions_latex: The ambient topology is fixed before closedness or solidity is assessed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is pointed if and only if it contains no nonzero linear subspace.
\(K\) is solid if and only if there exist \(x\in K\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\) with \(x+U\subseteq K\).
In finite dimensions, \(K\) is generating if and only if it is solid.
special_cases_latex: \(\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\mathbb S_+^n\) are proper cones in their natural Euclidean spaces.
A nontrivial linear subspace is neither pointed nor solid unless it is the whole ambient space for the latter property.
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper cone induces the partial order \(x\preccurlyeq_K y\Longleftrightarrow y-x\in K\).
Failure of any defining property excludes a cone from the finite-dimensional proper class.
boundary_notes: Some authors use different conventions for “proper” outside finite dimensions; the definition here is explicitly finite-dimensional.
Closedness and solidity depend on the selected topology, whereas pointedness and generatingness are algebraic.

children.title: Pointed Cones
children.top_down_role: Cones without nontrivial reversible directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness and Antisymmetric Cone Orders
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preorder induced by a convex cone is antisymmetric, and hence a partial order, exactly when the cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(x\preceq_K y\) by \(y-x\in K\). This relation is a preorder, and it is a partial order precisely when \(K\) is pointed: \[x\preceq_K y\text{ and }y\preceq_K x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in K\cap(-K).\] Thus antisymmetry is equivalent to \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent order-theoretic formulation of pointedness; no topology or closedness is required.

notation.meaning: Cone-induced preorder defined by membership of the difference in K.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is pointed when the only vector it contains together with its negative is zero, equivalently when it contains no nontrivial line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is pointed when \[K\cap(-K)=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, the lineality space \(\operatorname{lin}(K):=K\cap(-K)\) is trivial. Thus, if \(x\in K\) and \(-x\in K\), pointedness forces \(x=0\). Since a convex cone contains the entire line \(\{tx:t\in\mathbb{R}\}\) whenever it contains both \(x\) and \(-x\), this condition is also equivalent to saying that \(K\) contains no nontrivial linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is pointed if and only if \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), equivalently its lineality space is trivial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic pointedness through trivial lineality.

notation.meaning: Cone obtained by negating every element of the cone.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointedness and the Extreme Vertex at the Origin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization of pointedness through extremality of the cone vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\) in a real vector space, \[K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\text{ is an extreme point of }K.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is pointed exactly when its origin is an extreme point.

notation.meaning: Set of extreme points of the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness and the Extreme Vertex at the Origin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic meaning of pointedness for the translation-invariant preorder induced by a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(x\preceq_K y\) by \(y-x\in K\). For every convex cone \(K\), this relation is reflexive and transitive. It is antisymmetric, and therefore a partial order, exactly when \(K\) is pointed: \[x\preceq_Ky\ \text{and}\ y\preceq_Kx\Longrightarrow x=y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\cap(-K)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preorder induced by a convex cone is a partial order precisely when the cone is pointed.

notation.meaning: Translation-invariant preorder induced by the cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointed Cones and Antisymmetric Cone Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic order consequence of pointedness; no topology or closedness is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq X\) be a convex cone and define \(x\preceq_K y\iff y-x\in K\). Then \(\preceq_K\) is reflexive and transitive, and it is antisymmetric if and only if \(K\) is pointed. Indeed, \[x\preceq_K y\ \text{and}\ y\preceq_K x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in K\cap(-K),\] so pointedness forces \(x=y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preorder induced by a cone is a partial order exactly when the cone is pointed.

notation.meaning: The cone order defined by \(y-x\in K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hereditary and Product Rules for Pointedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary constructions whose pointedness is determined entirely by lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every subcone \(C\subseteq K\) of a pointed cone is pointed. For convex cones \(K_i\subseteq X_i\), \[\operatorname{lin}\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^mK_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{lin}(K_i),\] and consequently \(\prod_{i=1}^mK_i\) is pointed if and only if every \(K_i\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointedness passes to subcones, and a finite product cone is pointed exactly when every factor is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) and \(K_i\) are convex cones in real vector spaces.
The displayed product has finitely many factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\subseteq K\text{ and }K\text{ pointed}\Rightarrow C\text{ pointed},\qquad \prod_iK_i\text{ pointed}\iff\forall i,\ K_i\text{ pointed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solidity and Full Dimensionality of a Finite-Dimensional Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence is finite-dimensional and uses ambient norm topology. It is not asserted for arbitrary infinite-dimensional cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is called solid when \(\operatorname{int}_E K\ne\varnothing\), and it is called full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{span}K=E\), equivalently \(\dim K=\dim E\), where \(\dim K:=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\). In finite dimensions these two classes coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional convex cone is solid when it has a usable ambient interior and full-dimensional when its linear span equals the entire ambient space. For nonempty convex cones in finite-dimensional spaces, these conditions are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is solid if and only if there exist \(x\in K\) and \(r>0\) such that \(B(x,r)\subseteq K\).
\(K\) is full-dimensional if and only if \(K-K=E\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), \(\operatorname{int}K=\mathbb R_{++}^n\), so \(K\) is solid and full-dimensional.
A ray in \(\mathbb R^n\) is not solid when \(n>1\), although it has nonempty relative interior.
If \(E=\{0\}\), the cone \(K=\{0\}\) is both solid and full-dimensional in that zero-dimensional ambient space.
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper cone is necessarily full-dimensional.
If \(\operatorname{span}K\ne E\), then ambient interior is empty and relative interior must be used instead.
boundary_notes: In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, a closed pointed cone may span densely or even algebraically generate the space while still having empty interior.
The dimension of a cone means the dimension of its linear span, not its cardinality.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Specific Stability of the Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior of a solid convex cone is invariant under positive scaling and remains in the interior after addition of any cone element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a solid convex cone in a real topological vector space \(X\). Then, for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\lambda\operatorname{int}_XK=\operatorname{int}_XK,\qquad \operatorname{int}_XK+K\subseteq\operatorname{int}_XK.\] Thus positive rescaling preserves the interior exactly, and adding any cone element to an interior cone element preserves interiority.

knowledge_statements.title: Solid Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is solid when it has a nonempty ordinary interior in its ambient topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is solid in \(X\) if its ordinary ambient interior is nonempty: \[\operatorname{int}_XK\neq\varnothing.\] Equivalently, there exist \(u\in K\) and an ambient neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\) such that \(u+U\subseteq K\). In a normed space this is equivalent to the existence of \(u\in K\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfying \(B_X(u,\varepsilon)\subseteq K\). Solidity therefore depends on the chosen ambient topology and space.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is solid if and only if \(\operatorname{int}_XK\neq\varnothing\).

Full-Dimensional Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is full-dimensional when its linear span equals its ambient finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex cone \(C\subseteq X\) is full-dimensional in \(X\) when its linear span is the entire ambient space:
\[
\operatorname{span}C=X.
\]
Equivalently, the affine hull of \(C\) is \(X\), because \(0\in C\) implies \(\operatorname{aff}C=\operatorname{span}C\). Full-dimensionality is relative to the specified ambient space; the same cone is always full-dimensional when regarded as a subset of \(\operatorname{span}C\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is full-dimensional if and only if \(\operatorname{span}C=X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses ambient, rather than relative, dimension in finite-dimensional spaces.

notation.meaning: interior in the topology of the ambient space

knowledge_statements.title: Full Span Does Not Imply Solidity in Infinite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone in l2 is closed and spans all of l2 but has empty norm interior, so full span need not imply solidity in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the Hilbert space \(\ell^2\), the positive cone \[\ell^2_+=\{x=(x_n)\in\ell^2:x_n\geq0\text{ for every }n\}\] is closed and convex and satisfies \[\operatorname{span}\ell^2_+=\ell^2,\qquad \operatorname{int}_{\ell^2}\ell^2_+=\varnothing.\] Hence algebraic full dimensionality does not imply solidity in infinite-dimensional normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{span}K=\ell^2\) and \(\operatorname{int}_{\ell^2}K=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete Hilbert-space counterexample to the infinite-dimensional extension of the finite-dimensional equivalence.

knowledge_statements.title: Solidity–Dimension Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a convex cone has nonempty ambient interior exactly when it spans the whole space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty convex cone \(C\subseteq X\), solidity and full-dimensionality are equivalent:
\[
\operatorname{int}_X C\neq\varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{span}C=X.
\]
More generally, \(C\) has nonempty relative interior in \(\operatorname{span}C\). The displayed ambient-interior equivalence relies on finite dimensionality; in infinite-dimensional spaces a cone may linearly span the ambient space while having empty interior.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real topological vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence; it need not extend to infinite-dimensional spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper cone is a closed convex cone that is pointed and has nonempty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex cone \(C\subseteq X\) is proper when all three conditions hold:
\[
C\text{ is closed},
\qquad C\cap(-C)=\{0\},
\qquad \operatorname{int}C\neq\varnothing.
\]
The second condition is pointedness, and the third is solidity. Thus a proper cone contains no nonzero line, is full-dimensional, and contains all of its limit points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is proper exactly when it is closed, pointed, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard finite-dimensional conic-optimization convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional examples showing that closedness, pointedness, and solidity are independent requirements in the standard definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), each condition in the definition of a proper cone is indispensable. The cone \[K_1=\{0\}\cup\{(x_1,x_2):x_1>0,\ x_2>0\}\] is convex, pointed, and solid but not closed. The halfspace cone \[K_2=\{(x_1,x_2):x_1\geq0\}\] is closed and solid but not pointed. The ray \[K_3=\{(t,0):t\geq0\}\] is closed and pointed but has empty ambient interior. Thus no two of closedness, pointedness, and solidity imply the third.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness, pointedness, and solidity are independent: explicit planar cones satisfy each pair while failing the remaining properness condition.
assumptions_latex: The ambient space is \(\mathbb R^2\) with its usual topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No two of closedness, pointedness, and solidity imply the third.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_i\subseteq X_i\) be proper cones. Then \(\prod_{i=1}^mK_i\) is a proper cone in \(\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\). If \(T:X\to Y\) is a linear isomorphism and \(K\subseteq X\) is proper, then \(T(K)\) is proper in \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite products and linear isomorphic images of proper cones are proper.
assumptions_latex: All spaces are finite-dimensional real normed spaces.
The product has finitely many factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_i\text{ proper for all }i\Rightarrow\prod_iK_i\text{ proper},\qquad K\text{ proper}\Rightarrow T(K)\text{ proper}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a topology-sensitive umbrella definition spanning finite-dimensional, Hilbert, and Hausdorff locally convex regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ambient-space regime for cone geometry is a datum \((E,\tau,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{E,E'})\), together with a convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), where closure and interior are \(\overline K^{\tau}\) and \(\operatorname{int}_{\tau}K\), and the continuous dual cone is \[K^+:=\{x'\in E':\langle x,x'\rangle_{E,E'}\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}.\] A finite-dimensional regime takes \(E\cong\mathbb R^n\); a Hilbert regime identifies \(E'\) with \(E\) by the inner product; a locally convex regime retains the chosen topology and continuous dual explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone geometry is specified relative to an ambient vector space, a topology, and its continuous dual pairing. The topology determines closure and interior, while the pairing determines the continuous dual cone. Euclidean, Hilbert, and general locally convex settings are distinct regimes of this datum.

\(E'\) is the continuous dual determined by \(\tau\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex cone in finite dimensions equals its bipolar and admits a unique nearest point for every ambient vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual cone \(C^*\) is closed and convex, and finite-dimensional separation yields the bipolar identity
\[
C^{**}=C.
\]
Moreover, for each \(x\in X\), there exists a unique point \(P_Cx\in C\) satisfying
\[
\lVert x-P_Cx\rVert=\min_{c\in C}\lVert x-c\rVert.
\]
Thus closed convex cones in finite dimensions admit exact bipolar recovery and single-valued metric projection.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{**}=C\), and every \(x\in X\) has a unique metric projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records two fundamental consequences of finite-dimensional closed convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Hilbert-space vector decomposes uniquely into orthogonal projections onto a closed convex cone and its negative polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), the metric projections onto \(C\) and its negative polar \(C^\circ\) give the orthogonal decomposition
\[
x=P_Cx+P_{C^\circ}x,
\qquad
\langle P_Cx,P_{C^\circ}x\rangle=0.
\]
The two summands are uniquely determined. Equivalently, \(P_{C^\circ}x=x-P_Cx\), so Hilbert-space cone geometry couples polarity to metric projection through the inner product.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in H\) satisfies \(x=P_Cx+P_{C^\circ}x\) with orthogonal summands.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Cones in a Real Hilbert Space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \((\mathcal H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a real Hilbert space with norm \(\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}\), and \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition emphasizes the inner-product, polar, and metric-projection structures available for closed convex cones, including infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Hilbert-space convex cone is a set \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) satisfying \[(\forall x,y\in K)(\forall\alpha,\beta\ge0)\quad \alpha x+\beta y\in K.\] Its polar and dual cones are \[K^{\ominus}=\{u\in\mathcal H:\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle\le0\},\qquad K^{\oplus}=-K^{\ominus}.\] If \(K\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, its metric projector is the single-valued map \[P_Kx:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in K}\|x-y\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hilbert-space cone is a convex cone in a complete inner-product space. The inner product identifies polar and dual cones within the same space. When the cone is nonempty, closed, and convex, every point has a unique nearest point in the cone, defining the metric projector.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K^{\ominus}=\{u\in\mathcal H:(\forall x\in K)\ \langle x,u\rangle\le0\}\).
For closed convex \(K\), \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\ell_+^2(I)\), \(K\) is self-dual and \((P_Kx)_i=\max\{x_i,0\}\).
Finite-dimensional Euclidean cones are Hilbert-space cones.
A closed linear subspace is a cone whose polar equals its orthogonal complement.
immediate_consequences_latex: Moreau decomposition gives \(x=P_Kx+P_{K^{\ominus}}x\) with orthogonal summands.
Closedness is essential for a globally defined nearest-point projector.
boundary_notes: A Hilbert-space cone can be pointed and closed while having empty norm interior.
The metric projector generally has no analogue in an arbitrary locally convex space without additional geometry.

metric projector onto a nonempty closed convex cone

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Separation Certificate for Closed Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies outside a closed convex cone in a Hausdorff locally convex space exactly when a continuous functional is nonnegative on the cone and strictly negative at that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a closed convex cone in a Hausdorff locally convex space \(X\). For every \(x\notin C\), there is a continuous linear functional \(x^*\in X^*\) satisfying \[\langle x^*,c\rangle\geq0\quad(c\in C),\qquad \langle x^*,x\rangle<0.\] Equivalently, \[x\in C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle x^*,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x^*\in C^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
\(C\subseteq X\) is a closed convex cone, and \(x\in X\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x^*\in X^*\) such that \(\langle x^*,c\rangle\geq0\) for every \(c\in C\) and \(\langle x^*,x\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-functional certificate separating a point from a closed convex cone in a Hausdorff locally convex space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Continuous-Dual Recovery without Local Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary example showing the need for continuous-linear separation in bipolar recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<p<1\), let \(X=L^p([0,1])\) over Lebesgue measure with its usual quasi-norm topology, and let \(C=\{0\}\). The continuous dual is trivial, \(X^*=\{0\}\), and therefore \[C^\circ=X^*=\{0\},\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=X\ne C=\overline C.\] Thus continuous-dual bipolar recovery can fail outside the locally convex, continuously separated setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonatomic L-p with zero less than p less than one, the continuous dual is trivial, so the bipolar of the closed zero cone is the whole space.
assumptions_latex: \(X=L^p([0,1])\) is formed over Lebesgue measure and carries its usual quasi-norm topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Cones in a Hausdorff Locally Convex Space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \((X,\tau)\) is a real Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space, \(X'\) is its continuous dual, and \(\langle x,x'\rangle:=x'(x)\) is the canonical dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition is topology-dependent and does not assume a norm, inner product, metrizability, or reflexivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally convex-space cone is a subset \(K\subseteq X\) such that \[(\forall x,y\in K)(\forall\alpha,\beta\ge0)\quad\alpha x+\beta y\in K.\] Its \(\tau\)-closure and \(\tau\)-interior are \(\overline K^{\tau}\) and \(\operatorname{int}_{\tau}K\), and its continuous dual cone is \[K^+:=\{x'\in X':(\forall x\in K)\ \langle x,x'\rangle\ge0\}.\] The weak closure uses \(\sigma(X,X')\), while weak-star closure on subsets of \(X'\) uses \(\sigma(X',X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally convex-space cone is a convex cone in a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space. Its closure and interior are relative to the selected topology, and its dual cone is formed from continuous linear functionals rather than the full algebraic dual.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\tau)\) is a real Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^+=\bigcap_{x\in K}\{x'\in X':\langle x,x'\rangle\ge0\}\] is a weak-star closed convex cone in \(X'\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is \(\tau\)-closed if and only if it contains the limit of every \(\tau\)-convergent net in \(K\).
\(K^+\) is the intersection of all weak-star closed halfspaces of \(X'\) determined by elements of \(K\).
special_cases_latex: Every Banach space with its norm topology is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
Every real Hilbert space is a locally convex space whose continuous dual is identified with the space itself.
In finite dimensions, the locally convex and Euclidean cone regimes coincide.
immediate_consequences_latex: The algebraic properties of pointedness and lineality do not depend on \(\tau\), but closedness and solidity do.
Sequences do not characterize closure in every locally convex space; nets may be required.
boundary_notes: No inspected local source supplies a precise locator for this full locally convex-space formulation.
Metric projection and orthogonal polarity are not included without Hilbert structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the continuous negative polar of \(C\) by
\[
C^\circ=\{x^*\in X^*: \langle x^*,c\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }c\in C\}.
\]
Taking the polar again in \(X\) gives
\[
C^{\circ\circ}=\overline C.
\]
Hence a convex cone is recovered exactly from all continuous linear inequalities valid on it if and only if it is closed in the chosen locally convex topology.

children.top_down_role: Intrinsic failures caused by lineality, empty interior, or missing boundary points.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(E\) is a real topological vector space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone. Define \(L(K):=K\cap(-K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is an aggregate classification of three standard failure modes: nontrivial lineality, empty ambient interior, and nonclosedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regularity-failure signature of \(K\) is \[\mathfrak F(K):=\bigl(\mathbf 1_{L(K)\ne\{0\}},\ \mathbf 1_{\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing},\ \mathbf 1_{K\ne\overline K}\bigr)\in\{0,1\}^3.\] The first component is the lineality failure, the second the solidity failure, and the third the closure failure. The cone lies in the corresponding failure boundary whenever at least one component equals \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularity-failure signature records whether a convex cone has nonzero lineality, empty ambient interior, or missing limit points. Each condition marks a different obstruction to proper-cone behavior, and several can occur simultaneously.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The lineality component equals \(1\) if and only if \(K\) contains a nonzero linear subspace.
The closure component equals \(1\) if and only if \(\overline K\setminus K\ne\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: A finite-dimensional proper cone has signature \((0,0,0)\).
An infinite-dimensional positive orthant \(\ell_+^2(I)\) for infinite \(I\) has empty interior despite being closed and pointed.
An open convex cone can be pointed and solid but fail closedness.
immediate_consequences_latex: The signature separates algebraic failure from topology-dependent failures.
Replacing \(K\) by \(\overline K\) removes closure failure but can change neither lineality nor interior automatically.
boundary_notes: The symbol \(\mathfrak F\) and the three-bit packaging are local to this record; the constituent notions are standard.
Empty ambient interior does not imply empty relative or quasi-relative interior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality and Span Degeneracy of a Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(E\) is a real vector space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone. Set \(\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\) and \(V_K:=\operatorname{span}K=K-K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates algebraic degeneracies independently of closedness and topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is lineality-degenerate when \(\operatorname{lin}K\ne\{0\}\), span-deficient when \(V_K\ne E\), and algebraically degenerate when at least one of these conditions holds. It is algebraically nondegenerate when \[K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{span}K=E.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is lineality-degenerate if it contains a nonzero direction together with its negative, and span-deficient if it lies in a proper linear subspace. Algebraic degeneracy means that at least one of these defects occurs.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}K\ne\{0\}\) if and only if \(K\) contains a nontrivial linear subspace.
\(\operatorname{span}K\ne E\) if and only if \(K-K\ne E\).
special_cases_latex: A proper finite-dimensional cone is algebraically nondegenerate.
A nonzero linear subspace is lineality-degenerate because \(K=-K\).
A pointed ray in \(\mathbb R^n\) with \(n>1\) is span-deficient but not lineality-degenerate.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nontrivial lineality prevents antisymmetry of the cone-induced preorder.
Span deficiency forces empty ambient interior in finite dimensions.
Passing to the quotient \(V_K/\operatorname{lin}K\) removes lineality, while restricting the ambient space to \(V_K\) removes span deficiency.
boundary_notes: Closedness is not part of algebraic degeneracy.
The word “degenerate” is used here for the stated disjunction; other literature may reserve it for narrower conditions.

notation.meaning: linear span or generating subspace of the cone

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Annihilation of Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual functionals annihilate a nonpointed cone's lineality, forcing the dual into a proper subspace and preventing strictly positive ray normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(L=C\cap(-C)\neq\{0\}\), then every \(y\in C^*\) annihilates \(L\), so
\[
C^*\subseteq L^\perp,
\qquad
\operatorname{int}_X C^*=\varnothing.
\]
Moreover, no linear functional is strictly positive on all of \(C\setminus\{0\}\); hence a nonpointed cone admits no base obtained by strictly positive ray normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual and normalization obstructions caused by nonzero primal lineality.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpointed Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is nonpointed exactly when it contains a nonzero line, which destroys antisymmetry of its induced ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone \(C\) is nonpointed precisely when its lineality space is nontrivial:
\[
L=C\cap(-C)\neq\{0\}.
\]
For every nonzero \(\ell\in L\), both \(\ell\in C\) and \(-\ell\in C\). Consequently, the cone-induced relation \(x\preceq_C y\) fails antisymmetry, since \(x\preceq_C x+\ell\) and \(x+\ell\preceq_C x\) while \(x\neq x+\ell\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies lineality as the precise obstruction to pointedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Every Nonempty Face Contains the Lineality Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial obstruction caused by nonzero cone lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is a nonempty face of a convex cone \(C\), then \[L=C\cap(-C)\subseteq F.\] Consequently, when \(L\ne\{0\}\), the cone has no zero-dimensional face and no extreme ray in the usual facial sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face contains the cone's lineality, so a nonpointed cone has neither a vertex at the origin nor an extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.title: Every Nonempty Face Contains the Lineality Space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointed Quotient of a Nonpointed Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical algebraic removal of lineality and induced-order interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=C\cap(-C)\) and \(q:X\to X/L\) be the quotient map. Then \(q(C)\) is pointed. Moreover, \[q(x)\preceq_{q(C)}q(y)\iff y-x\in C+L=C.\] Thus the preorder induced by \(C\) becomes a partial order on equivalence classes modulo \(L\), identifying exactly the mutually comparable points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting by lineality produces a pointed cone and converts the induced preorder into a partial order on equivalence classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(C)\subseteq X/L\) is pointed, and the preorder induced by \(C\) descends to a partial order.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Quotient of a Nonpointed Cone
Ambient and Intrinsic Duals of a Lower-Dimensional Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ambient dual of a lower-dimensional cone is its intrinsic dual plus the orthogonal complement of its span; this orthogonal complement is exactly the ambient dual's lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W=\operatorname{span}C\), and compute the positive dual either in \(X\) or intrinsically in \(W\). Then
\[
C_X^*=C_W^*\oplus W^\perp,
\qquad
\operatorname{lin}(C_X^*)=W^\perp.
\]
Thus \(C\) is lower-dimensional in \(X\) exactly when its ambient dual has nonzero lineality arising from \(W^\perp\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional dual degeneracy caused solely by deficient ambient span.

notation.meaning: dual cone computed in the ambient space
dual cone computed intrinsically in the span

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional finite-dimensional cone has empty ambient interior but nonempty relative interior within its span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone \(C\) is lower-dimensional in \(X\) when
\[
\operatorname{span}C\neq X.
\]
In finite dimensions this is equivalent to \(\operatorname{int}_X C=\varnothing\). Nevertheless, every nonempty convex cone has nonempty relative interior in its span:
\[
\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing,
\]
where relative interior is computed within \(\operatorname{span}C\). Thus loss of ambient interior does not imply loss of relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real topological vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundary between ambient and relative interior.

notation.meaning: relative interior in the affine hull

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Lineality Forced by Deficient Span
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual obstruction created by lower dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite-dimensional inner-product space, if \(S=\operatorname{span}C\), then \[C^*\cap(-C^*)=S^\perp.\] Consequently, \[S\ne X\iff C^*\text{ is nonpointed}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is lower-dimensional exactly when its dual has nonzero lineality orthogonal to the cone's span.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Lineality Forced by Deficient Span

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical intrinsic repair of deficient ambient span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{span}C\). Although a lower-dimensional cone has \(\operatorname{int}_X C=\varnothing\), it is full-dimensional in \(S\), and \[\operatorname{int}_S C=\operatorname{ri}_X C\ne\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the ambient space to the cone's span converts its relative interior into ordinary interior.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Repair by Span Restriction
Two-Stage Reduction of Combined Cone Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combined degeneracy is canonically removed by restricting to the cone's span and then quotienting by its full lineality space; a closed cone becomes proper in the resulting quotient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{span}C\) and \(L=C\cap(-C)\). Regard \(C\) as a cone in \(S\), and then form its image \[C/L\subseteq S/L.\] This quotient cone spans \(S/L\) and is pointed. Thus restricting to \(S\) removes the dimensional defect, while quotienting by \(L\) removes exactly the lineality. If \(C\) is closed, then \(C/L\) is closed and hence is a proper cone in the finite-dimensional space \(S/L\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
Closedness of \(C\) is required only for the final properness conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{span}(C/L)=S/L\), \((C/L)\cap(-(C/L))=\{0+L\}\), and \(C\text{ closed}\Rightarrow C/L\text{ is proper in }S/L\).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical simultaneous removal of deficient ambient span and nontrivial lineality.

notation.meaning: Intrinsic ambient subspace of the cone.
Image of C in the quotient space S/L.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combined degeneracy occurs when a cone both contains a nonzero line and lies in a proper ambient subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cone lies in the combined degeneracy regime when
\[
C\cap(-C)\neq\{0\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{span}C\neq X.
\]
The first condition supplies nonzero lineality and prevents pointedness; the second confines \(C\) to a proper linear subspace and forces \(\operatorname{int}_X C=\varnothing\). Passing to \(S=\operatorname{span}C\) repairs the dimensional defect but does not remove the lineality \(C\cap(-C)\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real topological vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous failure of pointedness and ambient full dimensionality.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous dual consequences of deficient span and nonzero lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite-dimensional inner-product space, let \[C^*=\{y:\langle y,c\rangle\ge0\ \forall c\in C\},\quad S=\operatorname{span}C,\quad L=C\cap(-C).\] Then \[S^\perp=C^*\cap(-C^*),\qquad C^*\subseteq L^\perp.\] Hence, when \(S\ne X\) and \(L\ne\{0\}\), the dual cone is both nonpointed and lower-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deficient primal span creates dual lineality, while primal lineality confines the dual to a proper orthogonal subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Signature of Combined Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simultaneous Span Restriction and Lineality Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical reduction repairing both dimensional deficiency and lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{span}C\), \(L=C\cap(-C)\), and let \(q:S\to S/L\) be the quotient map. Then \(C\) is full-dimensional when regarded in \(S\), while \(q(C)\) is pointed and \[\operatorname{span}q(C)=S/L.\] Restricting to \(S\) repairs only the ambient dimensional defect; quotienting by \(L\) repairs only lineality; applying both yields a pointed full-dimensional cone in \(S/L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting to the span and quotienting by lineality are the two respective reductions required to repair both defects.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.

notation.meaning: Canonical quotient by the lineality space.

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Span Restriction and Lineality Quotient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences attributable specifically to the conjunction of both degeneracies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(L=C\cap(-C)\neq\{0\}\) and \(S=\operatorname{span}C\neq X\), then the cone-induced relation on \(X\) is not antisymmetric and \(\operatorname{int}_X C=\varnothing\). Therefore \(C\) cannot be proper in \(X\), even if it is closed. Restricting to \(S\) restores possible solidity but leaves nonantisymmetry; quotienting by \(L\) restores pointedness but does not by itself change the original deficient ambient placement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jointly nonpointed and lower-dimensional cone simultaneously loses order antisymmetry and ambient interior, so neither a span restriction nor a lineality quotient alone repairs both defects.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \preceq_C\text{ is not antisymmetric},\qquad\operatorname{int}_X C=\varnothing,\qquad C\text{ is not proper in }X.
knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Obstructions to Proper-Cone Geometry

children.title: Empty-Interior Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cones requiring relative or generalized interior notions.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Spanning Empty-Interior Cone in L2
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone in L2 spans the whole space but has empty norm interior and empty relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
C=L^2_+([0,1])=\{u\in L^2([0,1]):u\geq0\text{ almost everywhere}\},
\]
one has
\[
\operatorname{span}C=L^2([0,1]),
\qquad
\operatorname{int}C=\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing.
\]
Thus in infinite dimensions empty interior need not imply deficient linear span, and a nonempty convex cone need not have nonempty relative interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional counterexample to the finite-dimensional spanning and relative-interior conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a nonempty convex cone has empty ambient interior exactly when it is lower-dimensional, while its relative interior remains nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty convex cone \(C\subseteq X\) in a finite-dimensional space, the empty-interior condition satisfies
\[
\operatorname{int}_X C=\varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{span}C\neq X.
\]
Even in this regime, relative interior remains nonempty:
\[
\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing,
\]
where relative interior is taken in \(\operatorname{span}C\). In infinite-dimensional spaces, empty interior need not imply failure of linear spanning.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real topological vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes ambient-interior failure from relative-interior feasibility in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical full-span cone for which ambient and relative interiors are empty but quasi-relative interior is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\ell^2_+:=\{x\in\ell^2:x_n\geq0\ \forall n\}\). Then
\[
\operatorname{span}C=\ell^2,
\qquad \operatorname{int}C=\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing.
\]
For
\[
\operatorname{qri}C:=\{x\in C:\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}\text{ is a linear subspace}\},
\]
one has
\[
\operatorname{qri}C=\{x\in\ell^2:x_n>0\ \forall n\}\neq\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone in ℓ2 spans the whole space but has empty norm and relative interior; its quasi-relative interior consists of the coordinatewise strictly positive sequences.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambiently Thin Cones and Generalized Interior Substitutes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(E\) is a real topological vector space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone. In the Hilbert specialization, generalized interiors are defined using conical hulls of \(K-x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The primary condition is empty ambient interior; relative and generalized interiors are recorded as distinct replacement regimes, not identified with ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is in an empty-interior regime when \[\operatorname{int}_E K=\varnothing,\] equivalently, for every \(x\in K\) and every neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\), \(x+U\nsubseteq K\). In a Hilbert space its intrinsic substitutes include \[\operatorname{ri}K=\{x\in K:\operatorname{cone}(K-x)=\operatorname{span}(K-x)\}\] and \[\operatorname{qri}K=\{x\in K:\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(K-x)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(K-x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone has empty ambient interior when no point contains a full ambient neighborhood inside the cone. Such a cone may still have relative, strong-relative, or quasi-relative interior, which use its intrinsic span or closed span.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_E K=\varnothing\) if and only if every nonempty open subset of \(E\) meets \(E\setminus K\).
In finite dimensions, \(\operatorname{int}_E K=\varnothing\) if and only if \(\operatorname{span}K\ne E\).
special_cases_latex: Every proper linear subspace has empty ambient interior but equals its relative interior.
For infinite \(I\), \(\ell_+^2(I)\) is closed and pointed but has empty norm interior.
A lower-dimensional ray in \(\mathbb R^n\), \(n>1\), has empty ambient interior and nonempty relative interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict feasibility expressed through \(\operatorname{int}K\) is unavailable in this regime.
Constraint qualifications may require \(\operatorname{ri}K\), \(\operatorname{sri}K\), or \(\operatorname{qri}K\) instead.
boundary_notes: Empty interior alone does not imply nonclosedness or nonpointedness.
Generalized interior sets can themselves be empty in infinite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Cone Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex cone is recovered only up to closure by bipolarity, and nearest-point minimizers may fail to exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonclosed convex cone \(C\), the bipolar theorem gives
\[
C^{**}=\overline C\supsetneq C.
\]
Thus continuous homogeneous linear inequalities recover only the closure, not the original cone. Moreover, for some \(x\in X\), the distance
\[
\inf_{c\in C}\lVert x-c\rVert
\]
need not be attained by any \(c\in C\), even though it is attained on the closed cone \(\overline C\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a convex cone that is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{**}=\overline C\supsetneq C\), so bipolar data cannot distinguish \(C\) from its closure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bipolar failure boundary for a nonclosed convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Missing Boundary Points Have No Strict Dual Separator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation failure caused by a nonclosed cone's omitted boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space and let \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\). Then
\[
\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C^*.
\]
Thus no \(y\in C^*\) satisfies \(\langle y,x\rangle<0\). Strict dual-cone certificates characterize exclusion from \(\overline C\), not exclusion from \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point omitted only from a nonclosed cone's boundary has no strict dual-cone separator because dual inequalities test membership in the closure.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in C^*\), so strict dual separation is impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Boundary Points Have No Strict Dual Separator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exactly when distance minimization over a possibly nonclosed cone attains its infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space and set \(p=P_{\overline C}x\). Then
\[
\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|=\operatorname{dist}(x,\overline C)=\|x-p\|.
\]
The infimum over \(C\) is attained if and only if \(p\in C\); when attained, \(p\) is its unique minimizer. In particular, every \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\) has distance zero from \(C\) but no nearest point in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a cone equals distance to its closure, and a nearest point exists exactly when the closure projection belongs to the original cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distance infimum over \(C\) is attained if and only if \(P_{\overline C}x\in C\).

notation.meaning: metric projection of x onto the closed convex cone \(\overline C\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Convex Cones and Their Closure Completion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \((E,\tau)\) is a Hausdorff topological vector space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure is taken in the specified topology. Sequential characterizations are restricted to metrizable ambient spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is nonclosed when \[K\ne\overline K^{\tau},\] equivalently when its closure defect \(\Delta_{\tau}(K):=\overline K^{\tau}\setminus K\) is nonempty. Its closure completion is \(K^{\mathrm{cl}}:=\overline K^{\tau}\), which is a closed convex cone containing \(K\) and is the smallest \(\tau\)-closed cone containing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is nonclosed when it omits at least one of its topological limit points. The omitted points form its closure defect, and adjoining all of them gives the smallest closed cone containing the original cone.
assumptions_latex: \((E,\tau)\) is a Hausdorff topological vector space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(E\) is metrizable, \(K\) is nonclosed if and only if there exist \(x_n\in K\) and \(x\notin K\) with \(x_n\to x\).
In a general topological vector space, nonclosedness is characterized by a convergent net in \(K\) whose limit is outside \(K\).
special_cases_latex: The image of a closed convex cone under a linear map need not be closed.
The Minkowski sum of two closed convex cones need not be closed.
The open positive orthant together with the origin is a convex cone but is not closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Polarity cannot distinguish \(K\) from \(\overline K\), since they have the same polar cone.
Replacing \(K\) by \(\overline K\) can restore projection and separation statements that require closedness.
boundary_notes: Closure can add boundary rays or other limit points but preserves convexity and conicity.
A nonclosed cone may still be pointed and may have nonempty interior.

notation.meaning: set of closure points missing from the cone
topological closure completion of the cone

children.title: Cone Operations and Closedness
children.top_down_role: Cone-preserving constructions and the regularity changes they can introduce.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(E,F\) are real topological vector spaces, \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) are convex cones, and \(A:E\to F\) is linear and continuous whenever topology is relevant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The calculus distinguishes algebraic cone preservation from preservation of closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone-operation closure calculus consists of the operations \[\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i,\qquad K_1+K_2,\qquad K_1\times K_2,\qquad A(K),\qquad A^{-1}(L),\qquad\operatorname{cone}S,\] together with their closure-regularized forms \(\overline{K_1+K_2}\), \(\overline{A(K)}\), and \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\). An operation is cone-preserving when its algebraic output is a convex cone; it is closed-cone-preserving on a stated class when closed cone inputs always produce a closed output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-operation closure calculus tracks intersections, sums, products, linear images and inverse images, and generated conic hulls. It records separately whether each construction preserves conicity and whether the resulting cone is closed, applying topological closure when necessary.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_i\) and \(L\) is a convex cone in its stated ambient space.
The topology is fixed for every closure operation.
\(A\) is linear; it is continuous for claims involving inverse images of closed cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{cone}S)}\] is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(S\), while sums and linear images may require explicit closure.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For convex cones, \(K_1+K_2\) is the least convex cone containing \(K_1\cup K_2\).
\((K_1+K_2)^{\ominus}=K_1^{\ominus}\cap K_2^{\ominus}\) in a Hilbert space.
special_cases_latex: Arbitrary intersections and finite Cartesian products of closed convex cones are closed convex cones.
Continuous linear inverse images preserve closed convex cones.
Finite generation in a finite-dimensional space yields a closed conic hull.
immediate_consequences_latex: The closure operator is unnecessary for intersections and products of closed cones but may be essential for sums and images.
Polarity converts Minkowski sums into intersections of polar cones.
boundary_notes: A linear image of a closed convex cone need not be closed.
A Minkowski sum of closed convex cones need not be closed.
The phrase “closure calculus” is an umbrella term local to the tree; the individual operations are standard.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Duality for Sums and Intersections of Convex Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone-operation polarity with the closure boundary and its relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K_1,\ldots,K_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty convex cones. Then (K_1+\cdots+K_m)^\circ=K_1^\circ\cap\cdots\cap K_m^\circ and (\operatorname{cl}K_1\cap\cdots\cap\operatorname{cl}K_m)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}(K_1^\circ+\cdots+K_m^\circ). If \bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}K_i\neq\varnothing, closure can be omitted from the second identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity converts a finite Minkowski sum of nonempty convex cones into the intersection of their polars. It converts the intersection of their closures into the closure of the sum of their polars. If the cones' relative interiors share a point, the latter sum needs no closure.
assumptions_latex: K_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a nonempty convex cone for }i=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\sum_{i=1}^m K_i\right)^\circ=\bigcap_{i=1}^m K_i^\circ,\qquad \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{cl}K_i\right)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m K_i^\circ\right),\qquad \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m K_i\right)^\circ=\sum_{i=1}^m K_i^\circ\text{ under the stated qualification}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product and Additive Assembly of Convex Cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(E_i\) is a real vector space and \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a convex cone. For additive assembly, all \(K_i\) lie in a common space \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates componentwise product assembly from Minkowski addition in a common ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The product assembly and additive assembly of \((K_i)_{i=1}^m\) are respectively \[\prod_{i=1}^mK_i:=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\prod_{i=1}^mE_i:x_i\in K_i\ \forall i\}\] and \[\sum_{i=1}^mK_i:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m x_i:x_i\in K_i\ \forall i\right\}.\] Both outputs are convex cones. The first retains component coordinates; the second combines all factors through vector addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone assembly has two basic forms. A Cartesian product collects independent cone coordinates in a product space. A Minkowski sum adds one element from each cone in a common ambient space. Both constructions preserve convex conicity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sum_iK_i\) is the image of \(\prod_iK_i\) under \(A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i x_i\).
For two cones, \(K_1+K_2=\{x_1+x_2:x_i\in K_i\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(E=E_1\oplus\cdots\oplus E_m\) and each \(K_i\subseteq E_i\), the internal sum is naturally isomorphic to the product cone.
If every \(K_i\) is closed, the finite product is closed; the Minkowski sum need not be closed.
For \(K_i=\mathbb R_+^{n_i}\), the product is \(\mathbb R_+^{\sum_i n_i}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Product membership is componentwise.
The polar of a two-cone Minkowski sum is the intersection of the two polar cones.
boundary_notes: Infinite products require a specified product space and topology.
Additive assembly can lose factor identifiability and closedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: External and Internal Factorizations of a Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(E_i\) is a real vector space and \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a convex cone. Let \(E\) be another real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorization requires an explicit product-space or direct-sum identification; it is stronger than expressing a cone as an arbitrary Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An external factorized cone is \[K_{\mathrm{ext}}:=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\subseteq E_1\times\cdots\times E_m.\] A cone \(K\subseteq E\) has an internal factorized decomposition when there exists a linear isomorphism \[T:E_1\oplus\cdots\oplus E_m\to E\] such that \[K=T(K_1\times\cdots\times K_m).\] Equivalently, after identifying \(E\) with the direct sum, each \(x\in K\) has a unique representation \(x=x_1+\cdots+x_m\) with \(x_i\in K_i\subseteq E_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorized cone is a Cartesian product of component cones, or the image of such a product under a linear isomorphism onto a direct-sum ambient space. Internal factorization gives every cone element a unique tuple of component coordinates.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a convex cone.
For an internal factorization, \(T\) is a linear isomorphism.
The direct-sum decomposition makes component representations unique.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under \(E=E_1\oplus\cdots\oplus E_m\), \(K=K_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K_m\) if and only if \(K\cap E_i=K_i\) and every \(x\in K\) has a unique componentwise decomposition.
Membership in an external factorization satisfies \((x_i)_i\in\prod_iK_i\) if and only if \(x_i\in K_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: A block-separable nonnegative orthant factors as \(\mathbb R_+^{n_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R_+^{n_m}\).
For closed convex factors in a finite Hilbert direct sum, projection onto the product acts componentwise.
A one-factor decomposition recovers the original cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Pointedness and closedness of a finite product hold exactly when they hold componentwise.
The product has nonempty interior exactly when every factor has nonempty interior in its own ambient space.
boundary_notes: A Minkowski sum in overlapping subspaces need not be a factorization because representations may be nonunique.
Infinite factorizations require a specified direct-sum topology.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior, Span, and Lineality of Product Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Span, lineality, relative interior, and their dimensions factor componentwise for finite product cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex cones \(C_i\subseteq X_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(C=\prod_iC_i\), \[\operatorname{span}C=\prod_i\operatorname{span}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{lin}C=\prod_i\operatorname{lin}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{ri}C=\prod_i\operatorname{ri}C_i.\] Hence dimension and lineality dimension are additive across factors.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\subseteq X_i\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products in finite-dimensional spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces and Extreme Rays of Product Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces factor componentwise, and every extreme ray of a finite product cone is supported in exactly one factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^mC_i\). Every nonempty face of \(C\) is uniquely of the form \(\prod_{i=1}^mF_i\), where each \(F_i\) is a face of \(C_i\). Consequently, the nonzero extreme rays of \(C\) are exactly \[\{0\}\times\cdots\times R_i\times\cdots\times\{0\},\] where \(R_i\) is an extreme ray of one factor.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F(C)=\{\prod_iF_i:F_i\in\mathcal F(C_i)\},\text{ and each nonzero extreme ray has exactly one nonzero factor}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty faces under the standard face convention.

notation.meaning: Family of nonempty faces of the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Product Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product of finite-dimensional convex cones is a convex cone; its dual, closedness, pointedness, and solidity factor componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Cartesian product
\[
C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i
=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m):x_i\in C_i\text{ for every }i\}
\]
is a convex cone in \(X=\prod_{i=1}^m X_i\). Under the product inner product,
\[
C^*=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i^*.
\]
Because the product is finite and carries its Euclidean product topology, \(C\) is closed, pointed, or solid exactly when every factor has the corresponding property.
assumptions_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(X_i\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and \(C_i\subseteq X_i\) is a convex cone.
\(X=\prod_{i=1}^m X_i\) carries the product inner product and its Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\) is a convex cone and \(C^*=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i^*\); moreover, closedness, pointedness, and solidity hold for \(C\) exactly when they hold for every factor.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products of finite-dimensional inner-product-space cones, with product topology and componentwise duality.

notation.meaning: dual cone under the corresponding inner product
