knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polarity Relative to a Separating Dual Pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a real separating dual pair: \(X,Y\) are real vector spaces and the bilinear pairing separates points of both spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unlike Hilbert-space polarity, the two polar operations change ambient spaces: subsets of \(X\) polarize into \(Y\), and subsets of \(Y\) polarize into \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C\subseteq X\), its nonpositive polar in \(Y\) is \[C^{\circ}_Y:=\{y\in Y:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}.\] For \(D\subseteq Y\), its nonpositive polar in \(X\) is \[D^{\circ}_X:=\{x\in X:(\forall y\in D)\ \langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}.\] The corresponding nonnegative dual cones are \(C^*_Y=-C^{\circ}_Y\) and \(D^*_X=-D^{\circ}_X\). A bipolar is formed by alternating spaces, namely \(C^{\circ\circ}:=(C^{\circ}_Y)^{\circ}_X\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a dual pair, a subset of the primal space has a polar in the paired dual space, defined by nonpositive pairing with every primal element. A subset of the dual space polarizes back into the primal space. Thus a bipolar alternates the two ambient spaces. The positive dual convention is obtained by negating the nonpositive polar.
assumptions_latex: The pairing separates points of \(X\) and \(Y\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in C^{\circ}_Y\iff\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\).
\(C^*_Y=\{y:(\forall x\in C)\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\}=-C^{\circ}_Y\).
special_cases_latex: For a Hilbert space identified with its continuous dual, the two ambient spaces coincide.
For \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=(\mathbb R^n)^*\), the pairing is functional evaluation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Polarity reverses inclusion across the pairing.
Every polar is an intersection of homogeneous closed halfspaces in the weak topology generated by the paired space.
boundary_notes: Writing both polar cones as subsets of one space requires an explicit identification, such as a Hilbert-space Riesz identification.
Changing the paired subspace \(Y\) can change both the polar and the closure recovered by the bipolar.

notation.meaning: nonpositive polar of C in Y
bipolar obtained by alternating Y and X

knowledge_statements.title: Antitonicity and Closed-Conic-Hull Invariance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner-product dualization reverses inclusion and is unchanged when a set is replaced by its closed convex conic hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary subsets \(A,B\subseteq H\),
\[
A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow B^*\subseteq A^*,
\qquad
A^*=\left(\overline{\operatorname{cone}_{\mathrm{cvx}}(A)}\right)^*.
\]
Thus the dual depends only on the closed convex conic hull of the original set.
assumptions_latex: Closure is in the Hilbert-space norm topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational order and hull invariance of nonnegative inner-product dualization.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cones under Inner Products
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Hilbert space, the dual cone consists of vectors having nonnegative inner product with every vector of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(K\subseteq H\), its nonnegative dual cone is \[K^*:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\] The inner product identifies \(H\) with its continuous dual, so both \(K\) and \(K^*\) lie in the same ambient space. The set \(K^*\) is always a closed convex cone, whether or not \(K\) itself is convex or closed.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the nonnegative inner-product convention for dual cones.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual cone of the cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic structural behavior of the nonnegative inner-product dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B\subseteq H\) in a real Hilbert space. If \(A\subseteq B\), then \(B^*\subseteq A^*\). Moreover,
\[
A^*=\operatorname{cone}(A)^*=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(A)}^{\,*}.
\]
Thus the dual depends only on the closed convex cone generated by the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner-product dualization reverses inclusion and is unchanged when a set is replaced by its convex conic hull or the closure of that hull.

notation.meaning: Vectors pairing nonnegatively with every element of A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Cone of a Linear Subspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical self-paired example for nonnegative cone duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(M\subseteq H\) is a linear subspace of a real Hilbert space, then
\[
M^*=M^\perp.
\]
In particular, \(\{0\}^*=H\) and \(H^*=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative dual cone of a linear subspace is its orthogonal complement; consequently, the zero cone and whole space are dual to one another.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational order and closure properties of the nonnegative dual in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary subsets \(A,B\subseteq H\),
\[
A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow B^*\subseteq A^*,
\qquad
A^*=\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{cone}(A)}\bigr)^*,
\qquad
A^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(A)}.
\]
Hence a cone \(K\) satisfies \(K^{**}=\overline K\) when it is convex, and \(K^{**}=K\) exactly when it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner-product dualization reverses inclusion, depends only on the closed convex conic hull, and bidualization produces that hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner products of oppositely oriented convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by equality of maximin and minimax values, extensions through indicator functions, an existence regime, and conditional homogeneity and additivity laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets, with \(C\) supremum oriented and \(D\) infimum oriented. If \[\sup_{x\in C}\inf_{y\in D}\langle x,y\rangle=\inf_{y\in D}\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle,\] their common value is denoted by \(\langle C,D\rangle=\langle D,C\rangle\); otherwise this inner product is undefined. Equivalently, it agrees with the convex-concave function pairing for \(f=\delta(\cdot\mid C)\) and \(g=-\delta(\cdot\mid D)\). It exists whenever \(C\) and \(D\) are closed and at least one is bounded. For proper concave \(h\), define \[\langle C,h\rangle=\sup_{x\in C}h^*(x)=\inf_y\{\langle C,y\rangle-h(y)\}\] when the two extrema agree, and leave it undefined otherwise. For proper convex \(h\), define \[\langle h,D\rangle=\inf_{y\in D}h^*(y)=\sup_x\{\langle x,D\rangle-h(x)\}\] when the two extrema agree, and leave it undefined otherwise. If \(C,C'\) are nonempty supremum-oriented convex sets and \(D,D'\) are nonempty infimum-oriented convex sets, then, whenever all displayed pairings exist and no expression \(+\infty-\infty\) occurs, for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\langle\lambda C,D\rangle=\lambda\langle C,D\rangle=\langle C,\lambda D\rangle,\] \[\langle C+C',D\rangle\geq\langle C,D\rangle+\langle C',D\rangle,\qquad \langle C+C',y\rangle=\langle C,y\rangle+\langle C',y\rangle\ \ (\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n),\] and \[\langle C,D+D'\rangle\leq\langle C,D\rangle+\langle C,D'\rangle,\qquad \langle x,D+D'\rangle=\langle x,D\rangle+\langle x,D'\rangle\ \ (\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner product of a supremum-oriented convex set and an infimum-oriented convex set is their common maximin-minimax pairing value, when those values agree; otherwise it is undefined. The definition extends through indicator functions to pairings with proper concave or convex functions. Closedness of both sets and boundedness of either guarantees existence. Whenever all relevant pairings exist and no indeterminate infinity subtraction occurs, the pairing is positively homogeneous, superadditive in its supremum-oriented set argument, subadditive in its infimum-oriented set argument, and exactly additive when the opposite argument is a single vector.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\neq C,C'\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are convex and supremum oriented}
\varnothing\neq D,D'\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are convex and infimum oriented}
\text{Each set or set-function pairing is defined only when its displayed extrema are equal}
\text{The algebraic laws require all relevant pairings to exist and exclude }+\infty-\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle C,D\rangle:=\sup_{x\in C}\inf_{y\in D}\langle x,y\rangle=\inf_{y\in D}\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle,\text{ with the stated set-function extensions, existence condition, homogeneity, superadditivity, subadditivity, and vector-additivity laws}

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Sign Conventions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonpositive polar cone is the negative of the nonnegative dual cone, so formulas cross conventions by negating every polar object.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the nonpositive convention, define \(K^\circ:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). Under the nonnegative convention, define \(K^*:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). These conventions translate exactly by \[K^\circ=-K^*,\qquad K^*=-K^\circ.\] Therefore any formula stated with one convention must reverse the sign of each polar cone when translated to the other; omitting this sign change generally reverses the asserted inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation between the two common sign conventions for cone polarity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonpositive Polar versus Nonnegative Dual Convention
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition fixes the translation boundary between the two dominant sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonpositive polar convention is \[C^{\ominus}:=\{u\in\mathcal H:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,u\rangle\leq0\}.\] The nonnegative dual convention is \[C^{\oplus}:=\{u\in\mathcal H:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,u\rangle\geq0\}.\] They are related exactly by \(C^{\oplus}=-C^{\ominus}\) and \(C^{\ominus}=-C^{\oplus}\). Consequently, a formula written with one convention is translated to the other by negating every polar cone while retaining the underlying primal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the nonpositive convention, polar vectors pair at most zero with the original set. Under the nonnegative convention, usually called the dual cone convention, they pair at least zero. The two cones differ only by a sign: the dual cone is the negative of the polar cone. Any formula mixing sources must therefore record which convention is being used.
assumptions_latex: \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) is the real Hilbert inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Antitone Galois Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive dualization across paired spaces is an inclusion-reversing Galois correspondence; bidualization is extensive and taking three duals returns the first dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For cones \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\),
\[
K\subseteq{}^+L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subseteq K^+.
\]
Consequently \(K\subseteq{}^+(K^+)\), \(L\subseteq({}^+L)^+\), and triple dualization returns the first dual:
\[
({}^+(K^+))^+=K^+,
\qquad
{}^+(({}^+L)^+)={}^+L.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\subseteq{}^+L\iff L\subseteq K^+\), with bidual extensivity and triple-dual identities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order structure of positive cone dualization across a real dual pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Pair Cone Bipolar Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive bidual of a cone in a separating dual pair is its weakly closed convex conic hull; a convex cone equals its bidual exactly when weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating real dual pair and let \(K\subseteq X\) be a cone. Then
\[
{}^+(K^+)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}_{\mathrm{cvx}}(K)}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.
\]
Thus, for a convex cone, \({}^+(K^+)=\overline K^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}\), and \(K={}^+(K^+)\) exactly when \(K\) is \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closed and convex. The symmetric statement holds for cones in \(Y\).
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separating real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipolar closure in the weak topology induced by a separating dual pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Cones in Dual-Paired Spaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a separating dual pair, a cone is sent to the cone of elements in the opposite space that pair nonnegatively with all its elements; algebraic and continuous duals are special cases when their required structures are present.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating real dual pair. For cones \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\), define \[K^+:=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\] and \[{}^+L:=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }y\in L\}.\] These cones lie in opposite members of the pair. The choice \(Y=X^*\) gives the algebraic-dual construction. If \(X\) is a real topological vector space whose continuous dual \(X'\) separates points, the choice \(Y=X'\) gives the continuous-dual construction.
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separating real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^+=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\) and \({}^+L=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }y\in L\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex cone in a Hilbert space is recovered exactly by taking its nonnegative dual cone twice.

Thus a closed convex cone is completely determined by the homogeneous linear inequalities satisfied by all of its points.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Is Necessary for Pointwise Bipolar Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the paired space does not separate points, the bipolar of the zero cone is the annihilator rather than the zero cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a bilinear pairing and define its left annihilator \[N:=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle=0\ \forall y\in Y\}.\] Under the nonnegative cone-dual convention, for \(K=\{0\}\) one has \(K^+=Y\) and \[{}^+(K^+)={}^+Y=N.\] Hence, if \(N\ne\{0\}\), even the zero cone is not recovered by bipolarization.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are in bilinear duality, not necessarily separating.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of bipolar recovery when the selected pairing does not separate the original space.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual cone in the paired space

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity of Bipolar Completion under Dual Enlargement
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger paired dual yields a smaller or equal bipolar completion because it supplies more separating inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1\subseteq Y_2\subseteq X^\#\), and suppose both \((X,Y_i)\) are separating dual pairs. For a cone \(K\subseteq X\), let \(B_i={}^+(K^+_{Y_i})\). Then \[B_2\subseteq B_1.\] Thus enlarging the paired dual supplies more separating inequalities and can only shrink the bipolar completion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order relation between bipolar closures formed from two separating paired spaces.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual cone formed in the paired space Yi

knowledge_statements.title: Compatible Topologies Have the Same Closed Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally convex topologies compatible with a fixed dual pair have the same closed convex sets, so bipolar closure changes only when the paired dual space changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y)\) be a separating dual pair. If \(\mathcal T\) is a locally convex topology on \(X\) whose continuous dual is exactly \(Y\), then every convex set \(C\subseteq X\) satisfies \[\overline C^{\,\mathcal T}=\overline C^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.\] In particular, \(\sigma(X,Y)\) and \(\tau(X,Y)\) have the same closed convex cones.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is locally convex and \((X,\mathcal T)'=Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology variation while the separating paired dual space remains fixed.

notation.meaning: Weak topology induced by the dual pairing
Mackey topology of the dual pair

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar Closure Depends on the Paired Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separating dual pairs on the same vector space whose weak closures of one cone differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\ell^1\) and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1+e_n:n\ge2\}\). Both \((\ell^1,c_0)\) and \((\ell^1,\ell^\infty)\) are separating dual pairs under \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_nx_ny_n\). Since \(e_1+e_n\to e_1\) in \(\sigma(\ell^1,c_0)\), \[e_1\in\overline K^{\sigma(\ell^1,c_0)}.\] In contrast, \(y=(-1,1,1,\ldots)\in\ell^\infty\) is nonnegative on \(K\) but \(\langle e_1,y\rangle=-1\), so \[e_1\notin\overline K^{\sigma(\ell^1,\ell^\infty)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the paired space from all bounded sequences to null sequences weakens the available inequalities and enlarges the weak closure, hence can change the bipolar.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\ell^1\) is paired with either \(c_0\) or \(\ell^\infty\) by the coordinate pairing.

notation.meaning: The nth standard unit vector in sequence space

knowledge_statements.title: Bipolar Closure Depends on the Paired Space
Topological Bipolar Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipolar recovery relative to the weak topology induced by a dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,F,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separated real dual pair and let \(S\subseteq E\). For \(A\subseteq E\) and \(B\subseteq F\), define \[A^+=\{y\in F:\langle x,y\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in A\},\qquad B^+=\{x\in E:\langle x,y\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }y\in B\}.\] Then \[S^{++}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(S)}^{\,\sigma(E,F)},\] where \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is the convex conic hull of \(S\). Thus bipolar recovery uses closure in the weak topology generated by the selected paired space \(F\). If \(S\) is a convex cone, then \[S^{++}=\overline S^{\,\sigma(E,F)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a separated dual pair, the positive bipolar of a set is its weakly closed convex conic hull, so bipolar recovery depends on the selected paired space.
assumptions_latex: \((E,F,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separated real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^{++}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(S)}^{\,\sigma(E,F)}\); for a convex cone \(S\), this equals \(\overline S^{\,\sigma(E,F)}\).

positive dual in F of a subset A of E
positive dual in E of a subset B of F

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating dual pair, and equip \(X\) with the weak topology \(\sigma(X,Y)\), the coarsest topology making every map \(x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle\), \(y\in Y\), continuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the standard dual-pair formulation. The exact recovered closure depends on the paired space and its induced weak topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C\subseteq X\), define \[C^{\circ}:=\{y\in Y:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,y\rangle\leq0\},\qquad C^{\circ\circ}:=\{x\in X:(\forall y\in C^{\circ})\ \langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}.\] The topology-relative bipolar completion is \[\operatorname{bip}_{X,Y}(C):=C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}\bigl(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{conv}C)\bigr).\] A cone \(K\) is bipolar closed in this regime when it is convex and \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closed, equivalently \(K=K^{\circ\circ}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a separating dual pair, polar inequalities generate the weak topology determined by the chosen paired space. The bipolar completion of a set is its convex conical hull closed in that weak topology. Consequently, changing the paired dual can change the polar inequalities and the closure represented by the bipolar. A convex cone is fixed by bipolarization exactly when it is closed in the topology induced by the pairing.
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y)\) is a separating real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{conv}C))\), and a convex cone \(K\) satisfies \(K=K^{\circ\circ}\) exactly when it is \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\bigcap_{y\in C^{\circ}}\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}\).
For a convex cone \(K\), \(K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}K\).
special_cases_latex: In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, weak and norm closures coincide.
In a Hilbert space paired with itself through the inner product, the standard Hilbert bipolar formula is recovered.
immediate_consequences_latex: If two separating duals induce different weak closures, their bipolar completions may differ.
Every polar cone is \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-closed and convex.
boundary_notes: The norm closure and weak closure of a convex set agree in Banach spaces with the full continuous dual, but this must not be assumed for an arbitrary restricted pairing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar Completion through the Separated Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deferred because it subsumes the immutable deferred dual-pair bipolar theorem rather than supplying a nonduplicative local result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a bilinear pairing, let \(N=\{x:\langle x,y\rangle=0\ \forall y\in Y\}\), and let \(q:X\to X/N\) be the quotient map. After also quotienting the right annihilator, the induced pairing is separating. For every cone \(K\subseteq X\), \[{}^+(K^+)=q^{-1}\!\left(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(qK)}^{\,\sigma(X/N,Y)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonseparating pairing, bipolar completion can be described by quotienting invisible directions and then applying the separating dual-pair bipolar theorem.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) is its left annihilator and \(K\subseteq X\) is a cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \({}^+(K^+)=q^{-1}(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(qK)}^{\,\sigma(X/N,Y)})\), with the right annihilator understood in the induced separated pairing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-cone calculus under a fixed inner product
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone. For any set \(S\subseteq E\), write \(\operatorname{cone}S\), \(\operatorname{cl}S\), and \(S^\perp\) for its conic hull, closure, and orthogonal complement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry uses the nonnegative dual convention. Rockafellar's polar cone has the opposite sign: \(K^*=-K^\circ\). All closure statements are finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone and polar cone of \(K\) are \[K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\},\qquad K^\circ:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}=-K^*.\] Dualization is antitone and insensitive to conic generation and closure: \[K_1\subseteq K_2\Rightarrow K_2^*\subseteq K_1^*,\qquad S^*=(\operatorname{cone}S)^*=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}S)^*.\] The cone \(K^*\) is always closed and convex, and the bidual relation is \[K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K.\] Consequently, dualization is an order-reversing involution on the class of closed convex cones. The basic terminal cases are \(\{0\}^*=E\), \(E^*=\{0\}\), and \(L^*=L^\perp\) for every linear subspace \(L\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a cone K in a finite-dimensional inner-product space, its dual consists of all vectors having nonnegative inner product with every vector of K; its polar uses the opposite inequality. Dualization reverses inclusion, is unchanged by taking conic hull or closure, always produces a closed convex cone, and satisfies K bidual equals the closure of K. Thus it is an order-reversing involution on closed convex cones. The duals of the zero cone, the whole space, and a subspace are respectively the whole space, the zero cone, and the orthogonal complement.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional and carries the displayed inner product.
\(K,K_1,K_2\subseteq E\) are convex cones whenever the corresponding identities are invoked.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in K^*\iff \inf_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\).
For closed convex cones, \(K_1=K_2\iff K_1^*=K_2^*\).
special_cases_latex: \(L^*=L^\perp\) for a subspace \(L\).
\((\mathbb R_+^n)^*=\mathbb R_+^n\) under the Euclidean pairing.
immediate_consequences_latex: \((\operatorname{cl}K)^*=K^*\).
The equality \(K=K^{**}\) characterizes closed convex cones among convex cones.
boundary_notes: Changing the pairing changes the representing dual cone.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the bidual formula depends on the chosen dual topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duality rules for sums and intersections of cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Let \(K_1,K_2\subseteq E\) be nonempty convex cones, and define \(K_1+K_2:=\{x_1+x_2:x_i\in K_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formulas use nonnegative dual cones. Closure is retained where it is genuinely needed; it cannot generally be deleted from the dual of an intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sum-intersection duality calculus is the pair of identities \[(K_1+K_2)^*=K_1^*\cap K_2^*,\qquad (K_1\cap K_2)^*=\operatorname{cl}(K_1^*+K_2^*)\] when \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are closed convex cones. More generally, for a family \((K_i)_{i\in I}\), \[\left(\sum_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i^*,\] where the sum denotes the cone of finite sums. If \(K_1^*+K_2^*\) is closed, the closure in the intersection formula is unnecessary. A standard sufficient qualification is \(\operatorname{ri}K_1\cap\operatorname{ri}K_2\neq\varnothing\); polyhedrality of both cones is another sufficient regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a Minkowski sum of convex cones is the intersection of their dual cones. For closed convex cones, the dual of their intersection is the closure of the sum of their duals. The closure may be omitted when that dual sum is already closed, including standard relative-interior-qualified and polyhedral cases. The sum rule extends to arbitrary families when the primal sum means finite sums.
assumptions_latex: For \((K_1\cap K_2)^*=\operatorname{cl}(K_1^*+K_2^*)\), both cones are closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in(K_1+K_2)^*\iff y\in K_1^*\text{ and }y\in K_2^*\).
If \(K_1^*+K_2^*\) is closed, then \(y\in(K_1\cap K_2)^*\iff y=y_1+y_2\) for some \(y_i\in K_i^*\).
special_cases_latex: \((K+L)^*=K^*\cap L^\perp\) for a cone \(K\) and subspace \(L\).
For polyhedral cones, \((K_1\cap K_2)^*=K_1^*+K_2^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite systems of homogeneous inequalities dualize to finitely generated cones.
Finite conic generators dualize to intersections of homogeneous half-spaces.
boundary_notes: The algebraic sum of two closed convex cones need not be closed.
For nonclosed cones, bidualization introduces closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary-Family Sum Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the algebraic finite-support sum of any family of cones is the intersection of their dual cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space and let \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) be cones. Define
\[
\sum_{i\in I}K_i:=\left\{\sum_{i\in F}x_i:F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ x_i\in K_i\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\left(\sum_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i^*.
\]
assumptions_latex: \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) is an arbitrary family of cones.
The indexed sum is algebraic and uses only finite supports.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic sum of an arbitrary family, formed from finite-support selections.

notation.meaning: Algebraic finite-support sum of the indexed cones

knowledge_statements.title: Duals of Cone Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative dual of a cone sum is exactly the intersection of the two dual cones, without any closure qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary cones \(K,L\subseteq H\), their Minkowski sum satisfies \[(K+L)^*=K^*\cap L^*.\] No convexity or closedness assumption is required, and the resulting dual cone is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sum-to-intersection rule; no closedness assumption is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of an Arbitrary Algebraic Cone Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed extension of the exact binary sum-to-intersection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) be any family of cones in a real inner-product space \(H\), and define
\[
\sum_{i\in I}K_i:=\left\{\sum_{i\in F}x_i:F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ x_i\in K_i\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\left(\sum_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i^*.
\]
No convexity, closedness, completeness, or finite-dimensionality assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of an arbitrary algebraic sum of cones is exactly the intersection of all factor duals, without a closure or regularity assumption.
assumptions_latex: \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of cones in \(H\).

notation.meaning: Algebraic cone sum whose elements use finitely many summands

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of an Arbitrary Algebraic Cone Sum
Arbitrary-Family Intersection Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of an arbitrary intersection of closed convex cones is the closure of the finite-support sum of their duals; the unclosed formula is exact precisely when that sum is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) be closed convex cones. Then
\[
\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\overline{\sum_{i\in I}K_i^*},
\]
where \(\sum_{i\in I}K_i^*\) consists of finite sums. The closure may be omitted exactly when this algebraic sum is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\((K_i)_{i\in I}\) is an arbitrary family of closed convex cones.
\(\sum_{i\in I}K_i^*\) denotes the algebraic finite-support sum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary-family extension in finite dimensions; the dual-cone sum is the algebraic finite-support sum.

notation.meaning: Set of all finite sums of elements drawn from distinct indexed dual cones

knowledge_statements.title: Duals of Cone Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of an intersection of closed convex cones is the closure of the sum of their duals; closure disappears when that sum is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\subseteq H\) be closed convex cones. Then \[(K\cap L)^*=\overline{K^*+L^*}.\] The closure is taken in the Euclidean topology and cannot generally be omitted because the sum of two closed convex cones may fail to be closed. If \(K^*+L^*\) is closed, the formula simplifies to \((K\cap L)^*=K^*+L^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intersection-to-sum rule with the necessary closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of an Arbitrary Cone Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed Hilbert-space extension of the binary intersection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\neq\varnothing\) and let \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) be closed convex cones in a real Hilbert space \(H\). Then
\[
\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\overline{\operatorname{cone}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i^*\right)},
\]
where the closure is in the norm topology. Equivalently, the right-hand side is the closure of all finite sums of elements drawn from the cones \(K_i^*\). For finite \(I\), this is \((\bigcap_iK_i)^*=\overline{\sum_iK_i^*}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of an arbitrary nonempty intersection of closed convex cones in a Hilbert space is the norm closure of the cone generated by all factor duals.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\subseteq H\) is a closed convex cone for every \(i\in I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K_1,\ldots,K_m\subseteq H\) be closed convex cones. Then
\[
\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m K_i\right)^*=\overline{\sum_{i=1}^m K_i^*}.
\]
If \(\sum_{i=1}^mK_i^*\) is closed, the closure may be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a finite intersection of closed convex cones is the closure of the sum of their dual cones, with exact equality to the unclosed sum precisely when that sum is closed.

\(K_1,\ldots,K_m\subseteq H\) are closed convex cones and \(m<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Family Intersection Duality
Closure-Sensitive Dual Correspondences
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a sum gives an intersection exactly, while dualizing that intersection back recovers the sum's closure and equals the sum precisely when the sum is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closed convex cones \(K,L\subseteq H\), \[(K^*\cap L^*)^*=\overline{K+L}.\] Therefore \[(K^*\cap L^*)^*=K+L\] if and only if \(K+L\) is closed. Thus reverse sum-intersection duality requires closure unless a separate criterion guarantees that the cone sum is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((K^*\cap L^*)^*=\overline{K+L}\), and \((K^*\cap L^*)^*=K+L\) if and only if \(K+L\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows exactly where closure enters sum-intersection duality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Conditions for Closure-Free Reverse Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional conditions ensuring that closure is unnecessary in reverse sum-intersection duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\) be closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. The sum \(K+L\) is closed, and hence \[(K^*\cap L^*)^*=K+L,\] if either (i) one of \(K,L\) is polyhedral or (ii) \(K\cap(-L)=\{0\}\). These conditions are sufficient, not necessary; the exact criterion is closedness of \(K+L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedrality of one summand or absence of a nonzero opposite common direction guarantees closure-free reverse duality.
assumptions_latex: \(K,L\) are closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
Either one cone is polyhedral or \(K\cap(-L)=\{0\}\).

children.title: Product-Direct-Sum Duality Calculus
children.top_down_role: Componentwise duality for decomposable cones.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(E_i\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces and let \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) be convex cones. Equip \(E:=E_1\oplus\cdots\oplus E_m\) with \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: In finite products the Cartesian product and external direct sum have the same underlying set; the terminology records whether the construction is viewed set-theoretically or as a decomposition of the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The product cone is \[\prod_{i=1}^mK_i:=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in E:x_i\in K_i\ \forall i\}.\] Its dual is componentwise: \[\left(\prod_{i=1}^mK_i\right)^*=\prod_{i=1}^mK_i^*.\] Equivalently, if mutually orthogonal subspaces \(E_i\) decompose \(E\) and \(K_i\subseteq E_i\), then for the external conic direct sum \(K_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K_m\), \[(K_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K_m)^*=K_1^*\oplus\cdots\oplus K_m^*,\] with each \(K_i^*\) computed inside \(E_i\). Thus membership, closedness, pointedness, solidity relative to the product space, and self-duality are determined componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an orthogonal direct sum of finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, the dual of a Cartesian product of cones is the Cartesian product of their dual cones. The same formula is written as a direct-sum identity when the ambient space is decomposed into orthogonal components. Consequently, dual membership and the usual regularity or self-duality properties can be checked factor by factor.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a convex cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in(\prod_iK_i)^*\iff y_i\in K_i^*\ \forall i\).
\(\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in\prod_iK_i\iff \langle y_i,x_i\rangle_i\geq0\ \forall x_i\in K_i,\forall i\).
special_cases_latex: A finite product of self-dual cones is self-dual under the product inner product.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(\prod_iK_i)=\prod_i\operatorname{lin}K_i\).
\(\operatorname{int}(\prod_iK_i)=\prod_i\operatorname{int}K_i\).
boundary_notes: For nonorthogonal decompositions, the formula must be transported through the adjoint of the chosen identification.
Infinite products require a specified topology and continuous dual.

knowledge_statements.title: Duals of Product Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the canonical product inner product, the dual of a finite product cone is the product of the factor dual cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(H=\prod_{i=1}^m H_i\) with the product inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_{H_i}\). For cones \(K_i\subseteq H_i\), let \(K=\prod_{i=1}^m K_i\). Then \[K^*=\prod_{i=1}^m K_i^*.\] Thus a vector \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) is dual-feasible for the product cone exactly when each component \(y_i\) is dual-feasible for its corresponding factor. No convexity or closedness assumption is required.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\subseteq H_i\) is a cone for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products under the canonical product inner product.

notation.meaning: Hilbert product space with componentwise inner product

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary on extending the finite Cartesian-product formula to infinitely many Hilbert factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For countably many factors \(H_i=\mathbb R\), the Hilbert direct sum is \(H=\ell^2\), not the full Cartesian product \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\). If \(K_i=\mathbb R_+\), then \[K=\{x\in\ell^2:x_i\ge0\ \forall i\},\qquad K^*=K.\] Thus coordinatewise nonnegativity must be accompanied by \(y\in\ell^2\); the unrestricted product \(\prod_iK_i^*=\mathbb R_+^{\mathbb N}\) is not the Hilbert-space dual cone. In particular, \((1,1,\ldots)\) lies in the unrestricted product but not in \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite product identity does not extend to an unrestricted Cartesian product over infinitely many Hilbert factors; summability remains part of dual membership.
assumptions_latex: The countable Hilbert product is interpreted as the Hilbert direct sum \(\ell^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Hilbert Products Require Summability
Duals of Direct-Sum Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the finite-support pairing, the dual of an algebraic direct sum of cones is the Cartesian product of their factor duals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\) and \(\prod_{i\in I}Y_i\) with the pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_i\), whose sum is finite because \(x\) has finite support. Then \(y\) is nonnegative on \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}K_i\) exactly when every coordinate \(y_i\) is nonnegative on \(K_i\). Consequently, \[\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\prod_{i\in I}K_i^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an index set and each \(K_i\) is a convex cone in a real vector space \(X_i\).
Each \(X_i\) is paired nondegenerately with a space \(Y_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic direct sums with the finite-support pairing; no topological-dual assertion is made.

notation.meaning: Algebraic direct sum, whose elements have finite support
Cartesian product of the factor dual cones

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous-Dual Boundary for Algebraic Direct Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the seed's algebraic paired dual from the continuous dual induced by an infinite-dimensional norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_{00}=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb N}\mathbb R\) carry the \(\ell^2\)-norm, and let \(K=c_{00,+}\). Under the finite-support pairing, the algebraic paired dual cone is \(\mathbb R_+^{\mathbb N}\). In contrast, every continuous linear functional on \((c_{00},\|\cdot\|_2)\) is represented by a sequence in \(\ell^2\), so the continuous positive dual cone is \(\ell_+^2\). Thus \[K^*_{\mathrm{cont}}=\ell_+^2\subsetneq\mathbb R_+^{\mathbb N}=K^*_{\mathrm{alg}}.\] The sequence \((1,1,\ldots)\) defines a positive algebraic functional on finite-support vectors but is not continuous for the \(\ell^2\)-norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an infinite algebraic direct sum, the full product is the algebraic paired dual, while a chosen topology can reduce the continuous dual to a proper subcone.

notation.meaning: Space of finitely supported real sequences
Cone of coordinatewise nonnegative square-summable sequences

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Dual Boundary for Algebraic Direct Sums
Factorwise Dual Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product vector belongs to the dual of the algebraic direct-sum cone precisely when each coordinate belongs to the corresponding factor dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y=(y_i)_{i\in I}\in\prod_{i\in I}Y_i\), membership in the dual of the direct-sum cone is determined factorwise: \[y\in\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\forall i\in I)\;y_i\in K_i^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an index set, and \(K_i\subseteq X_i\) is a convex cone for every \(i\in I\).
Each \(X_i\) is paired nondegenerately with a real vector space \(Y_i\), and \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i\) is paired with \(\prod_{i\in I}Y_i\) coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise membership formulation for the dual of an algebraic direct-sum cone under the finite-support pairing.

notation.meaning: The coordinate of a product element in the paired factor
Dual cone of the factor cone under the pairing between the factor spaces
Algebraic direct sum, whose elements have finite support

children.title: Duals under Linear Maps
children.top_down_role: Adjoint relationships for images, inverse images, sections, and projections.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Is Necessary in the Pullback-Dual Rule
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite pullback has a dual equal only to the closure of the adjoint image, so closure in the general inverse-image rule is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \(A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb S^2\) by \[A(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u&v/2\\v/2&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(A^{-1}C=\mathbb R_+\times\{0\}\), while \[A^*C=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\] is not closed. Consequently, \[\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R=\overline{A^*C}\neq A^*C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^2\) carries the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional semidefinite example where the adjoint image of the dual cone is nonclosed.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of a Linear Inverse Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a cone pullback is the closure of the adjoint image of the dual; a relative-interior qualification removes the closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear and let \(C\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone. Then \[\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=\overline{A^*C^*}.\] If \(\operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\), then \(A^*C^*\) is closed and \[\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=A^*C^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pullback rule, including the closure term and a relative-interior qualification that removes it.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of a Cone Section
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual within a subspace of a cone section is the closure of the orthogonal projection of the ambient dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone and let \(L\subseteq E\) be a linear subspace. Forming the dual inside \(L\), \[(K\cap L)^{*_{L}}=\overline{P_L(K^*)}^{\;L}.\] If \(L\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\), the closure may be omitted.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subspace-section specialization of inverse-image duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of a Projected Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing an orthogonal projection produces the section of the ambient dual cone by the projection subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a cone and let \(L\subseteq E\) be a linear subspace. Then the dual formed inside \(L\) satisfies \[\bigl(P_LK\bigr)^{*_{L}}=K^*\cap L.\] No convexity or closedness of \(K\) or \(P_LK\) is required.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal-projection specialization of the exact image formula.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projection of K onto L

knowledge_statements.title: Duals under Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a linear image converts the map into an adjoint inverse image of the original dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone of the linear image of \(K\) is the adjoint inverse image of its dual: \[(AK)^*=\{y\in Y:A^*y\in K^*\}=(A^*)^{-1}(K^*).\] Equivalently, \(y\in(AK)^*\) if and only if \(\langle A^*y,x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in K\). This identity requires no closedness of \(K\) or \(AK\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(K\subseteq X\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact adjoint formula for an image cone in finite dimensions.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122
2.3 Linear Operators and Functionals p. 31

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Cannot Be Dropped from the Pullback Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional pullback whose adjoint image of the dual cone is nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=\mathbb S^2\), \(C=\mathbb S_+^2\), and define \(A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb S^2\) by \[A(x_1,x_2)=\begin{pmatrix}x_1&x_2/2\\x_2/2&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Under the trace pairing, \(A^*Z=(z_{11},z_{12})\), and \[A^*C^*=\{(u,v):u>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] which is not closed. Moreover, \[A^{-1}C=\{(x_1,0):x_1\ge0\},\qquad (A^{-1}C)^*=\{(u,v):u\ge0\}=\overline{A^*C^*}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite pullback has a nonclosed adjoint dual image, so the general inverse-image formula genuinely requires closure.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^2\) has the trace inner product.

notation.meaning: Cone of positive-semidefinite real symmetric 2-by-2 matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Cannot Be Dropped from the Pullback Rule

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duals of Linear Inverse Images, Sections, and Projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pullback rule with its closure correction and its subspace-section and projection specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear and let \(C\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone. Then \[(A^{-1}C)^*=\overline{A^*C^*}.\] If \(A^*C^*\) is closed, the closure may be omitted; this holds, in particular, if \(\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\) or if \(C\) is polyhedral. For a subspace \(S\subseteq Y\), with inclusion \(\iota:S\hookrightarrow Y\) and orthogonal projection \(P_S=\iota^*\), \[(C\cap S)^{*_{S}}=\overline{P_SC^*},\qquad (P_SC)^{*_{S}}=C^*\cap S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pullbacks dualize to closed adjoint images; sections dualize to closed projected duals, while projections dualize exactly to sections of the dual cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A^{-1}C)^*=\overline{A^*C^*}\), with the displayed section and projection specializations.

notation.meaning: Inverse image of C under A
Dual cone taken in the inner-product space S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint calculus for images, inverse images, sections, and projections
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E,F\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:F\to E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\), \(L\subseteq F\) be closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image formulas describe the dual exactly even when the primal image is not closed. The inverse-image and section formulas retain closure unless a standard closedness qualification applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual-cone rules for a linear map are \[(AK)^*=\{y\in F:A^*y\in K^*\}=(A^*)^{-1}(K^*),\] and \[(A^{-1}L)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*L^*),\qquad A^{-1}L:=\{x\in E:Ax\in L\}.\] If \(M\subseteq E\) is a subspace and \(P_M\) is the orthogonal projection, then, with duals of cones in \(M\) computed using the induced inner product, \[(P_MK)^*=K^*\cap M,\qquad (K\cap M)^{*_{M}}=\operatorname{cl}(P_MK^*).\] Thus projection and section are dual operations, while image and inverse image are related through the adjoint. The closures may be removed whenever the displayed adjoint images are closed, including appropriate polyhedral or relative-interior-qualified cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the image of a cone under a linear map consists exactly of vectors whose adjoint images lie in the original dual cone. The dual of an inverse image is the closure of the adjoint image of the dual. For an orthogonal projection onto a subspace, the dual of the projected cone is the intersection of the original dual with that subspace, while the dual within the subspace of a section is the closure of the projected dual.
assumptions_latex: \(A:E\to F\) is linear and \(A^*\) is its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((AK)^*=(A^*)^{-1}(K^*)\) and \((A^{-1}L)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*L^*)\), with the stated projection-section specializations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in(AK)^*\iff \langle A^*y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\).
\(y\in(P_MK)^*\iff y\in M\cap K^*\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \((AK)^*=A^{-*}K^*\).
For a coordinate projection, the dual of the projection is the corresponding coordinate section of the dual.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonclosed linear image and its closure have the same dual cone.
Lifted conic formulations turn projection questions into sections of dual cones.
boundary_notes: The image \(AK\) of a closed cone need not be closed.
Dropping closure from \((A^{-1}L)^*\) requires an additional qualification.

notation.meaning: inverse of the adjoint when A is invertible

children.title: Duality of Cone Regularity Properties
children.top_down_role: Dual relationships among lineality, span, pointedness, solidity, and generation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity dictionary for a cone and its dual
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Define \(\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\) and \(\operatorname{span}K:=K-K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solidity means nonempty interior in the stated ambient space. When intrinsic topology is intended, replace interior and full dimensionality by relative interior and the span of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The principal regularity properties are: \(K\) is pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\); solid when \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\); generating when \(K-K=E\); and proper when it is closed, convex, pointed, and solid. Duality exchanges these properties through \[\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}K)^\perp.\] Hence \[K\text{ pointed}\iff K^*\text{ solid},\qquad K\text{ solid}\iff K^*\text{ pointed},\] and, in finite dimensions, solidity is equivalent to generation. Consequently, \(K\) is proper if and only if \(K^*\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex cone, lineality is the largest reversible subspace and the span is the space generated by differences of cone elements. A cone is pointed when its lineality is zero, solid when it has nonempty ambient interior, generating when its span is the whole space, and proper when it is closed, convex, pointed, and solid. The dual's lineality is the orthogonal complement of the primal span, and the dual span is the orthogonal complement of primal lineality. Therefore pointedness and solidity are exchanged by dualization, while properness is preserved.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp\), \(\operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}K)^\perp\), and pointedness and solidity are dual properties.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is pointed \(\iff \operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).
\(K\) is generating \(\iff K^*\cap(-K^*)=\{0\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a subspace, \(K^*=K^\perp\), so neither cone is pointed unless its subspace is zero.
A full-dimensional polyhedral cone is pointed exactly when its dual has nonempty interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(K\) and \(K^*\) have complementary lineality and span dimensions.
Dualizing a proper cone remains within the class used for finite-dimensional conic optimization.
boundary_notes: A cone can be pointed without being full-dimensional.
Relative solidity inside \(\operatorname{span}K\) is automatic for nonempty convex cones and is not the ambient solidity used here.

notation.meaning: lineality space K intersect minus K

children.title: Pointedness–Solidity Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence between lineality-free and interior-bearing regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Characterization of Dual Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior of the dual consists exactly of functionals strictly positive on every nonzero primal cone vector; such a functional exists exactly when the closed cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\). Then
\[
\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle>0\text{ for every }x\in K\setminus\{0\}\}.
\]
Consequently, \(K\) is pointed exactly when some \(y\in E\) is strictly positive on every nonzero element of \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointwise characterization underlying pointedness–solidity duality.

notation.meaning: Ordinary ambient interior of the dual cone

knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness–Solidity Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed finite-dimensional cones, pointedness of either cone is equivalent to solidity of its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cone is pointed when \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), and it is solid when \(\operatorname{int}K
eq\varnothing\). For a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), dualization exchanges these properties: \[K	ext{ is pointed}\iff\operatorname{int}(K^*)
eq\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{int}(K)
eq\varnothing\iff K^*	ext{ is pointed}.\] Thus absence of reversible primal directions is equivalent to full-dimensional dual interior, and conversely.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-cone version using ordinary ambient interior.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the fixed inner product

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise characterization of dual solidity for a closed finite-dimensional convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\). Then
\[
\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle>0\text{ for every }x\in K\setminus\{0\}\}.
\]
Consequently, \(K\) is pointed exactly when there exists a vector strictly positive on every nonzero element of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector lies in the interior of the dual exactly when it pairs strictly positively with every nonzero primal cone vector; existence of such a vector certifies pointedness.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Certificate for Dual Interior

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is Necessary for Pointedness–Solidity Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed nonconvex conic counterexample in the finite-dimensional ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(K\) be the union of the three rays generated by
\[
(1,0),\qquad\left(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),\qquad\left(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right).
\]
Then \(K\) is closed, positively homogeneous, and pointed, but it is not convex and \(K^*=\{0\}\). Thus \(K^*\) has empty interior. Moreover, \(K^*\) is pointed while \(K\) itself has empty interior, so both exchanges can fail without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A union of three rays separated by 120 degrees is a closed pointed nonconvex cone whose dual is only zero; it also has empty interior despite its dual being pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb R^2\) with its Euclidean inner product.
\(K\) is the union of the three displayed rays.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Necessary for Pointedness–Solidity Exchange

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness Is Necessary for Pointedness to Imply Dual Solidity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional counterexample at the closedness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
K=\{(s,t):t>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
Then \(K\) is a convex pointed cone but is not closed, whereas
\[
K^*=\{(0,b):b\geq0\},
\]
which has empty ambient interior. Thus pointedness need not imply solidity of the dual when closedness is dropped.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open upper half-plane together with the origin is a pointed convex cone, but its dual is a ray with empty ambient interior.
assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb R^2\) with its Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Is Necessary for Pointedness to Imply Dual Solidity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Dimensionality Is Necessary for Ambient-Interior Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional failure of pointedness-to-solidity under norm interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the Hilbert space \(\ell^2\), let
\[
K=\{x=(x_n):x_n\geq0\text{ for every }n\}.
\]
The cone \(K\) is closed, convex, pointed, and self-dual, but its norm interior is empty. Hence a closed pointed cone in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space need not have a solid dual when solidity means nonempty ambient norm interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative cone in l2 is closed, convex, pointed, and self-dual, yet has empty norm interior, so the finite-dimensional equivalence does not extend using ordinary ambient interior.

notation.meaning: Square-summable real sequences with nonnegative coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Dimensionality Is Necessary for Ambient-Interior Duality

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone with dual \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior is ambient interior in \(E\), not merely relative interior in the cone's span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Pointedness and solidity are defined by \[K	ext{ pointed}\iff K\cap(-K)=\{0\},\qquad K	ext{ solid}\iff\operatorname{int}K
eq\varnothing.\] Their dual correspondence is \[K	ext{ pointed}\iff\operatorname{int}K^*
eq\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{int}K
eq\varnothing\iff K^*\cap(-K^*)=\{0\}.\] Moreover, an element \(y\) lies in \(\operatorname{int}K^*\) exactly when \[\langle y,xangle>0\quad	ext{for every }x\in K\setminus\{0\}.\] Thus absence of reversible primal directions is equivalent to existence of a strictly positive dual functional, and ambient thickness of the primal cone is equivalent to absence of reversible dual directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is pointed if it contains no nonzero vector together with its negative, and solid if it has nonempty interior. For a nonempty closed convex cone in finite dimensions, pointedness is equivalent to the dual cone having nonempty interior, while solidity is equivalent to the dual being pointed. Interior dual vectors are precisely the functionals strictly positive on every nonzero primal cone vector.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is pointed if and only if \(K^*\) is solid, and \(K\) is solid if and only if \(K^*\) is pointed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\text{ pointed}\iff\exists y\in E\;\forall x\in K\setminus\{0\}:\langle y,x\rangle>0\).
\(K\text{ solid}\iff\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=\{0\}\).
special_cases_latex: \(\{0\}\) is pointed and its dual \(E\) is solid.
A linear subspace \(L\neq\{0\}\) is not pointed, and \(L^\perp\) has empty ambient interior unless \(L=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Strictly dual-feasible directions exist exactly for pointed closed cones.
The correspondence is symmetric because \(K^{**}=K\).
boundary_notes: Closedness is material for the stated bidirectional correspondence.
For a cone considered only inside its span, relative interior should not be confused with ambient solidity.

children.title: Span–Lineality Duality
children.top_down_role: Orthogonal relationships between intrinsic spans and reversible dual directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Boundary for Span-Lineality Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonclosed convex cone, dual lineality is still orthogonal to the primal span, but dual span is governed by the lineality of the cone's closure; the open upper-halfspace cone shows that using the original lineality can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), without assuming closedness, \[\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}\overline K)^\perp.\] Closedness permits \(\operatorname{lin}\overline K\) to be replaced by \(\operatorname{lin}K\). This replacement fails for \(K=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t>0\}\cup\{0\}\): here \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\), while \(K^*=\{(0,b):b\geq0\}\) has one-dimensional span.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\); closedness is not assumed.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Set \(L_K:=K\cap(-K)\) and \(S_K:=\operatorname{span}K=K-K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The span-lineality duality identities are \[\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}K)^\perp.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{span}K=(\operatorname{lin}K^*)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{lin}K=(\operatorname{span}K^*)^\perp.\] Hence the directions on which every dual functional vanishes are exactly the primal lineality directions, while dual reversible directions are precisely the vectors orthogonal to the entire primal span. In dimension form, \[\dim\operatorname{span}K+\dim\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=\dim E,\quad \dim\operatorname{lin}K+\dim\operatorname{span}(K^*)=\dim E.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex cone, the lineality of the dual is the orthogonal complement of the primal span, and the span of the dual is the orthogonal complement of primal lineality. knowledge_statements.title: Properness under Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed finite-dimensional convex cone is proper exactly when its dual is proper, and its second dual is the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), \[K\text{ is proper}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^*\text{ is proper},\qquad K^{**}=K.\] Thus dualization preserves proper-cone regularity and is involutive on this finite-dimensional closed-cone class.

Then \(K\) is convex, pointed, solid, and nonclosed, while \[K^*=\mathbb R_+^2,\qquad K^{**}=\overline K=\mathbb R_+^2\ne K.\] Thus the closed-cone hypothesis is essential for both the properness equivalence and exact bidual recovery.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. A cone \(K\subseteq E\) is called proper here when it is nonempty, closed, convex, pointed, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Some texts use “proper cone” with slightly different conventions. This record fixes the convention explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), properness is self-dual: \[K\text{ is proper}\iff K^*\text{ is proper}.\] More explicitly, closedness and convexity of \(K^*\) are automatic; primal pointedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\) is equivalent to pointedness of \(K^*\). Since \(K^{**}=K\), the same exchanges apply in both directions. Thus dualization preserves the class of proper cones while interchanging its two nontrivial regularity components, pointedness and solidity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated convention, a proper cone is closed, convex, pointed, and solid. The dual of every proper cone is proper, and conversely. Dual closedness and convexity are automatic, while pointedness of the primal becomes solidity of the dual and solidity of the primal becomes pointedness of the dual. Biduality makes the correspondence symmetric.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-dual cones and distinguished dual pairs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and let \(K,L\subseteq E\) be closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality is always relative to the displayed pairing. A dual pair need not consist of equal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone \(K\) is self-dual under \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) when \[K=K^*=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}.\] Two cones \((K,L)\) form a mutually dual pair when \[L=K^*\quad\text{and}\quad K=L^*.\] For closed convex cones the second equality follows from the first by biduality. The pair is non-self-dual when \(K\neq L\). Self-dual cones are necessarily closed and convex; if they are pointed, they are also solid, and conversely. Distinguished regimes therefore include self-dual proper cones, product cones assembled from self-dual factors, and asymmetric mutually dual pairs whose geometry is exchanged rather than fixed by dualization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex cone is self-dual when it equals the cone of vectors nonnegative on it under the chosen inner product. Two closed convex cones are a mutually dual pair when each is the other's dual; one equality implies the other by biduality. Such a pair is non-self-dual when the two cones differ. Self-dual pointed cones are automatically solid, and product constructions preserve self-duality under product pairings.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional and has a fixed inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distinguished regimes are characterized by \(K=K^*\) for self-duality and \(L=K^*,\ K=L^*\) for mutual duality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is self-dual \(\iff x\in K\) exactly when \(\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\).
For closed convex cones, \(L=K^*\iff K=L^*\).
special_cases_latex: A product of self-dual cones is self-dual under the sum inner product.
The nonnegative orthant is self-dual under the Euclidean pairing.
immediate_consequences_latex: A self-dual cone has identical primal and dual feasibility geometry.
A non-self-dual pair still supports symmetric bidualization after exchanging its two members.
boundary_notes: An arbitrary linear isomorphism between \(K\) and \(K^*\) does not make \(K\) self-dual under the original pairing.
Negative-polar conventions replace equality with a sign change.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-duality relative to a chosen inner product
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean product, let \(M\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), and define \(\langle x,y\rangle_M:=x^TMy\). Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formula compares two inner products on the same coordinate space. More general identifications with the algebraic dual give the same principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone relative to the \(M\)-inner product is \[K^{*_{M}}:=\{y:y^TMx\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}=M^{-1}K^*,\] where \(K^*\) is the Euclidean dual. Therefore \(K\) is self-dual relative to \(M\) exactly when \[K=K^{*_{M}}\iff MK=K^*.\] If \(T\) is invertible and \(M=T^TT\), this is equivalently \[TK=(TK)^*\] under the Euclidean product. Thus self-duality is not solely a property of the underlying set: it is a property of the cone together with a positive-definite pairing or an identification of \(E\) with \(E^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the inner product defined by a positive-definite matrix M, the dual of K is M inverse applied to the Euclidean dual. Hence K is self-dual for that pairing exactly when M maps K onto its Euclidean dual. Factoring M as T transpose T shows equivalently that the transformed cone T K is Euclidean self-dual. Self-duality therefore depends on the chosen pairing, not only on the set K.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in \(\mathbb R^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(M=T^TT\), then \(K\) is \(M\)-self-dual \(\iff TK\) is Euclidean self-dual.
\(y\in K^{*_{M}}\iff My\in K^*\).
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic norm, changing \(M\) exchanges the norm with the corresponding inverse-metric dual norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: A cone may fail to be self-dual in one metric and become self-dual after a suitable positive-definite change of pairing.
Orthogonal changes of coordinates preserve Euclidean self-duality.
boundary_notes: A general nonsymmetric bilinear form is not an inner product and is outside this definition.
Existence of some linear isomorphism \(K\to K^*\) does not automatically provide a symmetric positive-definite \(M\) with \(MK=K^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), define \[\mathcal{CP}_n=\operatorname{cone}\{xx^\top:x\in\mathbb R_+^n\},\qquad \mathcal{COP}_n=\{A\in\mathbb S^n:x^\top Ax\ge0\ \forall x\in\mathbb R_+^n\}.\] Under the trace pairing, \[\mathcal{CP}_n^*=\mathcal{COP}_n,\qquad \mathcal{COP}_n^*=\mathcal{CP}_n,\] and the two cones are distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The completely positive and copositive matrix cones form a distinct mutual-dual pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Norm cones as canonical asymmetric dual pairs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\), with dual norm \(\|y\|_*:=\max\{y^Tx:\|x\|\leq1\}\). Equip \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\) with \(\langle(s,y),(t,x)\rangle=st+y^Tx\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This construction includes both self-dual and non-self-dual pairs. It is asymmetric whenever the norm and its dual norm differ in the fixed coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the norm cone and its dual-norm cone by \[K_{\|\cdot\|}:=\{(t,x):t\geq\|x\|\},\qquad K_{\|\cdot\|_*}:=\{(s,y):s\geq\|y\|_*\}.\] They form a mutually dual pair: \[K_{\|\cdot\|}^*=K_{\|\cdot\|_*},\qquad K_{\|\cdot\|_*}^*=K_{\|\cdot\|}.\] For conjugate exponents \(1\leq p,q\leq\infty\) satisfying \(1/p+1/q=1\), this yields \[K_p^*=K_q,\qquad K_p:=\{(t,x):t\geq\|x\|_p\}.\] Thus \((K_1,K_\infty)\) is a canonical non-self-dual polyhedral pair, while \(K_2\) is the self-dual Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph cone of any norm is dual to the epigraph cone of its dual norm under the standard product pairing. In particular, the p-norm cone and q-norm cone are mutually dual when p and q are conjugate exponents. The one-norm and infinity-norm cones form a canonical asymmetric polyhedral pair, whereas the Euclidean norm cone is the self-dual Lorentz cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\|\cdot\|\) is a norm on finite-dimensional \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(\|\cdot\|_*\) is defined by the displayed support-function formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{\|\cdot\|}^*=K_{\|\cdot\|_*}\), and in particular \(K_p^*=K_q\) for conjugate exponents.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K_{\|\cdot\|}\) is self-dual in the fixed coordinates exactly when \(\|\cdot\|=\|\cdot\|_*\).
special_cases_latex: \(K_1^*=K_\infty\) and \(K_\infty^*=K_1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Dualizing a conic constraint over a norm cone replaces the norm by its dual norm.
Polyhedral norm cones provide explicit non-self-dual pairs with finite inequality and generator descriptions.
boundary_notes: Linear isomorphism between two cones does not mean equality under the fixed pairing.
At \(p=1\) or \(p=\infty\), conjugacy uses the standard extended convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces, exposed faces, extreme rays, and minimal faces of a cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space. For \(S\subseteq K\), let \(\operatorname{face}_K(S)\) denote the intersection of all faces of \(K\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extremal-generation statement requires closedness and absence of lines. The facial definitions themselves apply to arbitrary convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex subset \(F\subseteq K\) is a face, written \(F\unlhd K\), when \[x,z\in K,\ 0<\lambda<1,\ (1-\lambda)x+\lambda z\in F\Rightarrow x,z\in F.\] It is exposed when \(F=K\cap y^\perp\) for some \(y\in K^*\). A ray \(R=\mathbb R_+r\), \(r\neq0\), is extreme when it is a face; equivalently, \(r=x+z\) with \(x,z\in K\) implies \(x,z\in R\). The minimal face containing \(S\) is \[\operatorname{face}_K(S):=\bigcap\{F:F\unlhd K,\ S\subseteq F\}.\] If \(K\) is closed and pointed, then it is generated by its extreme rays: \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{r:\mathbb R_+r\text{ is an extreme ray of }K\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of a cone is a convex subset that contains both endpoints whenever it contains an interior point of a segment in the cone. An exposed face is obtained by intersecting the cone with the zero hyperplane of a dual-cone vector. Extreme rays are one-dimensional faces and admit an equivalent additive characterization. The minimal face containing a set is the intersection of all faces containing it. Every closed pointed cone is generated by representatives of its extreme rays.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone for the facial definitions.
\(K\) is closed and pointed for generation by extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditions define the conic facial-extremal hierarchy, and a closed pointed cone is generated by its extreme rays.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\unlhd K\iff x,z\in K,\ x+z\in F\Rightarrow x,z\in F\).
\(\mathbb R_+r\) is extreme \(\iff r=x+z\), \(x,z\in K\), forces \(x,z\in\mathbb R_+r\).
special_cases_latex: For pointed \(K\), \(\{0\}\) is the minimal nonempty face.
Every exposed ray is extreme, but an extreme ray need not be exposed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Faces are ordered by inclusion and form a complete lattice.
Minimal-face localization identifies the smallest conic stratum containing a feasible point or set.
boundary_notes: A cone with nonzero lineality has no extreme rays in the quotient-free one-dimensional sense sufficient to generate the whole cone.
Not every face of a nonpolyhedral cone is exposed.

notation.meaning: F is a face of K
minimal face of K containing S
