children.top_down_role: Inclusion and dimensional organization of conic faces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone, and let \(\mathcal F(K):=\{F:F\unlhd K\}\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(K\). Order \(\mathcal F(K)\) by set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The lattice definition is order-theoretic and does not require polyhedrality. Dimension gives a finite rank bound in finite-dimensional spaces but need not make the lattice graded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The face lattice of \(K\) is the complete lattice \((\mathcal F(K),\subseteq)\). For any family \((F_i)_{i\in I}\subseteq\mathcal F(K)\), its meet and join are \[\bigwedge_{i\in I}F_i=\bigcap_{i\in I}F_i,\qquad \bigvee_{i\in I}F_i=\bigcap\{F\in\mathcal F(K):\bigcup_{i\in I}F_i\subseteq F\}.\] Thus the join is the minimal face containing the union. The least and greatest elements are \(\varnothing\) and \(K\). In finite dimensions, strict inclusion of nonempty faces implies strict increase of dimension, so every strictly nested facial chain has finite length bounded by \(\dim K+1\), apart from the optional empty bottom element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces of a cone, including the empty face and the cone itself, form a complete lattice under inclusion. The meet of any family is its intersection, while its join is the smallest face containing the union. The empty set and the whole cone are the bottom and top elements. In finite dimensions, strict containment of nonempty faces strictly increases dimension, so facial chains are finite, although the lattice need not be graded for arbitrary nonpolyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal F(K),\subseteq)\) is a complete lattice with the displayed meet and join operations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F_1\vee F_2=\operatorname{face}_K(F_1\cup F_2)\).
\(F_1\wedge F_2=F_1\cap F_2\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is pointed, \(\{0\}\) is the least nonempty face.
For a polyhedral cone, \(\mathcal F(K)\) is finite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every subset \(S\subseteq K\) has a unique minimal containing face.
Facial inclusion supplies a dimension-monotone stratification of the cone.
boundary_notes: A complete lattice can have infinitely many elements; completeness does not imply polyhedrality.
Dimension alone need not determine joins or comparability.

notation.meaning: collection of all faces of K
meet and join in the face lattice

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Improper, proper, boundary, and minimal faces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty convex cone and let \(L:=\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)\). Faces are ordered by inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record uses the convention that a proper face is neither empty nor the whole cone. Some authors allow the empty face among proper faces; the convention must be checked when comparing sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The improper faces are \(\varnothing\) and \(K\). A face \(F\unlhd K\) is proper when \[\varnothing\neq F\subsetneq K.\] Every proper face lies in the relative boundary \(\operatorname{rbd}K:=\operatorname{cl}K\setminus\operatorname{ri}K\), and therefore \(\dim F<\dim K\) in finite dimensions. Every nonempty face contains the lineality space \(L\), and \(L\) is itself the unique minimal nonempty face. Consequently, when \(K\) is pointed, the unique minimal nonempty face is \(\{0\}\). A nonempty face \(F\) is minimal precisely when it has no nonempty proper subface, equivalently when \(F=L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empty face and the whole cone are the improper faces. Under the stated convention, a proper face is nonempty and strictly smaller than the cone. Every proper face lies on the relative boundary and has smaller dimension. The lineality space is contained in every nonempty face and is itself the unique minimal nonempty face. For a pointed cone this minimal face is the origin.
assumptions_latex: Dimension and relative-boundary assertions use finite-dimensional \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proper faces are the nonempty strict faces; all lie in \(\operatorname{rbd}K\), and \(\operatorname{lin}K\) is the unique minimal nonempty face.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\text{ proper}\iff F\unlhd K,\ \varnothing\neq F\neq K\).
\(F\text{ minimal nonempty}\iff F=\operatorname{lin}K\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is pointed, the minimal nonempty face is \(\{0\}\).
If \(K\) is a subspace, its only nonempty face is \(K\) itself.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty facial chain begins at \(\operatorname{lin}K\).
Passing to \(K/\operatorname{lin}K\) converts minimal faces to the pointed zero face.
boundary_notes: The whole cone is a face but is not a boundary face.
For nonclosed cones, relative boundary is taken using the relative topology of the affine hull and the displayed closure convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper face is a nonempty face strictly smaller than the cone, under the convention that the empty set is a face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subset \(F\subseteq C\) is a face of \(C\) when it is convex and, whenever \(x,y\in C\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and \(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in F\), one has \(x,y\in F\). Under the convention that \(\varnothing\) is a face, a proper face is a face satisfying \[\varnothing\subsetneq F\subsetneq C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex cone in a real vector space.
The face lattice includes the empty face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F\text{ is proper}\iff F\text{ is a face of }C\text{ and }\varnothing\subsetneq F\subsetneq C.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the extended face lattice containing the empty face.

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality and Existence of Proper Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural characterization of the nonempty proper-face class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex cone and let \(L=C\cap(-C)\) be its lineality space. The set \(L\) is a face of \(C\), and every nonempty face of \(C\) contains \(L\). Consequently, \(C\) has a nonempty proper face if and only if \(C\) is not a linear subspace; in that case \(L\) is its least nonempty face and is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the least nonempty face, and nonempty proper faces exist exactly when the cone is not a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonempty face contains \(L\), and \(C\) has a nonempty proper face exactly when \(L\subsetneq C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality and Existence of Proper Faces
Improper Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The improper faces are the empty face and the whole cone; conventions excluding empty faces retain only the whole cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the extended face lattice \(\mathcal F(C)\), the two improper faces are its least and greatest elements: \[F\text{ is an improper face of }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F=\varnothing\text{ or }F=C.\] Every other face is proper. If faces are required by convention to be nonempty, only \(C\) is called improper and \(\varnothing\) is omitted from the lattice.
assumptions_latex: The extended face lattice includes the empty face.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-lattice convention; some authors exclude the empty face entirely.

notation.meaning: The extended collection of faces of the cone

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Boundary as a Union of Proper Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative boundary of a closed finite-dimensional cone is the union of its proper exposed faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}C\) and let \(C_L^*\) be the dual cone in \(L\). If \(C\) is closed, then \[\operatorname{relbd}C=\bigcup\{C\cap y^\perp:y\in C_L^*\setminus\{0\},\ C\cap y^\perp\ne C\}.\] Thus every relative-boundary point belongs to a proper exposed face.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed finite-dimensional convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed finite-dimensional cones, with duality taken inside the cone's span.

notation.meaning: dual cone taken in the linear span of the cone

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Roles of Proper Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty proper face lies on the cone’s relative boundary; any face meeting the relative interior equals the whole cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonempty proper face of a finite-dimensional convex cone lies in its relative boundary: \[F\subseteq\operatorname{relbd}C.\] Equivalently, if a face \(F\) meets \(\operatorname{ri}C\), then \(F=C\). Thus proper faces stratify boundary portions of the cone, whereas the improper face \(C\) is the only face containing relative-interior points.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(F\) is a nonempty proper face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-boundary statement, valid without full dimensionality.

notation.meaning: Relative boundary in the affine hull of the cone

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper Faces Cover the Attained Relative Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes boundary points contained in a possibly nonclosed cone from missing points of its relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty finite-dimensional convex cone. Every point of \(C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\) belongs to a nonempty proper exposed face of \(C\), and \[C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C=\bigcup\{F:F\text{ is a nonempty proper face of }C\}.\] If \(C\) is closed, this union equals \(\operatorname{relbd}C\). If \(C\) is not closed, points in \(\operatorname{relbd}C\setminus C\) belong to no face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper faces cover exactly the relative-boundary points attained by the cone; for a closed cone they cover its entire relative boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The union of all nonempty proper faces is \(C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\), and it is \(\operatorname{relbd}C\) when \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Proper Faces Cover the Attained Relative Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facets as maximal proper faces of polyhedral cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral cone, regarded as a polyhedron in its linear span \(S:=\operatorname{span}K\). Let \(d:=\dim K=\dim S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence between maximal proper faces and codimension-one faces is asserted in the polyhedral regime. It can fail for general nonpolyhedral cones, where a maximal proper face may have larger codimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A facet of \(K\) is an inclusion-maximal proper face: \[F\text{ is a facet}\iff F\unlhd K,\ F\subsetneq K,\ \nexists G\unlhd K\text{ with }F\subsetneq G\subsetneq K.\] For a nonempty polyhedral cone this is equivalent to \[F\neq\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\dim F=d-1.\] Every facet is exposed: there exists a nonzero \(a\in K^*\cap S\) such that \[F=K\cap a^\perp=\{x\in K:a^Tx=0\}.\] If \(K=\{x\in S:a_i^Tx\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) is an irredundant homogeneous half-space representation, its inequalities correspond to the facets, up to positive rescaling and duplication of the same supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty polyhedral cone, a facet is a maximal proper face. Equivalently, it is a nonempty face of dimension one less than the cone. Every facet is exposed by a nonzero valid homogeneous inequality. In an irredundant homogeneous inequality description, the inequalities correspond to facets, modulo positive scaling and repeated descriptions of the same supporting hyperplane. The polyhedral qualification is essential because maximal proper faces of general cones need not have codimension one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For polyhedral \(K\), facets are exactly the maximal proper faces and exactly the nonempty faces of dimension \(\dim K-1\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\text{ facet}\iff F\text{ is a nonempty maximal element of }\mathcal F(K)\setminus\{K\}\).
\(F\text{ facet}\iff\dim F=\dim K-1\).
special_cases_latex: For a full-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone in \(\mathbb R^n\), every facet has dimension \(n-1\).
For a ray, the zero face is its unique facet under the nonempty-face convention.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper face of a polyhedral cone is contained in a facet.
Minimal irredundant homogeneous inequality descriptions are indexed by facets.
boundary_notes: For a Lorentz cone of dimension greater than three, extreme rays are maximal proper faces but are not facets by codimension.
If the empty face is admitted as a facet in zero-dimensional conventions, the degenerate case must be handled separately.

notation.meaning: dimension of K in its span

knowledge_statements.title: Exposure and Dual Certificate for a Facet
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facet of a closed finite-dimensional cone is exposed, and its supporting normal spans an extreme ray of the relative dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}C\) and let \(C_L^*\) be the dual cone in \(L\). If \(C\) is closed and \(F\) is a facet, then there exists \(y\in C_L^*\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[F=C\cap y^\perp,\qquad \mathbb R_+y\text{ is an extreme ray of }C_L^*.\] Thus every facet is exposed, and its relative supporting normal supplies a dual extreme-ray certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed finite-dimensional convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\in C_L^*\setminus\{0\}:F=C\cap y^\perp\text{ and }\mathbb R_+y\text{ is extreme in }C_L^*.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed finite-dimensional cones; the relative-dual formulation avoids ambient annihilator directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Facets of Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facet is a proper face whose dimension is exactly one less than the dimension of the cone’s linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a convex cone and let \(F\subsetneq C\) be a face. The face \(F\) is called a facet of \(C\) when it has relative codimension one in \(C\), namely
\[\dim(\operatorname{span}F)=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)-1.\]
Thus the definition is taken relative to the linear hull of \(C\), even when \(C\) is not full-dimensional in its ambient space.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper face \(F\) is a facet exactly when \(\dim F=\dim C-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative-dimension convention.

notation.meaning: dimension of the linear span of a cone or face

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative supporting-hyperplane characterization, valid without ambient full dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite-dimensional convex cone, let \(V=\operatorname{span}C\), and let \(F\) be a facet of \(C\). There is a nonzero functional \(y\in V^*\), unique up to multiplication by a positive scalar, such that \[y(x)\ge0\quad(x\in C),\qquad F=C\cap\ker y.\] Thus every facet is exposed, and \(\mathbb R_+y\) is an extreme ray of the relative dual cone \[C_V^*=\{z\in V^*:z(x)\ge0\ \text{for all }x\in C\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every facet is exposed by a unique relative normal ray, which is an extreme ray of the relative dual cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique ray \(\mathbb R_+y\subseteq C_V^*\) satisfying \(F=C\cap\ker y\), and this ray is extreme in \(C_V^*\).

notation.meaning: dual cone formed in the linear span of the primal cone
supporting normal ray of the facet

knowledge_statements.statement_title: An Extreme Dual Normal Need Not Expose a Facet
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse outside polyhedral or additional regularity regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the self-dual cone \(C=\mathbb S_+^3\), let \(Y=uu^{\mathsf T}\) with \(u\ne0\). The ray \(\mathbb R_+Y\) is extreme in \(C^*=C\), while its exposed face \[F_Y=\{X\succeq0:\langle Y,X\rangle=0\}=\{X\succeq0:Xu=0\}\] is linearly isomorphic to \(\mathbb S_+^2\). It has dimension \(3\), whereas \(C\) has dimension \(6\), so it is not a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the 3-by-3 positive-semidefinite cone, an extreme rank-one dual normal exposes a codimension-three face rather than a facet.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R_+Y\) is an extreme ray of \(C^*\), but \(C\cap Y^\perp\) is not a facet of \(C\).

notation.meaning: cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite n-by-n matrices

knowledge_statements.title: An Extreme Dual Normal Need Not Expose a Facet
Extension to a Maximal Proper Face
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper face of a finite-dimensional cone lies in a maximal proper face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite-dimensional convex cone. Every proper face \(F\unlhd C\) is contained in a maximal proper face \(M\unlhd C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a maximal proper face \(M\unlhd C\) satisfying \(F\subseteq M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional existence above an arbitrary proper face.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposure of Maximal Proper Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every maximal proper face of a closed finite-dimensional cone is exposed by a supporting dual functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a closed finite-dimensional convex cone and let \(M\) be a maximal proper face. Then there exists \(y\in C^*\) whose restriction to \(\operatorname{span}C\) is nonzero and such that \[M=C\cap y^\perp.\] Hence every maximal proper face is exposed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(M\) is a maximal proper face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a supporting dual vector \(y\) such that \(M=C\cap y^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative supporting representation; no polyhedrality assumption is required.

notation.meaning: The dual cone under the nonnegative-pairing convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Proper Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal proper face is a proper face with no distinct face strictly between it and the whole cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper face \(F\subsetneq C\) is a maximal proper face of \(C\) if, for every face \(G\) of \(C\),
\[F\subseteq G\subseteq C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G=F\ \text{or}\ G=C.\]
Equivalently, \(F\) is a maximal element, under inclusion, among all proper faces of \(C\). This notion is purely lattice-theoretic and does not itself prescribe the codimension of \(F\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone and \(F\) is a proper face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face \(F\) is maximal proper when no face lies strictly between \(F\) and \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic maximality in the face lattice.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper face of a finite-dimensional cone is contained in a maximal proper face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a maximal proper face \(M\) with \(F\subseteq M\lneq C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Cofinality of Maximal Proper Faces
Strict Failure of the Converse for Lorentz Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Lorentz cone of dimension at least three, maximal proper faces are rays and no facets exist, so maximality need not imply facet status outside the polyhedral regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge3\), every nonzero proper face of the Lorentz cone \(Q^d\) is an extreme ray. Thus every extreme ray is a maximal proper face, but \(Q^d\) has no face of dimension \(d-1\). Consequently, a maximal proper face of a nonpolyhedral cone need not be a facet.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximal proper faces of \(Q^d\) are one-dimensional, whereas \(Q^d\) has no facets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nonpolyhedral failure of maximal-proper-to-facet implication.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet–Maximality Coincidence Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every facet is a maximal proper face. For a polyhedral cone, every maximal proper face is a facet, so the two classes coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite-dimensional convex cone. Every facet of \(C\) is a maximal proper face. If, in addition, \(C\) is polyhedral, every maximal proper face has dimension \(\dim C-1\). Hence, for polyhedral cones, the facets are exactly the maximal proper faces.
assumptions_latex: For the converse assertion, \(C\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every facet is maximal proper; for polyhedral \(C\), the maximal proper faces are exactly the facets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General forward implication and polyhedral coincidence.

Then \[F_u:=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:Xu=0\}\] is a maximal proper face of \(K\), while \[\dim K-\dim F_u=n>1.\] Hence \(F_u\) is not a facet. In fact, \(\mathbb S_+^n\) has no facets for \(n\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the positive-semidefinite cone, matrices annihilating a fixed nonzero vector form a maximal proper face of codimension n. Thus maximal proper faces need not be facets outside the polyhedral regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_u\) is maximal proper and has codimension \(n>1\), so it is not a facet.

children.title: Facial Chain-Rank Geometry
children.top_down_role: Nested facial strata and their depth.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex set, \(\mathcal F(C)\) is its face lattice ordered by inclusion, and chain length means the number of strict inclusions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional facial geometry; the definition applies to cones as a special case and permits the empty face when explicitly stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{ht}_C(F):=\sup\{r:\varnothing=F_{-1}\subsetneq F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r=F,\ F_i\in\mathcal F(C)\},\qquad \operatorname{dp}_C(F):=\sup\{s:F=G_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq G_s=C\}.\] A facial chain is any totally inclusion-ordered family in \(\mathcal F(C)\); a saturated chain has no face strictly between consecutive members. The facial chain rank of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{rk}_{\mathcal F}(C):=\sup\{m:F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_m=C\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facial chain of a finite-dimensional convex set is a family of faces totally ordered by inclusion. Its length is the number of strict inclusions. The height of a face records the largest number of strict facial inclusions below it, while its depth records the largest number above it up to the whole set. The facial chain rank is the maximum length of a strict chain terminating at the whole set. A chain is saturated when consecutive faces admit no intermediate face. These quantities describe nested facial strata independently of a particular inequality representation. Because every proper nonempty face has strictly smaller dimension than its parent, all such chains are finite in finite dimensions, although conventions concerning the empty face shift numerical ranks by one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_m\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dim F_0<\cdots<\dim F_m,\] so every finite-dimensional facial chain has finite length.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{dp}_C(F)\) is the rank of the interval \([F,C]\) in the face lattice when that interval is graded.
A saturated chain from \(F\) to \(C\) successively crosses covering relations of \(\mathcal F(C)\).
special_cases_latex: For a full-dimensional polyhedral cone, maximal chains from \(\{0\}\) to the cone have one face at each attainable dimension.
If \(C\) has nonzero lineality, its lineality space is contained in every nonempty face and replaces \(\{0\}\) as the least nonempty facial stratum.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\operatorname{dp}_C(F)\leq \dim C-\dim F\).
Strictly decreasing sequences of nonempty faces terminate in finite dimensions.
boundary_notes: The face lattice need not be graded, so different saturated chains can have different lengths.
In infinite-dimensional spaces the supremum may be infinite or ordinal-valued; that regime is excluded.

notation.meaning: face lattice of the convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Extension to a Saturated Complete Chain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite strict face chain can be refined and completed to a saturated maximal chain from the lineality space to the whole cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite strict chain of nonempty faces of \(C\) can be refined and extended to a saturated complete chain \[L=G_0\subsetneq G_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq G_r=C,\] where no face lies strictly between consecutive terms. Equivalently, maximal chains in the nonempty face lattice are precisely saturated chains from \(L\) to \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-dimensional convex cone with lineality space \(L=C\cap(-C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite strict chain of nonempty faces is contained in a saturated complete chain from \(L\) to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonempty face lattice.

notation.meaning: The unique minimal nonempty face of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Face Chains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face chain is a nested sequence of faces. Its length counts strict inclusions; a complete chain runs from the lineality space to the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A face chain of \(C\) is a finite family \((F_i)_{i=0}^{m}\) of nonempty faces satisfying
\[F_0\subseteq F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_m.\]
It is strict if \(F_{i-1}\subsetneq F_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and complete from the minimal to the maximal face if \(F_0=L=C\cap(-C)\) and \(F_m=C\). Its length is the number \(m\) of strict inclusions, not the number of faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A face chain is a family of faces totally ordered by inclusion; it is strict when every displayed inclusion is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite chains in the nonempty face lattice.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension Grading of Nonempty Face Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic ordering restrictions for nonempty faces of a finite-dimensional cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite-dimensional convex cone with lineality space \(L=C\cap(-C)\). Every nonempty face \(F\unlhd C\) contains \(L\). If \(F\subsetneq G\) are nonempty faces of \(C\), then \[\dim F<\dim G.\] Thus dimension strictly grades every strict chain of nonempty faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face contains the lineality space, and dimension increases at every strict inclusion in a face chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\subseteq F\) for every nonempty face, and \(F\subsetneq G\Rightarrow\dim F<\dim G\).

notation.meaning: lineality space and least nonempty face of C

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Grading of Nonempty Face Chains
Facial Rank
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial rank is the greatest number of strict inclusions in a face chain from the cone’s lineality space to the whole cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The facial rank of \(C\) is
\[\rho(C)=\max\bigl\{m:\ L=F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_m=C,\ \text{each }F_i\text{ a face of }C\bigr\}.\]
Thus \(\rho(C)\) records the largest number of strict face-lattice steps from the unique minimal nonempty face \(L\) to \(C\). Under this convention, a linear subspace has facial rank \(0\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-dimensional convex cone with lineality space \(L=C\cap(-C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The facial rank \(\rho(C)\) is the maximum length of a strict face chain from \(L\) to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank defined by maximal strict-chain length.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The proposed rank convention is mathematically coherent, but “facial rank” and its normalization are not sufficiently supported by the cited general convex-cones section. A source explicitly defining this terminology and chain-length convention is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz-Cone Chain Length
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Lorentz cone has maximal complete facial-chain length two; for dimensions at least three this is strictly below the dimension bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Lorentz cone \(Q^d\), every proper nonzero face is an extreme ray. Therefore every complete strict chain of nonempty faces has length at most \(2\), and \[\{0\}\subsetneq\mathbb R_+(1,u)\subsetneq Q^d,\qquad \|u\|_2=1,\] attains length \(2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximal length of a complete strict chain of nonempty faces of \(Q^d\) is \(2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical rank-two cone family; strictness of the dimension bound occurs for \(d\ge3\).

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Chain Length
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of the PSD cone are ordered like subspaces, so its longest complete face chains have length n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) has the form \[F_U=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}X\subseteq U\}\] for a subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(F_U\subseteq F_W\) exactly when \(U\subseteq W\). Consequently, longest complete strict face chains correspond to complete flags of subspaces and have length \(n\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^n\) is the cone of real positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximal length of a complete strict face chain of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) is \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subspace-indexed facial representation used to determine chain depth; strictness of the dimension bound occurs for \(n\ge2\).

notation.meaning: The PSD face consisting of matrices whose ranges lie in U.

knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Length Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial rank cannot exceed dimension minus lineality dimension. Polyhedral cones attain this bound, while a nonpolyhedral cone may have smaller facial rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a finite-dimensional convex cone with lineality space \(L\), and let \(\rho(C)\) denote its facial rank under the strict-chain-length convention. Then
\[\rho(C)\leq \dim C-\dim L.\]
If \(C\) is polyhedral, then
\[\rho(C)=\dim C-\dim L.\]
For nonpolyhedral cones, the inequality may be strict.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-dimensional convex cone with lineality space \(L\).
For the equality assertion, \(C\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(\rho(C)\leq\dim C-\dim L\), with equality for polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension bound generally; equality in the polyhedral regime.

notation.meaning: facial rank defined by strict-chain length

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\mathbb S_+^n\), its faces are indexed by subspaces \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) as \[F_U:=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}X\subseteq U\}.\] The maximum number of strict inclusions in a nonempty face chain from \(\{0\}\) to \(\mathbb S_+^n\) is \(n\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PSD cone of order n has maximum strict facial-chain length n, while its dimension is n(n+1)/2. It therefore gives strict inequality in the general dimension bound.
assumptions_latex: Chain length counts strict inclusions between nonempty faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum strict chain length is \(n\), strictly less than \(\dim\mathbb S_+^n\) for \(n\geq2\).

children.title: Facial Exposure Classes
children.top_down_role: Facial strata classified by their relationship with supporting functionals.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(F\) is a face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets and cones; exposure is taken relative to the affine hull of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[F\text{ is exposed in }C\iff \exists a\neq0:\quad F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle=C\cap\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\},\] where \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle<+\infty\). A face that is not representable this way is nonexposed. For a cone \(K\), an exposed face has the form \(K\cap y^\perp\) for a nonzero \(y\in K^*\) under the dual-cone convention \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed face is a face selected exactly as the maximizer set of a nonconstant linear functional, equivalently as the intersection of the convex set with a supporting hyperplane. A face lacking such a global supporting functional is nonexposed. The whole set is commonly admitted as an improper exposed face by allowing a constant functional, whereas a proper exposed face requires a supporting hyperplane that does not contain the whole affine hull. For cones, homogeneity forces a supporting level through the origin, so exposed faces are orthogonal sections by dual vectors. Exposed extreme points and exposed rays are respectively zero- and one-dimensional exposed faces; every exposed face is a face, but a face need not be exposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{exp}}(C):=\{F\in\mathcal F(C):F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{C}\langle a,\cdot\rangle\text{ for some }a\}\subseteq\mathcal F(C).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper face \(F\) is exposed iff there is a supporting hyperplane \(H\) of \(C\) with \(F=C\cap H\).
For a cone under the nonnegative-dual convention, \(F\) is exposed iff \(F=K\cap y^\perp\) for some \(y\in K^*\).
special_cases_latex: An exposed point is a singleton exposed face.
An exposed ray is a one-dimensional exposed face of a cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is closed relative to a closed convex set.
Every exposed ray is extreme, while the converse can fail.
boundary_notes: Exposure in a face does not imply exposure in the ambient convex set.
Sign conventions for polar cones reverse maximization and minimization but not the exposed set.

notation.meaning: support function of the convex set
dual cone under the nonnegative pairing convention

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed face is exactly the intersection of the cone with a supporting hyperplane defined by one nonzero dual direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(C^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in C\}\). A proper face \(F\) of \(C\) is exposed if there exists \(y\in C^*\), nonzero on \(\operatorname{span}C\), such that
\[F=\{x\in C:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}=C\cap y^{\perp}.\]
The vector \(y\) is an exposing direction: its supporting hyperplane isolates precisely the points of \(F\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face \(F\) is exposed exactly when \(F=C\cap y^{\perp}\) for some nonzero \(y\in C^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-cone convention with nonnegative pairing.

notation.meaning: dual cone of nonnegative linear functionals
orthogonal hyperplane to the exposing direction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp condition for the zero face of a closed cone to be exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonzero closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Then \(\{0\}\) is an exposed face of \(C\) if and only if \(C\) is pointed. When this holds, every dual vector in the relative interior of \(C^*\), interpreted in the dual of \(\operatorname{span}C\), exposes \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonzero closed cone, the zero set is an exposed face exactly when the cone is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonzero closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{0\}\text{ is an exposed face of }C\iff C\cap(-C)=\{0\}.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of the dual cone after restriction to the span of C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Meet closure of exposed faces of a cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F_i=C\cap y_i^\perp\) with \(y_i\in C^*\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), then
\[\bigcap_{i=1}^m F_i=C\cap\left(\sum_{i=1}^m y_i\right)^\perp.\]
Consequently every finite intersection of exposed faces is exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite intersections of exposed faces are exposed, with the sum of the exposing directions exposing the intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Intersections of Exposed Faces

knowledge_statements.statement_title: All Exposing Directions of an Exposed Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior characterization of the dual directions exposing a fixed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a closed convex cone and let \(F\unlhd C\) be exposed. With \(F^\triangle=C^*\cap F^\perp\),
\[C\cap y^\perp=F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\in\operatorname{ri}(F^\triangle).\]
Thus the exposing directions of \(F\) are precisely the relative-interior points of its conjugate face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector exposes a fixed exposed face exactly when it lies in the relative interior of that face's conjugate dual face.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.title: All Exposing Directions of an Exposed Face

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Conic Generation by Exposed Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a nontrivial line-free closed convex cone by arbitrary selected generators of all exposed rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone with \(K\neq\{0\}\) that contains no affine line. Let \(T\subseteq K\) satisfy the condition that every exposed ray of \(K\) is generated by some \(x\in T\). Then \(K=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nontrivial closed convex cone containing no line, any set that supplies a generator for every exposed ray generates the whole cone after taking the conic hull and closure.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a closed convex cone}
\forall\text{ exposed rays }R\text{ of }K\;\exists x\in T:\ R=\mathbb{R}_+x

knowledge_statements.title: A Cone with Nonexposed Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing the convex hull of the unit disk and an exterior point gives a closed three-dimensional cone with nonexposed extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[D=\{u\in\mathbb R^2:\|u\|_2\leq1\},\quad C=\operatorname{conv}(D\cup\{(2,0)\}),\quad K=\operatorname{cone}\{(u,1):u\in C\}.\]
For \(q_\pm=(1/2,\pm\sqrt3/2)\), the rays
\[R_\pm=\mathbb R_+(q_\pm,1)\]
are extreme rays of the closed cone \(K\), but neither ray is exposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\pm=\mathbb R_+(q_\pm,1)\) are extreme rays of \(K\) that are not exposed faces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit closed three-dimensional homogenization cone.

notation.meaning: Rays over the two tangency points.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexposed face is a genuine face that cannot be isolated by intersecting the cone with one supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A face \(F\) of \(C\) is nonexposed if it is not an exposed face; explicitly,
\[\text{there is no }y\in C^*\text{ such that }F=C\cap\{x:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}.\]
Thus \(F\) still satisfies the facial decomposition property, but it cannot be recovered as the zero set on \(C\) of any single supporting dual functional.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face \(F\) is nonexposed when no \(y\in C^*\) satisfies \(F=C\cap y^{\perp}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negation of single-direction facial exposure.

notation.meaning: dual cone of nonnegative linear functionals

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Exposed Faces p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogenized Tangency Produces a Nonexposed Ray
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed finite-dimensional cone with a nonexposed face, also illustrating dependence on the ambient cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[B=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{u\in\mathbb R^2:\|u\|\le1\}\cup\{(2,0)\}\bigr),\qquad K=\operatorname{cone}\{(u,1):u\in B\}.\]
For either \(p=(1/2,\pm\sqrt3/2)\), the ray \(R=\mathbb R_+(p,1)\) is an extreme ray of \(K\) but is not exposed. Its unique supporting hyperplane also contains the two-dimensional exposed face
\[E=\operatorname{cone}\{(p,1),((2,0),1)\}.\]
Thus \(R\) is nonexposed as a face of \(K\), although it is exposed as a face of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing a disk joined tangentially to an exterior point produces a closed cone with a nonexposed extreme ray; exposure can change when the ambient cone changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is a nonexposed face of \(K\) but an exposed face of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.title: Homogenized Tangency Produces a Nonexposed Ray

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conjugate-face characterization of nonexposure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a closed convex cone and \(F\unlhd C\). With
\[F^\triangle=C^*\cap F^\perp,\qquad F^{\triangle\triangle}=C\cap(F^\triangle)^\perp,\]
the face \(F^{\triangle\triangle}\) is the smallest exposed face of \(C\) containing \(F\). Consequently,
\[F\text{ is nonexposed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\subsetneq F^{\triangle\triangle}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is nonexposed exactly when double conjugation enlarges it to a strictly larger exposed face.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is nonexposed if and only if \(F\subsetneq F^{\triangle\triangle}\).

notation.meaning: Conjugate face in the dual cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Double-Conjugation Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed cone is facially exposed exactly when every nonempty face is fixed by double conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each nonempty face \(F\unlhd K\), let \(F^\triangle=K^*\cap F^\perp\). Then
\[K\text{ is facially exposed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F^{\triangle\triangle}=F\quad\text{for every nonempty face }F\unlhd K.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
Faces are taken to be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is facially exposed if and only if \(F^{\triangle\triangle}=F\) for every nonempty face \(F\unlhd K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed finite-dimensional cones; faces are understood as nonempty.

notation.meaning: Conjugate face of F in the dual cone.
Double conjugate of F in K.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Cones Are Facially Exposed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-dimensional polyhedral cone is facially exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonempty face of a finite-dimensional polyhedral cone is exposed. Consequently, every polyhedral cone is facially exposed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a polyhedral convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every proper nonempty face of \(K\) is exposed, so \(K\) is facially exposed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedral cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Facially Exposed Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is facially exposed when every proper face can be isolated by some single supporting dual direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone \(C\) is facially exposed if every proper face \(F\) of \(C\) is exposed. Equivalently, for each proper face \(F\subsetneq C\), there exists a dual direction \(y\in C^*\), nonzero on \(\operatorname{span}C\), satisfying
\[F=C\cap y^{\perp}=\{x\in C:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}.\]
Hence the face lattice of a facially exposed cone contains no nonexposed proper faces.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cone \(C\) is facially exposed exactly when each proper face equals \(C\cap y^{\perp}\) for some \(y\in C^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global exposure property of the face lattice.

notation.meaning: dual cone of nonnegative linear functionals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial exposure passes from a cone to its faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is facially exposed and \(F\unlhd C\), then \(F\), regarded as a cone in \(\operatorname{span}F\), is facially exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a facially exposed cone is itself facially exposed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-dimensional facially exposed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is facially exposed as a cone in \(\operatorname{span}F\).

notation.meaning: F is a face of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Hereditary Facial Exposure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic closure properties of the facial-exposure class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Facial exposure is invariant under invertible linear maps. Moreover, for finite-dimensional convex cones \(C_1,C_2\),
\[C_1\times C_2\text{ is facially exposed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C_1\text{ and }C_2\text{ are facially exposed}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible linear images preserve facial exposure, and a finite product is facially exposed exactly when each factor is.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Facial exposure is invariant under linear isomorphism and componentwise under finite products.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic definition of extreme rays, supplemented by finite-dimensional closed and closure-qualified generation classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[R\in\operatorname{ExtRays}(K)\iff \bigl(x,y\in K,\ x+y\in R\bigr)\Longrightarrow x,y\in R.\] Define \(\operatorname{egen}(K):=\operatorname{cone}\bigl(\bigcup_{R\in\operatorname{ExtRays}(K)}R\bigr)\). The cone is extremally generated if \(K=\operatorname{egen}(K)\), and closed-extremally generated if \(K=\overline{\operatorname{egen}(K)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero ray of a convex cone is extreme when no point on that ray can be decomposed as a sum of two cone elements lying outside the same ray. Equivalently, the ray is a one-dimensional face. The extremal generating cone is the conic hull of all extreme rays. Equality with the original cone defines exact extremal generation; equality only after closure defines closed extremal generation. This distinction matters for nonpolyhedral or infinite-dimensional cones. If a cone contains a line, it has no one-dimensional pointed face outside its lineality in the usual sense, so extremal generation is naturally studied after removing lineality or under pointedness assumptions.

equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(u\in K\setminus\{0\}\), \(\mathbb R_+u\) is extreme iff \(u=(x+y)/2\) with \(x,y\in K\) implies \(x,y\in\mathbb R_+u\).
Exact extremal generation means every \(x\in K\) is a finite conic combination of vectors spanning extreme rays.
special_cases_latex: For a polyhedral pointed cone, the extreme rays form a finite generating family.
For a cone with a compact convex base, extreme rays correspond to extreme points of that base.
immediate_consequences_latex: An extreme ray is preserved as an extreme ray of any face containing it.
A conic representation by extreme directions is an internal representation of the cone.
boundary_notes: Extreme vectors are defined only up to positive scaling.
Closed-extremal generation does not assert a finite exact representation for every point.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays Are Inherited Through Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray contained in a face is extreme in that face exactly when it is extreme in the ambient cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is a face of a convex cone \(C\) and \(R\subseteq F\) is a ray, then \[R\text{ is an extreme ray of }F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R\text{ is an extreme ray of }C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a face of a convex cone \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\text{ is extreme in }F\iff R\text{ is extreme in }C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremality is inherited in both directions between a face and its ambient cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme ray is a one-dimensional face: any conic decomposition of one of its points uses vectors on the same ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The ray generated by \(r\) is \(R=\mathbb{R}_+r=\{\lambda r:\lambda\geq0\}\). It is an extreme ray of \(C\) if \(R\) is a face of \(C\). Equivalently, for all \(u,v\in C\),
\[u+v\in R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in R\ \text{and}\ v\in R.\]
Thus a nonzero direction on an extreme ray cannot be decomposed into two conic directions lying outside that ray.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone and \(r\in C\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ray \(\mathbb{R}_+r\) is extreme exactly when \(u+v\in\mathbb{R}_+r\), with \(u,v\in C\), implies \(u,v\in\mathbb{R}_+r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme rays characterized as one-dimensional faces.

notation.meaning: nonnegative ray generated by a nonzero vector

children.title: Exposed Extreme Rays
children.top_down_role: Extreme rays isolated by supporting dual directions.

knowledge_statements.title: A Nonexposed Extreme Ray
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing a disk joined to an exterior point produces a closed pointed cone with a nonexposed extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|_2\le1\}\cup\{(2,0)\})\), \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{(z,1):z\in K\}\), and \(q=(1/2,\sqrt3/2)\). The point \(q\) is extreme in \(K\), but its supporting line meets \(K\) in \([q,(2,0)]\). Hence \(\mathbb R_+(q,1)\) is an extreme ray of \(C\) that is not exposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb R_+(q,1)\text{ is extreme in }C\text{ but not exposed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonpolyhedral closed pointed cone with a nonexposed extreme ray.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Extreme Rays Are Exposed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme ray of a polyhedral cone is isolated by one supporting dual functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedral cone, every extreme ray \(R\) is exposed: there exists \(y\in C^*\) such that \[R=C\cap y^\perp.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedral convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral specialization of exposure of all polyhedral faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Density of Exposed Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exposed extreme rays are dense among extreme rays of a closed pointed finite-dimensional cone after compact-base normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonzero closed pointed finite-dimensional cone, let \(a\) be strictly positive on \(C\setminus\{0\}\), and set \(B=\{x\in C:a(x)=1\}\). Then \[\operatorname{ext}B\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{exp}B}.\] Moreover, \(b\in B\) is exposed in \(B\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_+b\) is an exposed extreme ray of \(C\). Thus exposed extreme rays are dense among normalized extreme rays.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonzero closed pointed finite-dimensional convex cone.
\(B\) is a compact base cut out by a strictly positive functional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density after normalization by a compact base; not every extreme ray need be exposed.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed extreme ray is an extreme ray isolated exactly as the zero set of one supporting dual functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An extreme ray \(R\) of \(C\) is exposed if it is an exposed face. Equivalently, there exists \(y\in C^*\) such that
\[R=C\cap y^{\perp}=\{x\in C:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}.\]
The functional defined by \(y\) is nonnegative throughout \(C\) and vanishes precisely on \(R\). Every exposed extreme ray is extreme, whereas an extreme ray need not be exposed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ray \(R\) is exposed exactly when \(R=C\cap y^{\perp}\) for some \(y\in C^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme rays that are also exposed faces.

notation.meaning: dual cone of nonnegative linear functionals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedral convex cone, every extreme ray \(R\) of \(C\) is exposed: there exists \(y\in C^*\) such that \[R=C\cap y^\perp.\] More generally, every face of a polyhedral cone is exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral cones have no nonexposed extreme rays.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedral convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Density of Exposed Rays among Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic finite-dimensional Straszewski approximation principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\ne\{0\}\) be a closed pointed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space. On any compact normalized base of \(C\), exposed points are dense in the extreme points. Equivalently, every extreme ray is a limit of exposed extreme rays in the corresponding normalized-base topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional closed pointed cone, exposed extreme rays are dense among all extreme rays, although the two classes need not coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonzero, closed, pointed, convex, and finite-dimensional.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Carathéodory Bound for Extreme-Ray Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every element of a d-dimensional closed pointed cone is a conic combination of at most d extreme-ray generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a nonzero closed pointed convex cone of dimension \(d\), every \(x\in C\) has a representation \[x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i r_i,\qquad m\le d,\quad\lambda_i\ge0,\] where every \(\mathbb R_+r_i\) is an extreme ray of \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonzero closed pointed finite-dimensional convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in C\ \exists m\le d:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i r_i.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite representation bound using the dimension of the cone's span.

notation.meaning: dimension of the cone's linear span

knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness Failure for Extreme-Ray Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real line is a closed nonpointed cone with no extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed convex cone \(C=\mathbb R\) is not pointed and has no extreme rays: each nonzero ray fails the face condition because a point on it can be decomposed using elements of opposite signs.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\mathbb R\), regarded as a cone in itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ has no extreme rays and is not generated by them}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when pointedness is removed.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Failure for Extreme-Ray Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open upper-half-plane cone with the origin adjoined is pointed but has no extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\] is nonzero, convex, and pointed but not closed. It has no extreme rays, because every nonzero element decomposes into two noncollinear elements of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is pointed and convex but has no extreme rays}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when closedness is removed.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Generation Principles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero finite-dimensional closed pointed cone has a compact base cut out by a strictly positive linear functional. That base is the convex hull of its extreme points, whose rays are exactly the extreme rays of the cone; consequently the cone is generated by its extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subseteq V\) be a nonzero closed pointed convex cone. There exists \(a\in V^*\) such that \(a(x)>0\) for every \(x\in C\setminus\{0\}\). For any such \(a\), the set
\[B=\{x\in C:a(x)=1\}\]
is a compact base of \(C\) and satisfies
\[B=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}B).\]
The rays through the points of \(\operatorname{ext}B\) are exactly the extreme rays of \(C\), and
\[C=\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{ext}B).\]
Thus every element of \(C\) is a finite conic combination of vectors lying on extreme rays.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq V\) is a nonzero closed pointed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cone \(C\) is generated by its extreme rays; equivalently, every compact base obtained from a strictly positive functional is the convex hull of its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed pointed cone generation.

notation.meaning: strictly positive functional in the algebraic dual
compact base cut out by the strictly positive functional
set of extreme points of the base

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent Failures Without Closedness or Pointedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Examples showing that neither seed hypothesis can be dropped from the universal generation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pointed nonclosed cone \[C_1=\{0\}\cup\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>|x|\}\] has no extreme rays and therefore is not generated by extreme rays. The closed nonpointed cone \(C_2=\mathbb R\) also has no extreme rays. Thus pointedness alone and closedness alone are each insufficient for the seed generation conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed open cone and a closed line both lack extreme rays, independently demonstrating the closedness and pointedness boundaries of the generation theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither pointedness without closedness nor closedness without pointedness guarantees generation by extreme rays.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a convex cone and \(B\subseteq K\) is a compact convex base: every \(u\in K\setminus\{0\}\) has a unique representation \(u=\lambda b\) with \(\lambda>0\) and \(b\in B\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The compact-base extreme-generation principle is the finite-dimensional mechanism that converts extreme points of a normalized cross-section into extreme rays of a cone. A base meets every nonzero ray exactly once. A point of the base is extreme precisely when its ray is extreme in the cone. Compact convexity ensures that every base point is a convex combination of extreme base points, and after rescaling this becomes a conic representation of every cone element by extreme-ray generators. The principle therefore specifies both the normalization object and the resulting generation family; it is stronger than merely taking the closure of the extreme-ray hull.

The radial projection \(K\setminus\{0\}\to B\) identifies extreme rays with extreme points of \(B\).
special_cases_latex: A pointed closed cone in finite dimensions has a compact base after choosing a strictly positive dual functional.
For a finitely generated cone, a minimal nonredundant generating family contains one representative from each extreme ray.
immediate_consequences_latex: A cone with a compact base is closed.

children.title: Minimal-Face Localization
children.top_down_role: Smallest facial strata containing points, subsets, or affine sections.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(S\subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets; the definition also applies to points and feasible affine sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{face}_C(S):=\bigcap\{F\in\mathcal F(C):S\subseteq F\}.\] This is the unique face \(F_{\min}\) satisfying \(S\subseteq F_{\min}\) and \(F_{\min}\subseteq F\) for every face \(F\) of \(C\) containing \(S\). For a point \(x\), write \(\operatorname{face}_C(x):=\operatorname{face}_C(\{x\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face of a subset is the intersection of all faces of the ambient convex set that contain that subset. It is therefore the smallest facial stratum in which the subset can be localized. For a point, this gives its minimal face. For an affine section or feasible region, one first takes the subset lying in the cone or convex set and then applies the same intersection. The construction is intrinsic to the ambient facial lattice and does not depend on a chosen inequality representation. Since arbitrary intersections of faces are faces, the localization is itself a face whenever the subset is contained in the ambient set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\) is the meet in \(\mathcal F(C)\) of all faces containing \(S\).
\(\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\operatorname{face}_C(\operatorname{conv}S)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(S=\{x\}\), the construction yields the minimal face of a point.
For an affine space \(A\) with \(C\cap A\neq\varnothing\), \(\operatorname{face}_C(C\cap A)\) is the minimal face containing the section.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(S\subseteq T\subseteq C\), then \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq\operatorname{face}_C(T)\).
If \(S\subseteq F\) for a face \(F\), then localization may be computed inside \(F\).
boundary_notes: The definition is ambient-dependent: the same subset can have different minimal faces in different convex supersets.
If \(S\not\subseteq C\), the localization is undefined under this convention.

notation.meaning: minimal face of the ambient set containing the subset
face lattice of the ambient convex set

children.title: Minimal Face of a Point
children.top_down_role: Facial localization of an individual cone element.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Face of the Origin
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face of the origin is the cone's lineality space and is the zero face exactly for pointed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The minimal face of the origin is the lineality space:
\[\operatorname{face}_K(0)=K\cap(-K)=\operatorname{lin}K.\]
In particular, \(\operatorname{face}_K(0)=\{0\}\) exactly when \(K\) is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{face}_K(0)=\operatorname{lin}K\), and this equals \(\{0\}\) if and only if \(K\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes nonpointed cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Order Representation of the Minimal Face
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone element y lies in the minimal face of x exactly when some positive multiple of x dominates y in the cone order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in K\),
\[\operatorname{face}_K(x)=\{y\in K:\exists\alpha>0\text{ such that }\alpha x-y\in K\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic membership representation valid without pointedness or closedness.

notation.meaning: Minimal face of K containing x.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Face of a Point
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face of a cone element is the intersection of all faces containing it and is the unique smallest such face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex cone \(K\subseteq V\) and a point \(x\in K\), the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(x\) is defined by
\[\operatorname{face}_K(x):=\bigcap\{F:F\unlhd K,\ x\in F\}.\]
It is the unique smallest face of \(K\) containing \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{face}_K(x)=\bigcap\{F:F\unlhd K,\ x\in F\}\) is the unique smallest face of \(K\) containing \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional facial localization inside a convex cone.

notation.meaning: F is a face of K.
Minimal face of K containing x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-Order Representation of the Minimal Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise algebraic membership test for a minimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in K\),
\[\operatorname{face}_K(x)=\{y\in K:\exists\,\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }x-\varepsilon y\in K\}.\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{face}_K(0)=K\cap(-K),\qquad \operatorname{face}_K(tx)=\operatorname{face}_K(x)\quad(t>0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face of a point consists of the cone elements dominated by that point in the cone order; at zero it is the lineality space and it is constant along positive rays.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Representative of a Section
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any relative-interior point of a nonempty convex subset has the same minimal face as the whole subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(S\subseteq K\) is nonempty and convex, then
\[x\in\operatorname{ri}S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{face}_K(x)=\operatorname{face}_K(S).\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to nonempty convex subsets, including affine or conic sections.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of S in its affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Join of Pointwise Minimal Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face of a nonempty subset is the face-lattice join of the minimal faces of its points.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed-Face Duality Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugation gives an inclusion-reversing bijection between exposed faces of a closed cone and its dual; double conjugation exposes the smallest exposed superface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F\in\mathcal E(K)\), set \(F^\triangle=K^*\cap F^\perp\); for \(G\in\mathcal E(K^*)\), set \(G^\triangle=K\cap G^\perp\). Then

Thus conjugation is an inclusion-reversing bijection between \(\mathcal E(K)\) and \(\mathcal E(K^*)\). For an arbitrary face \(F\unlhd K\), \(F^{\triangle\triangle}\) is the smallest exposed face of \(K\) containing \(F\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(\mathcal E(K)\) denotes the exposed faces of \(K\), including \(K\) and \(\{0\}\) when applicable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mapsto F^\triangle\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection from \(\mathcal E(K)\) to \(\mathcal E(K^*)\), with inverse \(G\mapsto G^\triangle\).

The regime therefore separates the universally involutive exposed correspondence from stronger cone classes in which every face participates. A nice cone, also called facially dual complete in some sources, satisfies a stronger closure compatibility between each face and the ambient dual cone: adding the orthogonal complement of the face to the dual cone yields a closed set, equivalently the full ambient dual of the face. These definitions classify cones according to how completely their facial structure is represented by dual certificates. They must not be conflated without an additional theorem specifying when one property implies the other.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Facial Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed finite-dimensional cones, closed dual-plus-orthogonal sums, closed projected duals, and exact face-dual extension are equivalent conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each face \(F\unlhd K\), the following conditions are equivalent:
\[K^*+F^\perp\ \text{is closed},\]
\[\Pi_{\operatorname{span}F}(K^*)\ \text{is closed},\]
\[\Pi_{\operatorname{span}F}(K^*)=F^*.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-induced preorders are translation invariant and preserved by nonnegative linear combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x_i\preceq_K y_i\) and \(\alpha_i\ge0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\preceq_K\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i y_i.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Induced Preorders

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[x\preceq_K y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in K.\]

\[x\preceq_K y\ \text{and}\ y\preceq_K x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in\operatorname{lin}K,\]

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(V\) is a real topological vector space, \(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone, and \(I(K)\subseteq K\) denotes a chosen interior-type set such as \(\operatorname{int}K\), \(\operatorname{ri}K\), \(\operatorname{sri}K\), or \(\operatorname{qri}K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[x\leq_Ky\iff y-x\in K,\qquad x<_Ky\iff y-x\in K\setminus\{0\},\] \[x\ll_Ky\iff y-x\in\operatorname{int}K,\qquad x\ll_{K,I}y\iff y-x\in I(K).\] These are respectively weak, nonzero, topologically strong, and generalized-interior comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic order strength is classified by the portion of the ordering cone in which the displacement lies. Weak comparison allows the boundary and zero. Nonzero comparison excludes equality but may still use boundary directions. Strong comparison requires an interior direction and is the standard strict generalized inequality for a solid cone. In lower-dimensional or infinite-dimensional settings, relative, strong-relative, or quasirelative interiors can replace the ordinary interior, producing explicitly named generalized-interior regimes. The relations are not interchangeable: an interior-based comparison is generally stronger than a nonzero comparison, and ordinary interior may be empty even when generalized interiors are useful.

Relative-strong comparison uses \(y-x\in\operatorname{ri}K\) when order is considered in \(\operatorname{span}K\).

For a lower-dimensional cone, \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\) in \(V\) while \(\operatorname{ri}K\) can be nonempty.

If \(I(K)+K\subseteq I(K)\), then \(x\ll_{K,I}y\leq_Kz\) implies \(x\ll_{K,I}z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Conic Orders
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointed cone, strict conic inequality means a nonzero cone difference. It defines an irreflexive, transitive strict partial order preserved by translations and positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y\in V\), define
\[x\prec_K y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in K\setminus\{0\}.\]
For pointed \(K\), this is equivalently the relation \(x\preceq_K y\) with \(x\ne y\). It is an irreflexive, transitive strict partial order and satisfies
\[x\prec_K y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x+z\prec_K y+z\]
for every \(z\in V\), as well as
\[x\prec_K y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha x\prec_K\alpha y\]
for every \(\alpha>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior replacement for strong comparison when a cone has empty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(L=K\cap(-K)\), and define \(x\ll_K^{\mathrm{ri}}y\) by \(y-x\in\operatorname{ri}K\). This relation is translation-invariant and transitive, and it is invariant under adding elements of \(L\) to either argument. Hence it induces the relative-interior relation of the pointed quotient cone \(K/L\) on \(V/L\). If \(K\neq L\), the induced relation is irreflexive and remains nonempty even when \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior yields a strong comparison for lower-dimensional cones and becomes an irreflexive relation after quotienting out lineality, unless the cone is a subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty finite-dimensional convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generating, normal, and topologically closed ordered spaces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \((V,\|\cdot\|)\) is a normed real vector space, \(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone, and \(x\leq_Ky\iff y-x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normed ordered vector spaces; generating, normal, and closed-order properties are recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[K\text{ is generating}\iff K-K=V.\] \[K\text{ is normal}\iff \exists c>0\ \forall x,y\in V:\quad 0\leq_Ky\leq_Kx\Longrightarrow\|y\|\leq c\|x\|.\] The order is closed when \(K\) is closed, equivalently its graph \(\{(x,y):x\leq_Ky\}\) is closed in \(V\times V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordered normed space is controlled by several independent cone properties. A generating cone permits every vector to be written as a difference of positive vectors, giving order decomposability. A normal cone makes order intervals norm bounded in a uniform way: vectors between zero and a positive upper bound cannot have arbitrarily larger norm than that bound. A closed cone gives a topologically closed order relation, so inequalities persist under limits. Pointedness may additionally be imposed to obtain a partial order, but it is distinct from generating and normal behavior outside specialized finite-dimensional settings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(V,K)\text{ is a closed generating normal ordered normed space}\iff K-K=V,\ K\text{ is closed, and }\exists c>0:\ 0\leq_Ky\leq_Kx\Rightarrow\|y\|\leq c\|x\|.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Normality means every order interval \([0,x]_K=K\cap(x-K)\) lies in the norm ball of radius \(c\|x\|\).
Closedness of \(K\) is equivalent to sequential order stability in finite-dimensional or metrizable settings.
special_cases_latex: \(\mathbb R_+^n\) is pointed, generating, normal, and closed for every norm.
A cone may be pointed but fail to generate the ambient space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Generating cones support positive-minus-positive decompositions.
For a closed order, limits of ordered pairs remain ordered.
boundary_notes: The constant in normality depends on the chosen norm.
Infinite-dimensional duality between normal and generating cones requires additional topological hypotheses.

set of differences of positive vectors
