assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\sim_K y\iff \exists T\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\text{ such that }y=Tx\) partitions \(\partial K\) into boundary orbit classes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary classes are defined by the full linear automorphism group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y\in\partial K\), define
\[
x\sim_K y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{there exists }T\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\text{ with }y=Tx.
\]
This equivalence relation partitions \(\partial K\) into boundary orbit classes \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)x\). Each class is invariant under every cone automorphism, although distinct classes may have incident closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two boundary points have the same boundary orbit class when a cone automorphism maps one to the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Orbit Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit-equivalence definition fits the boundary-orbit leaf, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariants shared by boundary points in the same automorphism orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and let \(F_K(x)\) denote the unique minimal face of \(K\) containing \(x\). If \(y=Tx\) for some \(T\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\), then
\[
F_K(y)=T(F_K(x)).
\]
Hence orbit-equivalent boundary points have minimal faces of the same dimension and the same facial-lattice type. These invariants are necessary but need not be sufficient for two boundary points to lie in the same orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An automorphism carries the minimal face of a boundary point to the minimal face of its image, so minimal-face geometry is invariant along boundary orbits.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space.

notation.meaning: Minimal face of K containing x.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial Invariants of Boundary Orbits
Component Ranks for Reducible Symmetric Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a reducible symmetric cone, component-rank data up to permutations of isomorphic factors classify orbits; total rank alone may not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[K=K^{(1)}\times\cdots\times K^{(m)}\] be a product of irreducible symmetric cones, with permutations allowed among linearly isomorphic factors. Two elements \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) and \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) lie in the same \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)\)-orbit exactly when their componentwise Jordan-rank tuples agree after such a permutation. Therefore equality of total Jordan rank \[\sum_i\operatorname{rank}(x_i)=\sum_i\operatorname{rank}(y_i)\] is not sufficient in general for orbit equivalence.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite product of irreducible symmetric cones.
Factor permutations are restricted to linearly isomorphic factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Orbit equivalence is classified by component-rank tuples up to admissible factor permutations, not generally by total rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reducible-product extension and limitation of scalar-rank orbit classification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total Rank Does Not Classify Reducible Symmetric Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for extending the irreducible rank-classification statement to products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a product of irreducible symmetric cones, component ranks classify product-group orbits, and the full automorphism group additionally identifies permutations of isomorphic factors. Total rank alone can fail: in \(\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb S_+^2\), elements with component ranks \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) have equal total rank but are not automorphism-equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For reducible symmetric cones, component ranks up to permutations of isomorphic factors are needed; total rank can be insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite product of irreducible symmetric cones.
review_flags: The refinement uses the canonical decomposition into irreducible symmetric factors; isomorphic factors may be permuted.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Rank Does Not Classify Reducible Symmetric Cones

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-two symmetric-cone specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Lorentz cone \(L_n\), the Jordan-rank strata are \(\{0\}\), \(\partial L_n\setminus\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname{int}L_n\), of ranks \(0,1,2\), respectively. Each is a single orbit under \(\operatorname{Aut}(L_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lorentz cone has three automorphism orbits: zero, the nonzero boundary, and the interior.
assumptions_latex: \(L_n\) is a Lorentz cone of rank two.
knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz-Cone Rank Orbits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical matrix realization of rank-stratified automorphism orbits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), congruence maps \(X\mapsto AXA^{\mathsf T}\), with \(A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb R)\), act transitively on each fixed-rank stratum. Therefore \(X,Y\in\mathbb S_+^n\) lie in the same cone-automorphism orbit exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}X=\operatorname{rank}Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-semidefinite matrices are automorphism-equivalent exactly when they have the same matrix rank.

notation.meaning: Cone of real positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Rank Orbits

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is an irreducible symmetric cone realized as the cone of squares of a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra \(V\) of rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-orbit correspondence for irreducible symmetric cones, not arbitrary homogeneous cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(s\in\{0,\ldots,r\}\), the rank stratum
\[
K_s:=\{x\in K:\operatorname{rank}(x)=s\}
\]
is a single orbit under \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)\). Hence two elements \(x,y\in K\) lie in the same automorphism orbit if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(x)=\operatorname{rank}(y)\). In particular, \(K_r=\operatorname{int}K\), while the strata with \(s<r\) lie on the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an irreducible symmetric cone, two elements are automorphism-equivalent exactly when they have the same Jordan rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Stratified Orbits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-orbit property is appropriately restricted to irreducible symmetric cones and fits the leaf, but it requires a cited Euclidean-Jordan-algebra source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Tuples for Reducible Symmetric Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp extension and limitation of scalar-rank orbit classification for product symmetric cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K=K^{(1)}\times\cdots\times K^{(m)}
\]
be a product of irreducible symmetric cones, and group mutually isomorphic factors together. Under \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)\), two elements \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) and \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) lie in the same orbit exactly when their componentwise Jordan-rank tuples agree up to permutations of isomorphic factors. Consequently, equality of the total ranks
\[
\sum_i\operatorname{rank}(x_i)=\sum_i\operatorname{rank}(y_i)
\]
need not imply orbit equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For reducible symmetric cones, automorphism orbits are classified by component rank tuples, not generally by total rank alone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite product of irreducible symmetric cones.
Permutations are allowed only among mutually isomorphic factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\sim y\) iff their component-rank tuples agree up to permutations of isomorphic factors; total rank alone may be insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Tuples for Reducible Symmetric Cones
Orbit-Closure Incidence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of a rank-s orbit consists exactly of all strata having rank at most s.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(s\in\{0,\ldots,r\}\), the closure of the rank-\(s\) orbit satisfies
\[
\overline{K_s}=\bigcup_{j=0}^{s}K_j.
\]
Equivalently, a rank-\(j\) orbit is incident to the closure of a rank-\(s\) orbit exactly when \(j\leq s\). Thus orbit degeneration can decrease Jordan rank but cannot increase it.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is an irreducible symmetric cone of rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure incidence among rank orbits of an irreducible symmetric cone.

notation.meaning: Topological closure of the rank-s orbit

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The closure-incidence formula is correctly scoped to rank strata of an irreducible symmetric cone, but no supporting source is provided.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General incidence relation for automorphism orbits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For automorphism orbits \(\mathcal O,\mathcal O'\subseteq K\), define \(\mathcal O'\preceq\mathcal O\) when \(\mathcal O'\subseteq\overline{\mathcal O}\). This relation is reflexive and transitive and records which orbit types occur as limits of another orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orbit-closure incidence places one orbit below another when it lies in the other's closure.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
review_flags: Only a preorder is asserted in full generality; antisymmetry on orbit classes requires additional separation or regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbit-Closure Preorder

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Orbit Closures Remain on the Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence separation between boundary and interior orbits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\partial K\), then \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)x\subseteq\partial K\). Since every topological boundary is closed, \(\overline{\operatorname{Aut}(K)x}\subseteq\partial K\). Thus a boundary orbit cannot have an interior orbit in its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of a boundary orbit remains on the boundary and cannot enter the interior.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
review_flags: Closedness of K is not required because \(\partial K\) is closed for every subset K.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Orbit Closures Remain on the Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Is Incident to Every Cone Orbit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal minimal degeneration caused by scalar automorphisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in K\), \(tI\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\) for \(t>0\), and \(tx\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Hence \(\{0\}\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{Aut}(K)x}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cone orbit degenerates to the zero orbit through positive scalar dilations.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Is Incident to Every Cone Orbit

children.title: Homogeneous Cones
children.top_down_role: Cones whose automorphisms act transitively on their interiors.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[E\text{ is finite-dimensional},\qquad K\subseteq E\text{ is closed, convex, pointed, and has nonempty interior}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper cones and transitivity under their full linear automorphism groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is homogeneous if its automorphism group acts transitively on its interior: \[\forall x,y\in\operatorname{int}K\ \exists g\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\quad gx=y.\] Equivalently, after choosing any base point \(e\in\operatorname{int}K\), \[\operatorname{int}K=\operatorname{Aut}(K)\cdot e.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper cone is homogeneous when any interior point can be carried to any other interior point by an invertible linear transformation preserving the cone. Equivalently, the interior is a single orbit of the automorphism group. Homogeneity concerns only the interior action and does not itself impose self-duality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For some, and hence every, \(e\in\operatorname{int}K\), the orbit map \(g\mapsto ge\) is surjective onto \(\operatorname{int}K\).
The interior is isomorphic as a homogeneous space to \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)/\operatorname{Aut}(K)_e\).
special_cases_latex: \(\mathbb R_+^n\), Lorentz cones, and \(\mathbb S_+^n\) are homogeneous.
A direct product \(K_1\times K_2\) of homogeneous cones is homogeneous.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every automorphism-invariant function on \(\operatorname{int}K\) is constant.
All interior points have conjugate stabilizer subgroups.
A homogeneous self-dual cone is symmetric.
boundary_notes: Transitivity is required only on \(\operatorname{int}K\), not on the whole cone; the origin and boundary belong to other orbits.
Homogeneity does not imply self-duality.
Some authors work with open homogeneous cones; here \(K\) is closed and the action is on its open interior.

notation.meaning: Subgroup fixing the interior base point \(e\).

children.title: Irreducible Homogeneous Cones
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous cone factors without nontrivial product decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Invariance of Irreducibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a regular homogeneous cone is homogeneous, and dualization preserves irreducibility in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual cone \(K^*\) is a regular homogeneous cone. Dualization carries a product decomposition of \(K\) to a product decomposition of \(K^*\), and biduality gives the converse. Consequently,
\[
K\text{ is irreducible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^*\text{ is irreducible}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a regular homogeneous cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*\) is homogeneous, and \(K\) is irreducible if and only if \(K^*\) is irreducible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual invariance of product irreducibility for finite-dimensional regular homogeneous cones.

notation.meaning: Dual cone with respect to the specified inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Factor Decomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-dimensional regular homogeneous cone has an irreducible product decomposition, unique up to permutation and cone isomorphism of factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There are irreducible regular homogeneous cones \(K_1,\ldots,K_m\) such that
\[
K\cong K_1\times\cdots\times K_m.
\]
If also \(K\cong L_1\times\cdots\times L_n\) with all \(L_j\) irreducible, then \(m=n\) and, after a permutation, \(K_i\cong L_i\) for every \(i\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a regular homogeneous cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is linearly isomorphic to a finite product of irreducible regular homogeneous cones, uniquely up to permutation and linear cone isomorphism of the factors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional decomposition into product-indecomposable homogeneous factors.

notation.meaning: Linear cone isomorphism to a Cartesian product.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of the finite product decomposition into irreducible homogeneous factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite-dimensional regular homogeneous cone \(K\) is linearly isomorphic to a finite product \[K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\] of irreducible regular homogeneous cones. If also \(K\cong L_1\times\cdots\times L_s\) with all \(L_j\) irreducible, then \(r=s\) and, after a permutation of indices, \(K_i\cong L_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular homogeneous cone decomposes into irreducible homogeneous factors, uniquely up to factor order and linear isomorphism.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional closed, pointed, solid homogeneous convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) has a finite irreducible product factorization unique up to permutation and linear cone isomorphism.

notation.meaning: A linear isomorphism carries one cone onto the other

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The homogeneous cone \(K\) is irreducible if there do not exist nonzero vector spaces \(E_1,E_2\), proper cones \(K_i\subseteq E_i\), and a linear isomorphism \(T:E\to E_1\oplus E_2\) such that \[T(K)=K_1\times K_2.\] If such data exist, \(K\) is reducible and \(K_1,K_2\) are product factors.

Irreducibility is invariant under linear cone isomorphism and identifies the atomic factors in product decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Vinberg Cone as a Homogeneous Nonsymmetric Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The five-dimensional sparse positive-semidefinite Vinberg cone is homogeneous but cannot be made self-dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[\mathcal V=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&0&u\\0&b&v\\u&v&c\end{pmatrix}:a,b,c,u,v\in\mathbb R\right\},\qquad \Omega=\mathcal V\cap\mathbb S_{++}^3.\] Equivalently, \[\Omega=\left\{(a,b,c,u,v):a>0,\ b>0,\ c>\frac{u^2}{a}+\frac{v^2}{b}\right\}.\] The automorphism group of \(K=\overline\Omega\) acts transitively on \(\operatorname{int}K=\Omega\), but no inner product makes \(K\) self-dual. Thus \(K\) is a homogeneous nonsymmetric cone, commonly called the five-dimensional Vinberg cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S_{++}^3\) is the cone of positive-definite real symmetric matrices.
Homogeneity of \(K\) refers to transitivity on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional example separating homogeneity from symmetry.

notation.meaning: Interior of the five-dimensional Vinberg cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality Preserves Homogeneous Nonsymmetry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a homogeneous cone is homogeneous, and symmetry or nonsymmetry is preserved by duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\) is a regular homogeneous cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space, then \(K^*\) is homogeneous. Moreover, \(K\) is symmetric if and only if \(K^*\) is symmetric. Consequently, \[K\text{ is homogeneous nonsymmetric}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^*\text{ is homogeneous nonsymmetric}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a regular homogeneous cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*\) is homogeneous, and \(K\) is nonsymmetric iff \(K^*\) is nonsymmetric.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality behavior of finite-dimensional regular homogeneous cones.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual cone under the chosen inner product.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[E\text{ is finite-dimensional and }K\subseteq E\text{ is a proper cone}.\] For an inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_Q\), write \(K^{*Q}:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle_Q\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic nonsymmetry: the cone is homogeneous but cannot be made self-dual by choosing a positive-definite inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A homogeneous nonsymmetric cone is a proper cone \(K\) satisfying \[\operatorname{Aut}(K)\curvearrowright\operatorname{int}K\text{ transitively}\] but for which no positive-definite inner product makes it self-dual: \[K\ne K^{*Q}\qquad\text{for every positive-definite inner product }\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_Q.\] Equivalently, \(K\) is homogeneous and is not linearly isomorphic to a symmetric cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous nonsymmetric cone has an automorphism group transitive on its interior, but it lacks a compatible self-duality. Compatibility is quantified over positive-definite inner products: there is no such inner product for which the cone equals its dual. Thus homogeneity alone does not place the cone in the symmetric-cone class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\text{ homogeneous nonsymmetric}\iff K\text{ homogeneous and }\nexists Q\succ0\text{ with }K=K^{*Q}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: After fixing a reference inner product and identifying positive-definite inner products with positive-definite operators \(Q\), compatible self-duality would mean \(QK=K^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Positive Square Root
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive Jordan element has a unique positive square root, and interior points have invertible square roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in K\), there exists a unique \(y\in K\) such that \(y\circ y=x\). If \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i c_i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\), then
\[
x^{1/2}=\sum_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\,c_i.
\]
Moreover, \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) exactly when \(x^{1/2}\) is Jordan-invertible.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic square-root property of the cone of squares.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Representation Homogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic representations of invertible Jordan elements are cone automorphisms and explicitly establish interior homogeneity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(a\in V\), define
\[
P(a)=2L(a)^2-L(a^2),\qquad L(a)z=a\circ z.
\]
If \(a\) is Jordan-invertible, then \(P(a)\) is a linear automorphism of \(K\), with inverse \(P(a^{-1})\), and \(P(a)e=a^2\). Consequently, for every \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\), \(P(x^{1/2})e=x\).
assumptions_latex: \(a\) is invertible in the Euclidean Jordan algebra \(V\).

x\in\operatorname{int}K
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad

\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=y^2\text{ for some Jordan-invertible }y\in V.

knowledge_statements.title: Trace, Determinant, and Invertibility from the Spectrum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jordan trace, determinant and inverse are obtained by summing, multiplying and reciprocating eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i c_i\),
\[
\operatorname{tr}_J(x)=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i,
\qquad
\det_J(x)=\prod_{i=1}^r\lambda_i.
\]
The element \(x\) is Jordan-invertible exactly when every \(\lambda_i\ne0\), in which case \(x^{-1}=\sum_i\lambda_i^{-1}c_i\).
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frame-independent spectral invariants.

knowledge_statements.title: Jordan Functional Calculus and Spectral Idempotents
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar functions act on Jordan eigenvalues, and distinct-eigenvalue idempotents are uniquely recoverable as polynomials in the element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i c_i\) and \(f\) is defined on the spectrum of \(x\), set
\[
f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^r f(\lambda_i)c_i.
\]
This is independent of the Jordan frame refining the eigenspaces. For distinct eigenvalues \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\), the aggregate spectral idempotents are uniquely determined by
\[
e_j=\prod_{\ell\ne j}\frac{x-\mu_\ell e}{\mu_j-\mu_\ell},
\qquad x=\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_j e_j.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is defined on the finite spectrum of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_i f(\lambda_i)c_i\) is independent of frame refinements.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frame-independent functional calculus generated by the spectral theorem.

notation.meaning: Aggregate spectral idempotent for the distinct eigenvalue \(\mu_j\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical projection formula supplied by Jordan spectral decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i c_i\), define
\[
x_+=\sum_i\max\{\lambda_i,0\}c_i,
\qquad
x_-=\sum_i\max\{-\lambda_i,0\}c_i.
\]
Then \(x=x_+-x_-\), \(x_+,x_-\in K\), \(\langle x_+,x_-\rangle=0\), and
\[
\Pi_K(x)=x_+,
\]
where \(K\) is the cone of squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clipping negative Jordan eigenvalues to zero gives the metric projection onto the cone of squares and its orthogonal positive-negative decomposition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral organization of the cone interior, boundary, and rank strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in K\),
\[
x\in\operatorname{int}K\iff\operatorname{rank}(x)=r,
\qquad
x\in\partial K\iff\operatorname{rank}(x)<r.
\]
On \(K\), the Jordan rank is the number of strictly positive eigenvalues, so
\[
\{x\in K:\operatorname{rank}(x)=k\},\qquad k=0,\ldots,r,
\]
are the spectral rank strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the square cone, full rank characterizes the interior and deficient rank characterizes the boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.title: Rank and Boundary Stratification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial and continuous scalar functional calculus induced by a Jordan frame.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i c_i\) is a Jordan spectral decomposition, then for every real polynomial \(q\),
\[
q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^r q(\lambda_i)c_i.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{tr}x=\sum_i\lambda_i,
\qquad
\det x=\prod_i\lambda_i.
\]
A continuous scalar function on the spectrum similarly defines \(f(x)=\sum_i f(\lambda_i)c_i\), independently of frame choices within repeated eigenspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jordan spectral decomposition supports functional calculus, with trace and determinant equal to the sum and product of eigenvalues.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical families of irreducible symmetric cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\), let \(\operatorname{Herm}_n(\mathbb F)\) be the real vector space of Hermitian matrices over \(\mathbb F\), and let \(\mathcal L_m:=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{m-1}:t\ge\|u\|_2\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The nonexceptional irreducible symmetric-cone series: three Hermitian matrix series and the spin-factor or Lorentz series, modulo low-dimensional coincidences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical irreducible symmetric-cone family consists, up to linear isomorphism, of \[\operatorname{Herm}_n(\mathbb F)_+:=\{X\in\operatorname{Herm}_n(\mathbb F):X\succeq0\},\qquad \mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\},\] together with the Lorentz cones \[\mathcal L_m:=\{(t,u):t\ge\|u\|_2\}.\] These are the cones of squares of the simple special Euclidean Jordan algebras of Hermitian matrices and of the simple spin factors. Parameters are restricted to values for which the cone is irreducible, with duplicate low-dimensional isomorphism classes counted only once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical irreducible symmetric cones are the positive-semidefinite Hermitian matrix cones over \(\mathbb R\), \(\mathbb C\), and \(\mathbb H\), together with Lorentz cones arising from spin factors. They are called classical to distinguish them from the exceptional octonionic cone. Each is homogeneous, self-dual under its trace or standard Euclidean inner product, and irreducible in the nondegenerate parameter range.
equivalent_formulations_latex: These are the cones of squares of all simple Euclidean Jordan algebras except the exceptional Albert algebra.
For the matrix families, \(X\in\operatorname{Herm}_n(\mathbb F)_+\) if and only if every spectral eigenvalue of \(X\) is nonnegative.
special_cases_latex: \(\operatorname{Herm}_n(\mathbb R)_+=\mathbb S_+^n\).
The spin-factor cone is linearly represented by \(\mathcal L_m\).
The ray and certain low-dimensional Lorentz or matrix cones exhibit standard isomorphisms and should not be treated as new independent classes.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite products of classical irreducible cones are symmetric but generally reducible.
The exceptional cone \(\operatorname{Herm}_3(\mathbb O)_+\) is not a member of this classical family.
Each classical member has a Jordan spectral decomposition and a rank determined by its Jordan algebra.
boundary_notes: “Classical” is a classification label, not a claim that every member is an ordinary real symmetric-matrix cone.
Quaternionic Hermitian spaces are treated as real vector spaces.
The exact minimum parameters depend on whether rays and low-dimensional isomorphic cases are listed separately.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Repeated-squaring evaluation and gradient of a trace-power objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The quotient-form gradient requires a separate zero-matrix case because its displayed denominator then vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let p=2^k with k\in\mathbb{N}, let A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb{S}^n, and set A(y)=\sum_{j=1}^m y^{(j)}A_j. At any y with A(y)\succeq0, define X_0=A(y), Y_0=I_n, and, for r=1,\ldots,k, X_r=X_{r-1}^2 and Y_r=Y_{r-1}X_{r-1}. Then X_k=A(y)^p and Y_k=A(y)^{p-1}. Consequently, for f_p(y)=\tfrac12\langle A(y)^p,I_n\rangle_M^{2/p}, one has f_p(y)=\tfrac12\langle X_k,I_n\rangle_M^{2/p}. If \langle X_k,I_n\rangle_M>0, then for every i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, \nabla f_p(y)^{(i)}=\frac{2f_p(y)}{\langle X_k,I_n\rangle_M}\langle Y_k,A_i\rangle_M. If A(y)=0, each partial derivative is 0, while the quotient expression itself is undefined and must be interpreted through this separate boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-semidefinite symmetric matrix pencil and a power p that is a power of two, repeated squaring computes both the pth power and the preceding power. These matrices evaluate the squared trace-power objective and its partial derivatives. Away from the zero matrix the gradient has the stated quotient form; at the zero matrix the gradient is zero and the quotient must not be used literally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_k=A(y)^p,\quad Y_k=A(y)^{p-1},\quad f_p(y)=\tfrac12\langle X_k,I_n\rangle_M^{2/p},\quad \partial_i f_p(y)=\frac{2f_p(y)}{\langle X_k,I_n\rangle_M}\langle Y_k,A_i\rangle_M\ \text{when }A(y)\ne0,\quad \nabla f_p(y)=0\ \text{when }A(y)=0.

knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz Spectral Decomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lorentz-cone element has eigenvalues t plus and minus the norm of its vector component, whose product is the Lorentz determinant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x=(t,u)\) with \(u\ne0\), let
\[
c_\pm=\tfrac12(1,\pm u/\|u\|_2),\qquad \lambda_\pm=t\pm\|u\|_2.
\]
Then \(c_+,c_-\) form a Jordan frame and \(x=\lambda_+c_++\lambda_-c_-\). Hence \(x\in L_{d+1}\) exactly when \(\lambda_\pm\ge0\), and \(\det_J(x)=t^2-\|u\|_2^2\). For \(u=0\), the eigenvalues both equal \(t\).

knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz Cone Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lorentz cone consists of scalar-vector pairs whose scalar dominates the vector norm; it is self-dual, homogeneous, irreducible, and rank two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\ge2\), the Lorentz cone is
\[
L_{d+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d:t\ge\|u\|_2\}.
\]
Under the Euclidean inner product it is closed, pointed, self-dual, and homogeneous, hence symmetric. It is the cone of squares of the spin-factor Jordan algebra with product \((t,u)\circ(s,v)=(ts+\langle u,v\rangle,\,tv+su)\). For \(d\ge2\), it is irreducible and has Jordan rank \(2\). Its interior is characterized by \(t>\|u\|_2\), and every nonzero boundary point satisfies \(t=\|u\|_2\) and generates an extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{d+1}\) is an irreducible symmetric cone of Jordan rank \(2\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exceptional-specific cubic invariant and boundary stratification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{Herm}_3(\mathbb O)\), let \(\lambda_1(x),\lambda_2(x),\lambda_3(x)\) be its Jordan eigenvalues. Then \(\det x=\prod_{i=1}^3\lambda_i(x)\), and

\operatorname{int}K_{\mathrm{exc}}=\{x\in K_{\mathrm{exc}}:\det x>0\},\qquad
\partial K_{\mathrm{exc}}=\{x\in K_{\mathrm{exc}}:\det x=0\}.
\]
The nonzero boundary consists of the Jordan-rank-one and Jordan-rank-two strata.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exceptional symmetric cone of the Albert algebra
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb O\) be the real octonion algebra and let \(\mathfrak A=H_3(\mathbb O)\) be the \(27\)-dimensional real vector space of \(3\times3\) Hermitian octonionic matrices, equipped with the Jordan product \(X\circ Y=(XY+YX)/2\), identity \(e\), and trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan-algebra definition of the unique exceptional irreducible symmetric-cone family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exceptional symmetric cone is the cone of Jordan squares \[K_{\mathrm{exc}}:=\mathfrak A_+=\{Y\circ Y:Y\in\mathfrak A\}.\] Equivalently, if \(X=\sum_{i=1}^3\lambda_i c_i\) is a spectral decomposition relative to a Jordan frame \((c_1,c_2,c_3)\), then \[X\in K_{\mathrm{exc}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda_i\geq0\ \text{for }i=1,2,3.\] Thus \(K_{\mathrm{exc}}\) is a rank-three symmetric cone in the exceptional, nonrepresentable Albert algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exceptional symmetric cone is the cone of all Jordan squares in the 27-dimensional Albert algebra of 3-by-3 Hermitian octonionic matrices. An element belongs to it exactly when all three Jordan eigenvalues are nonnegative. Its ambient Euclidean Jordan algebra has rank three and is exceptional because its Jordan product is not induced by an associative algebra representation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K_{\mathrm{exc}}\) is the symmetric cone associated with the Albert algebra under the cone-of-squares correspondence.
\(X\in K_{\mathrm{exc}}\) if and only if its Jordan spectral decomposition has nonnegative coefficients.
special_cases_latex: The algebra has dimension \(27\) and rank \(3\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\operatorname{int}K_{\mathrm{exc}}=\{X:\lambda_i(X)>0\text{ for all }i\}.\)
The boundary consists of elements having at least one zero eigenvalue.
boundary_notes: This definition does not use ordinary associative matrix positivity; octonionic matrix multiplication is nonassociative.
The real, complex, and quaternionic positive-semidefinite cones belong to the classical families and are not exceptional.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-spectral facial stratification of a symmetric cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\), let \(K=\{x^2:x\in V\}\), and write \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i(x)c_i\) in a Jordan frame.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric cones; the strata use Jordan rank and the support idempotent of each positive element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in K\), define \(\operatorname{supp}(x):=\sum_{\lambda_i(x)>0}c_i\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(x):=\#\{i:\lambda_i(x)>0\}\). The rank-spectral facial stratification is the disjoint partition \[K=\bigsqcup_{k=0}^r\mathcal S_k,\qquad \mathcal S_k:=\{x\in K:\operatorname{rank}(x)=k\},\] refined by support idempotents as \[\mathcal S_k=\bigsqcup_{\substack{c^2=c\\ \operatorname{rank}(c)=k}}\operatorname{ri}F_c,\qquad F_c:=K\cap V(c,1),\] where \(V(c,1)=\{z:c\circ z=z\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank-spectral facial stratification partitions a symmetric cone by the number of positive Jordan eigenvalues. It is refined by support: each positive element has a support idempotent obtained by summing the primitive idempotents corresponding to its positive eigenvalues, and it lies in the relative interior of the face supported by that idempotent. Rank zero is the vertex, while rank equal to the algebra rank is the cone interior.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Two elements belong to the same support stratum precisely when their minimal faces coincide.
The rank of a stratum is the rank of its support idempotent.
special_cases_latex: \(\mathcal S_0=\{0\}\) and \(\mathcal S_r=\operatorname{int}K\).
For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), the strata are positive-semidefinite matrices of fixed matrix rank, refined by their range subspaces.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(x\in K\) belongs to exactly one relative interior \(\operatorname{ri}F_c\).
If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_c\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(x)=\operatorname{rank}(c)\).
boundary_notes: Rank alone need not identify a face; elements of equal rank may have different support idempotents.
The construction uses the spectral and facial structure of symmetric cones, not arbitrary closed convex cones.

children.title: Cone Rank
children.top_down_role: Algebraic rank attached to elements of symmetric and related cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Monotonicity and Invariance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank on a symmetric cone is order-monotone, obeys the standard sum bounds, and is invariant under positive scaling and cone automorphisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y\in K\),
\[
0\preceq_K x\preceq_K y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rank}(x)\le\operatorname{rank}(y),
\]
and
\[
\max\{\operatorname{rank}(x),\operatorname{rank}(y)\}
\le \operatorname{rank}(x+y)
\le \operatorname{rank}(x)+\operatorname{rank}(y).
\]
For every \(\alpha>0\) and \(g\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\),
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\alpha x)=\operatorname{rank}(x),\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(gx)=\operatorname{rank}(x).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the cone of squares of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank is order-monotone, satisfies \(\max\{\operatorname{rank}x,\operatorname{rank}y\}\le\operatorname{rank}(x+y)\le\operatorname{rank}x+\operatorname{rank}y\), and is invariant under positive scaling and cone automorphisms.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic structural laws for algebraic rank on positive elements of a symmetric cone.

notation.meaning: Order induced by the symmetric cone.
Linear automorphism group of the cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact tests for rank deficiency and full rank in a symmetric cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) have rank \(r\), let \(K\) be its cone of squares, and define the Jordan determinant by \(\det(x)=\prod_{i=1}^r\lambda_i(x)\). For \(x\in K\),
\[
\operatorname{rank}(x)=r
\iff \lambda_i(x)>0\ \text{for all }i
\iff \det(x)>0
\iff x\in\operatorname{int}K.
\]
Moreover, \(x=0\) exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}(x)=0\), and a nonzero \(x\in K\) lies on \(\partial K\) exactly when \(1\le\operatorname{rank}(x)<r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone element is full rank exactly when its Jordan determinant is positive and it is interior; positive rank deficiency exactly characterizes the nonzero boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\).

notation.meaning: Jordan determinant, equal to the product of the Jordan eigenvalues.
Rank of the Euclidean Jordan algebra and its symmetric cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Determinant and Interior Rank Tests

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank calculus for sums of positive elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y\in K\), their support idempotents satisfy \(s(x+y)=s(x)\vee s(y)\). Consequently,
\[
\max\{\operatorname{rank}(x),\operatorname{rank}(y)\}
\le \operatorname{rank}(x+y)
\le \operatorname{rank}(x)+\operatorname{rank}(y).
\]
If \(x\circ y=0\), then their supports are orthogonal and
\[
\operatorname{rank}(x+y)=\operatorname{rank}(x)+\operatorname{rank}(y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank of a sum of positive cone elements lies between the larger summand rank and the sum of ranks, with additivity for orthogonal elements.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the cone of squares of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Sum Rank Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Behavior of algebraic cone rank under cone automorphisms and direct products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(g\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\) for a symmetric cone \(K\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(gx)=\operatorname{rank}(x)\) for every \(x\in K\). If \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\) and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), then
\[
\operatorname{rank}_K(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\operatorname{rank}_{K_j}(x_j),
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(K)=\sum_{j=1}^m\operatorname{rank}(K_j).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone rank is invariant under cone automorphisms and additive across direct-product factors.
assumptions_latex: Direct products carry the product Euclidean Jordan algebra structure.

notation.meaning: Rank of the underlying Euclidean Jordan algebra.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Invariance and Product Additivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jordan rank of an element of a symmetric cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\), let \(K=\{x^2:x\in V\}\), and let \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i c_i\) be a spectral decomposition in a Jordan frame.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic element rank for symmetric cones; it is not the dimension of the ambient cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone rank of \(x\in V\) is \[\operatorname{rank}_K(x):=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}:\lambda_i(x)\neq0\}.\] For \(x\in K\), all eigenvalues are nonnegative, so \[\operatorname{rank}_K(x)=\#\{i:\lambda_i(x)>0\}=r-\operatorname{mult}_0(x).\] Equivalently, it is the rank of the support idempotent \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\sum_{\lambda_i(x)>0}c_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cone rank of an element is the number of its nonzero Jordan eigenvalues, counted with spectral multiplicity. For an element of the symmetric cone, these are exactly its positive eigenvalues. Equivalently, cone rank is the rank of the element's support idempotent or the algebra rank minus the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x\in K\), \(\operatorname{rank}_K(x)=\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{supp}(x))\).
Cone rank equals algebra rank minus corank.
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), cone rank is ordinary matrix rank.
For a Lorentz cone, nonzero boundary elements have rank one and interior elements have rank two.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}_K(x)=r\).
\(\operatorname{rank}_K(x)=0\) if and only if \(x=0\).
boundary_notes: The rank of the cone itself is \(r\); the rank defined here depends on the element \(x\).
Outside \(K\), nonzero eigenvalues may have either sign, but the same Jordan-rank formula remains meaningful.

notation.meaning: multiplicity of zero as a Jordan eigenvalue

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic rank for elements of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every \(x\in V\) has a spectral decomposition
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i(x)c_i
\]
for some Jordan frame \((c_1,\ldots,c_r)\). The cone rank of \(x\) is
\[
\operatorname{rank}(x)=\#\{i:\lambda_i(x)\ne0\}.
\]
This number is independent of the spectral decomposition. For the symmetric cone \(K=\{y\circ y:y\in V\}\), an element \(x\in K\) has nonnegative eigenvalues, so its rank is the number of strictly positive eigenvalues. The rank of \(K\) is \(r=\operatorname{rank}(e)\), where \(e\) is the Jordan identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone rank counts the nonzero Jordan eigenvalues of an element; on the cone, it counts the strictly positive eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Face Lattice and Complementation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The face lattice of a symmetric cone is represented by idempotents: inclusion is idempotent order, complementary idempotents expose faces, and conjugacy sends c to e-c.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The idempotent order and face inclusion agree:
\[
F_c\subseteq F_d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c\le d
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c\circ d=c.
\]
Every face is exposed, with
\[
F_c=\{x\in K:\langle e-c,x\rangle=0\}.
\]
Under the self-dual identification \(K^*=K\),
\[
F_c^{\triangle}=F_{e-c}.
\]
Thus complementation of support idempotents reverses face inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the self-dual cone of squares of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra \(V\) with identity \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Face inclusion corresponds to idempotent order, \(F_c\) is exposed by \(e-c\), and its conjugate face is \(F_{e-c}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order, exposure, and conjugacy of idempotent-supported faces in a symmetric cone.

notation.meaning: Conjugate face in the self-dual cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-dual facial complement formula for symmetric cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the self-dualizing inner product of a Euclidean Jordan algebra, the conjugate face of \(F_c\) is
\[
F_c^\triangle=K\cap F_c^\perp=F_{e-c}.
\]
Consequently every face of \(K\) is exposed, conjugation reverses inclusion, \((F_c^\triangle)^\triangle=F_c\), and
\[
\operatorname{rank}(F_c)+\operatorname{rank}(F_c^\triangle)=\operatorname{rank}(K).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of the face supported by c is the face supported by e−c, so symmetric-cone faces are exposed and have complementary ranks.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the cone of squares of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra with identity \(e\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Faces as Complementary Supports

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order structure of idempotent-indexed symmetric-cone faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For idempotents \(c,d\), write \(c\le d\) when \(c\circ d=c\). For \(F_c=K\cap V(c,1)\),
\[
F_c\subseteq F_d\iff c\le d,
\qquad
F_c\cap F_d=F_{c\wedge d},
\qquad
F_c\vee F_d=F_{c\vee d}.
\]
Thus \(c\mapsto F_c\) is an order isomorphism from the idempotent lattice onto the face lattice of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Containment, intersection, and join of symmetric-cone faces exactly match the order, meet, and join of their support idempotents.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the cone of squares of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_c\subseteq F_d\iff c\le d,\quad F_c\cap F_d=F_{c\wedge d},\quad F_c\vee F_d=F_{c\vee d}.

notation.meaning: Idempotent order defined by c being a sub-idempotent of d.

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Lattice Order by Support Idempotents

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inherited Symmetric-Cone Structure and Face Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jordan-algebra structure of every face, with the dimension formula for simple ambient algebras.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every idempotent \(c\), the Peirce space \(V(c,1)\) is a Euclidean Jordan algebra with identity \(c\), and \(F_c\) is its cone of squares. If the ambient algebra is simple with Peirce constant \(d\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(c)=k\), then
\[
\dim F_c=\dim V(c,1)=k+\frac d2k(k-1).
\]
Hence, in a fixed simple symmetric cone, all faces of rank \(k\) have the same dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face is itself a symmetric cone; in a simple ambient cone, a rank-k face has dimension k+d k(k−1)/2.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the cone of squares of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.
For the dimension formula, the ambient algebra is simple with Peirce constant \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_c\text{ is the cone of squares of }V(c,1),\qquad \dim F_c=k+\frac d2k(k-1)\text{ in the simple case}.

notation.meaning: Common dimension of the off-diagonal Peirce spaces in a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra.
Rank of the supporting idempotent and its face.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face Orbits in a Simple Symmetric Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Automorphism classification of faces by rank in the simple case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a simple symmetric cone of rank \(r\). For each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,r\}\), the automorphism group of \(K\) acts transitively on the faces of rank \(k\). Equivalently, if \(c\) and \(d\) are idempotents with \(\operatorname{rank}(c)=\operatorname{rank}(d)\), then some cone automorphism sends \(F_c\) onto \(F_d\). For reducible symmetric cones, total face rank alone need not determine the orbit because the ranks distributed among nonisomorphic factors are additional invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a simple symmetric cone, faces are automorphically equivalent exactly by rank; in reducible cones, the distribution of rank among factor types also matters.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional simple symmetric cone for the transitivity assertion.

notation.meaning: Face supported by the idempotent c.

knowledge_statements.title: Face Orbits in a Simple Symmetric Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact partition of a symmetric cone by support idempotent and minimal-face rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every idempotent \(c\),
\[
\operatorname{ri}(F_c)=\{x\in K:s(x)=c\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\{x\in K:\operatorname{rank}(x)=k\}
=\bigsqcup_{\operatorname{rank}(c)=k}\operatorname{ri}(F_c).
\]
Rank zero gives \(\{0\}\), rank one gives the relative interiors of the extreme rays, and maximal rank gives \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each support idempotent selects the relative interior of one face, and rank-k elements are exactly the union of the relative interiors of rank-k faces.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the cone of squares of a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.

notation.meaning: Support idempotent formed from the positive spectral components of x.
Relative interior of the face supported by c.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face \(F\unlhd K\) is a rank-\(k\) face if there exists an idempotent \(c\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(c)=k\) such that \[F=F_c:=K\cap V(c,1).\] The rank-\(k\) facial family is \[\mathfrak F_k(K):=\{F_c:c^2=c,\ \operatorname{rank}(c)=k\}.\] Its relative interior is characterized spectrally by \[x\in\operatorname{ri}F_c\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in F_c\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{supp}(x)=c,\] hence every relative-interior point of \(F_c\) has rank \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-k face of a symmetric cone is the cone of squares supported on the Peirce one-eigenspace of a rank-k idempotent. Its relative interior consists exactly of the positive elements whose support equals that idempotent. Consequently the rank of a face is the common Jordan rank of its relative-interior points, although lower-rank points occur on its relative boundary.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A face has rank \(k\) if and only if any, hence every, point in its relative interior has Jordan rank \(k\).
For \(x\in K\), the minimal face containing \(x\) is \(F_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}\).
special_cases_latex: \(\mathfrak F_0(K)=\{\{0\}\}\) and \(\mathfrak F_r(K)=\{K\}\).
For \(\mathbb S_+^n\), a rank-\(k\) face consists of matrices whose ranges lie in a fixed \(k\)-dimensional subspace.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F_d\subseteq F_c\), then the support idempotents satisfy the corresponding idempotent order \(d\leq c\).
The relative boundary of a rank-\(k\) face is the union of its faces of rank strictly below \(k\).
boundary_notes: The set of all cone elements of rank at most \(k\) is generally a union of faces, not one face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every idempotent \(c\in V\), define
\[
F_c=K\cap V(c,1).
\]
Then \(F_c\) is a face of \(K\), every face of \(K\) has this form for a unique idempotent \(c\), and its face rank is \(\operatorname{rank}(F_c)=\operatorname{rank}(c)\). If \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i c_i\in K\), its support idempotent is \(s(x)=\sum_{\lambda_i>0}c_i\), and
\[
\operatorname{face}_K(x)=F_{s(x)},\qquad \operatorname{rank}(F_{s(x)})=\operatorname{rank}(x).
\]
Consequently, rank organizes the boundary into minimal-face strata, while full-rank elements are precisely interior points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Atomic rank-one rays of a symmetric cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a Euclidean Jordan algebra, let \(K=\{x^2:x\in V\}\), and call a nonzero idempotent \(c\) primitive when it cannot be written as a sum of two nonzero idempotents.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-ray atoms in finite-dimensional symmetric cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The atomic rank-one ray associated with a primitive idempotent \(c\) is \[R_c:=\mathbb R_+c=\{\alpha c:\alpha\geq0\}.\] The atomic rank-one ray correspondence is the map \[c\longmapsto R_c.\] Its image is precisely the set of extreme rays of \(K\), and every nonzero \(x\in R_c\) has \(\operatorname{rank}(x)=1\). With the normalization \(c^2=c\), each extreme ray has a unique primitive-idempotent representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each primitive Jordan idempotent determines the ray of its nonnegative scalar multiples. These are exactly the rank-one extreme rays of a symmetric cone. Conversely, normalizing any nonzero generator of an extreme ray to be idempotent yields the unique primitive idempotent associated with that ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{extreme rays of }K\}=\{\mathbb R_+c:c^2=c\text{ and }c\text{ is primitive}\}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: A nonzero \(x\in K\) is atomic if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(x)=1\).
A ray is atomic if and only if its nonzero elements have spectral decompositions with exactly one positive coefficient.
special_cases_latex: For \(\mathbb S_+^n\), the atomic rays are \(\mathbb R_+uu^{\mathsf T}\) with \(u\neq0\).
For \(\mathbb R_+^n\), they are the coordinate rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(x\in K\) is a sum of finitely many mutually orthogonal atomic elements supplied by its spectral decomposition.
The number of nonzero atomic summands in a spectral decomposition equals \(\operatorname{rank}(x)\).
boundary_notes: A rank-one generator is unique only up to positive scaling; idempotent normalization removes that ambiguity.
Extreme points of a normalized base should not be confused with extreme rays of the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Primitive Idempotent Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primitive idempotents are normalized rank-one positive elements, and their nonnegative spans are exactly the extreme rays of a symmetric cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonzero idempotent \(c\in V\) is primitive when it cannot be written as \(c=c_1+c_2\) with nonzero orthogonal idempotents \(c_1\) and \(c_2\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{rank}(c)=1\). The extreme rays of \(K\) are precisely
\[
\{\mathbb R_+c:c\text{ is a primitive idempotent}\}.
\]
More generally, every nonzero rank-one element of \(K\) is a positive scalar multiple of a primitive idempotent, and every such multiple generates the same extreme ray. Thus primitive idempotents are normalized representatives of the atomic rays of \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the cone of squares of a Euclidean Jordan algebra \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rays \(\mathbb R_+c\) with primitive idempotent \(c\) are exactly the extreme rays of \(K\).

Exposure Certificate for a Rank-One Matrix Ray
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complementary orthogonal projector exposes exactly the positive-semidefinite rank-one ray generated by an outer product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
P_v=\frac{vv^*}{v^*v}.
\]
Then \(I-P_v\in K=K^*\), and
\[
\{X\in K:\langle I-P_v,X\rangle=0\}=\mathbb R_+(vv^*).
\]
Thus every rank-one matrix ray is exposed by the complementary orthogonal projector.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\), \(n\ge2\), and \(K=\operatorname{Herm}_n(\mathbb F)_+\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual matrix \(I-P_v\) exposes the extreme ray \(\mathbb R_+(vv^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit exposing functional for an atomic ray of a classical Hermitian positive-semidefinite cone.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal rank-one projector onto the line generated by v.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposing Certificate for a Rank-One PSD Ray
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual matrix certificate showing that every classical rank-one positive-semidefinite ray is exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0\ne v\in\mathbb F^n\), where \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\), and let \(P_v\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F}\{v\}\). With \(Y=I-P_v\succeq0\),
\[
\{X\succeq0:\langle Y,X\rangle=0\}=\mathbb R_+P_v=\mathbb R_+(vv^*),
\]
where the last equality is equality of rays. Thus \(Y\) exposes the rank-one ray generated by \(vv^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complementary orthogonal projection exposes the PSD ray generated by a rank-one outer product.
assumptions_latex: The Hermitian space carries its real trace inner product.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projection onto the one-dimensional subspace generated by v.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb F^n\), the matrix \(vv^*\) is Hermitian positive semidefinite and has matrix rank one. Conversely, every nonzero rank-one element \(X\in K\) admits a factorization \(X=vv^*\) for some nonzero \(v\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{ExtRays}(K)=\{\mathbb R_+(vv^*):v\in\mathbb F^n\setminus\{0\}\}.
\]
Two vectors \(v,w\ne0\) determine the same ray exactly when \(ww^*=\alpha vv^*\) for some \(\alpha>0\); equivalently, \(w=vq\) for some nonzero scalar \(q\in\mathbb F\).

knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Orbits in Product Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a product of irreducible symmetric cones, atomic-ray orbits are indexed by the isomorphism types of the irreducible factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every extreme ray of \(K\) has exactly one nonzero component and is of the form
\[
0\times\cdots\times R_i\times\cdots\times0,
\]
where \(R_i\) is an extreme ray of \(K_i\). Rays supported in factors \(K_i\) and \(K_j\) lie in the same \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)\)-orbit exactly when \(K_i\) and \(K_j\) are linearly isomorphic as cones. Thus the atomic rays form one orbit exactly when all irreducible factors have the same isomorphism type.
assumptions_latex: \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\) is a finite product of irreducible symmetric cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)\)-orbits of atomic rays correspond exactly to the linear cone-isomorphism classes represented among the factors \(K_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of atomic-ray transitivity from irreducible symmetric cones to finite products.

Let \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) be extreme rays of \(K\). There exists \(g\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\) such that \(g(R_1)=R_2\). Equivalently, after realizing \(K\) as the cone of squares of a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra, any two primitive idempotents \(c_1,c_2\) satisfy
\[
g(\mathbb R_+c_1)=\mathbb R_+c_2
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Certificate of Higher-Rank Nonextremality
Order-Interval Characterization of Eigenvalues
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest and largest Jordan eigenvalues are exactly the lower and upper cone-order bounds of an element relative to the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The extreme spectral coordinates are the endpoints of the cone-order interval generated by the identity:
\[
\lambda_{\min}(x)=\max\{t\in\mathbb R:x-te\in K\},
\qquad
\lambda_{\max}(x)=\min\{t\in\mathbb R:te-x\in K\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\lambda_{\min}(x)e\preceq_K x\preceq_K\lambda_{\max}(x)e.
\]
For scalars \(a\le b\),
\[
ae\preceq_K x\preceq_K be
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lambda_i(x)\in[a,b]\text{ for every }i.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a rank-\(r\) Euclidean Jordan algebra with identity \(e\) and cone of squares \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a spectral decomposition \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i(x)c_i\), membership and boundary geometry are determined coordinatewise:
\[
x\in K\iff\lambda_i(x)\ge0\ \text{for all }i,
\]
\[
x\in\operatorname{int}K\iff\lambda_i(x)>0\ \text{for all }i,
\]
and
\[
x\in\partial K\iff\lambda_i(x)\ge0\ \text{for all }i\text{ and }\min_i\lambda_i(x)=0.
\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{tr}_J(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i(x)\), \(\det_J(x)=\prod_i\lambda_i(x)\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(x)\) is the number of nonzero spectral coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jordan eigenvalues give coordinatewise tests for cone membership, interior, and boundary, and determine trace, determinant, and rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension and Genericity of Multiplicity Strata
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra, fixed multiplicity strata are smooth with the stated dimension, and simple spectrum is open and dense.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\) and Peirce constant \(d\). For an ordered composition \(\mathbf m=(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\models r\), the multiplicity stratum satisfies
\[
\dim S_{\mathbf m}=k+\frac d2\left(r^2-\sum_{j=1}^k m_j^2\right).
\]
Each \(S_{\mathbf m}\) is a smooth embedded submanifold. The simple-spectrum stratum \(S_{(1,\ldots,1)}\) is open and dense, and the repeated-spectrum locus is closed with empty interior.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\) with Peirce constant \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim S_{\mathbf m}=k+\frac d2(r^2-\sum_jm_j^2)\), and the simple-spectrum stratum is open and dense.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth-stratum geometry for simple Euclidean Jordan algebras.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb S^2\), both \[X=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\] have multiplicity pattern \((1,1)\), whereas \((X+Y)/2=I/2\) has pattern \((2)\). Hence \(S_{(1,1)}\cap\mathbb S_+^2\) is not convex and is not a face of \(\mathbb S_+^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two simple-spectrum positive-semidefinite matrices can have a repeated-spectrum midpoint, so multiplicity strata are not generally faces.
assumptions_latex: \(V=\mathbb S^2\) with its standard Jordan structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{(1,1)}\cap\mathbb S_+^2\) is not convex and is not a cone face.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity Strata Need Not Be Convex or Facial

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence relation generated by eigenvalue collisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered composition \(\mathbf m=(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\), the closure of \(S_{\mathbf m}\) is the union of the strata whose ordered compositions are obtained from \(\mathbf m\) by repeatedly merging adjacent blocks. Thus only adjacent ordered eigenvalue levels can collide without first passing through another collision stratum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure incidence is the coarsening order obtained by merging adjacent multiplicity blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.
Strata are indexed using increasingly ordered distinct eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{S_{\mathbf m}}=\bigcup_{\mathbf n\preceq\mathbf m}S_{\mathbf n}\), where \(\mathbf n\preceq\mathbf m\) denotes adjacent-block coarsening.

notation.meaning: The ordered composition \(\mathbf n\) is obtained by merging adjacent blocks of \(\mathbf m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Order of Multiplicity Strata

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic stratum and its collision boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \[S_{(1,\ldots,1)}=\{x:\lambda_i(x)\ne\lambda_j(x)\text{ for }i\ne j\}\] is open and dense in \(V\). Its complement is the zero set of \[\Delta(x)=\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_i(x)-\lambda_j(x))^2,\] and therefore consists exactly of elements with an eigenvalue collision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple-spectrum elements form an open dense stratum whose complement is the spectral-discriminant zero set.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{(1,\ldots,1)}\) is open and dense and \(V\setminus S_{(1,\ldots,1)}=\{x:\Delta(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Simple-Spectrum Stratum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension of Multiplicity Strata in a Simple Jordan Algebra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth-stratum dimension for the simple constant-Peirce-degree case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(V\) is simple of rank \(r\) and Peirce degree \(d\), then the stratum with ordered multiplicities \(\mathbf m=(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\) is a smooth embedded submanifold of dimension \[k+\frac d2\left(r^2-\sum_{j=1}^k m_j^2\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra, each multiplicity stratum is smooth and has a dimension determined by its block sizes and Peirce degree.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a simple Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\) and Peirce degree \(d\).

notation.meaning: Peirce degree of the simple Jordan algebra.

review_flags: The formula is restricted to simple Euclidean Jordan algebras; reducible products require componentwise orbit data.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension of Multiplicity Strata in a Simple Jordan Algebra

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic block decomposition at a fixed multiplicity pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\) has distinct eigenvalues \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\), define \[e_j(x)=\prod_{\ell\ne j}\frac{x-\mu_\ell e}{\mu_j-\mu_\ell}\] by Jordan polynomial calculus. The \(e_j(x)\) are uniquely determined pairwise orthogonal idempotents satisfying \[\sum_j e_j(x)=e,\qquad x=\sum_j\mu_j e_j(x),\] and \(\operatorname{rank}e_j(x)\) is the multiplicity of \(\mu_j\). Primitive refinements of a block of rank greater than one need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct eigenvalues determine unique spectral block idempotents, although primitive frames inside repeated blocks may be nonunique.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a unital Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block idempotents are intrinsic and their ranks equal the eigenvalue multiplicities.
review_flags: An authoritative Euclidean-Jordan-algebra locator remains desirable.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Idempotents of Repeated-Eigenvalue Blocks

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a rank-\(r\) Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sets \(S_{\mathbf m}\), indexed by ordered eigenvalue-multiplicity patterns \(\mathbf m\), form a disjoint partition of \(V\).

notation.meaning: Ordered composition of the rank recording multiplicities of increasingly ordered distinct eigenvalues.
Stratum having ordered multiplicity pattern \(\mathbf m\).

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports multiplicity stratification in Euclidean Jordan algebras; authoritative source required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic stratification by ordered equality patterns among Jordan eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbf m=(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\) be an ordered composition of \(r\), meaning that \(m_j\ge1\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^k m_j=r\). Define \(S_{\mathbf m}\subset V\) to consist of the elements having exactly \(k\) distinct Jordan eigenvalues \(\mu_1<\cdots<\mu_k\), where \(\mu_j\) has multiplicity \(m_j\). Then
\[
V=\bigsqcup_{\mathbf m\models r}S_{\mathbf m}.
\]
Each \(S_{\mathbf m}\) is invariant under Jordan algebra automorphisms. Eigenvalue collisions merge adjacent blocks of the ordered multiplicity pattern; within \(K\), an eigenvalue reaching zero can additionally lower cone rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elements are partitioned into strata by the ordered multiplicities of their increasingly ordered distinct Jordan eigenvalues; collisions merge adjacent multiplicity blocks, and reaching zero can lower cone rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Multiplicity Strata

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-separation data of a closed convex cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Define \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle u,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An umbrella definition collecting the projection, polarity, complementarity, and separation objects attached to a closed convex cone in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic metric-separation calculus of \(K\) is the system \[\mathfrak C(K):=(K,K^\circ,P_K,P_{K^\circ},\mathcal M_K,\mathcal S_K),\] where \(P_Cx:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\), \[\mathcal M_K:=\{(x,p,q):p=P_Kx,\ q=P_{K^\circ}x,\ x=p+q,\ \langle p,q\rangle=0\},\] and \[\mathcal S_K:=\{(x,u):u\in K^\circ\setminus\{0\},\ \langle u,x\rangle>0\}.\] Thus \(\mathcal M_K\) records metric primal-polar decompositions, while \(\mathcal S_K\) records strict certificates separating exterior points from \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic metric-separation calculus of a nonempty closed convex cone consists of the cone, its polar, their metric projectors, the graph of orthogonal primal-polar decompositions, and the set of strict polar separation certificates. A decomposition record expresses a point as orthogonal projections onto the cone and its polar. A separation record pairs an exterior point with a polar vector whose value at that point is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak C(K)=(K,K^\circ,P_K,P_{K^\circ},\mathcal M_K,\mathcal S_K)\) with \(\mathcal M_K\) and \(\mathcal S_K\) as defined above.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x,u)\in\mathcal S_K\) means \(\sup_{k\in K}\langle u,k\rangle=0<\langle u,x\rangle\).
\((x,p,q)\in\mathcal M_K\) is equivalent to \(p\in K\), \(q\in K^\circ\), \(x=p+q\), and \(p\perp q\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a closed subspace, then \(K^\circ=K^\perp\) and the calculus reduces to orthogonal subspace decomposition.
If \(K\) is self-dual, then \(K^\circ=-K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(x\in\mathcal H\), exactly one pair \((p,q)\) occurs in \(\mathcal M_K\).
If \(x\notin K\), then \(u=x-P_Kx\) belongs to \(K^\circ\) and yields a strict separation certificate.
boundary_notes: The name denotes a bundled formal system rather than an additional cone operation.
Closedness, convexity, and Hilbert geometry are essential for globally single-valued metric projectors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric projection onto a closed convex cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \(d_K(x)=\inf_{y\in K}\|x-y\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact metric projection in real Hilbert space; existence and uniqueness follow from nonempty closed convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in\mathcal H\), the projection of \(x\) onto \(K\) is the unique point \[P_Kx:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in K}\frac12\|x-y\|^2.\] Equivalently, \(p=P_Kx\) exactly when \[p\in K,\qquad x-p\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle p,x-p\rangle=0,\] where \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle u,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection of a Hilbert-space point onto a nonempty closed convex cone is the unique cone element minimizing squared distance to the point. It is equivalently characterized by feasibility of the projected point, membership of the residual in the polar cone, and orthogonality between the projection and residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_Kx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in K}\|x-y\|^2\), with \(p=P_Kx\iff p\in K,\ x-p\in K^\circ,\ \langle p,x-p\rangle=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p=P_Kx\) if and only if \(p\in K\) and \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in K\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a closed linear subspace, \(P_K\) is the ordinary orthogonal projector.
For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), \((P_Kx)_i=\max\{x_i,0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(P_K\) is positively homogeneous and idempotent.
\(P_K\) is firmly nonexpansive, hence \(1\)-Lipschitz.
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed cone, the distance infimum may fail to be attained.
In a general Banach space, existence or uniqueness may fail without additional geometric hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L^n=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\|x\|_2\leq t\}\). For \((x,s)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\), write \(r=\|x\|_2\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the Lorentz cone is the identity for points in the cone, zero for points in the negative-cone regime, and an explicit radial rescaling in the intermediate regime. The normalized cases avoid division by zero at the origin.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle u,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired metric approximation by a cone and its negative polar in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal H\), its primal-polar projection pair relative to \(K\) is \[\Pi_K(x):=(p_K(x),q_K(x)):=(P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x).\] The pair is equivalently the unique \((p,q)\in K\times K^\circ\) satisfying \[x=p+q\qquad\text{and}\qquad \langle p,q\rangle=0.\] The first component is the primal projection and the second is the polar projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-polar projection pair of a point consists of its projection onto a closed convex cone and its projection onto the cone's negative polar. It is uniquely characterized as an orthogonal pair, one component in each cone, whose sum is the original point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_K(x)=(P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x)\), equivalently the unique \((p,q)\in K\times K^\circ\) with \(x=p+q\) and \(p\perp q\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(q_K(x)=x-p_K(x)\) and \(p_K(x)=x-q_K(x)\).
\(p_K(x)=P_Kx\) is characterized by \(q_K(x)\in K^\circ\) and \(\langle p_K(x),q_K(x)\rangle=0\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed subspace \(V\), \(\Pi_V(x)=(P_Vx,P_{V^\perp}x)\).
For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), the pair is \((x_+,x_-)\), with \(x=x_++x_-\) under the negative-part convention \(x_-\leq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The residual of either projection is the other projection.
boundary_notes: The polar convention uses nonpositive pairings; using the positive dual cone changes the sign of the second component.
The pair is globally single-valued because both cones are nonempty, closed, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-cone projector is positively homogeneous, fixes exactly the cone, has that cone as its range, and vanishes exactly on the polar cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a closed convex cone is the unique nearest cone point and is characterized by a polar, orthogonal residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), the primal cone projection is the uniquely attained minimizer
\[
P_Kx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in K}\frac12\|x-y\|^2.
\]
With the polar cone defined by \(K^\circ=\{u\in H:\langle u,y\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in K\}\), a point \(p\in H\) equals \(P_Kx\) if and only if
\[
p\in K,\qquad x-p\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle p,x-p\rangle=0.
\]
Thus the variational minimizer and the primal-polar orthogonality conditions characterize exactly the same projection.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_Kx\) is the unique \(p\in K\) satisfying \(x-p\in K^\circ\) and \(\langle p,x-p\rangle=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Projection Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership gives an exact projection, while projection from outside a cone lands on its boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in C\), then \(p=x\) and \(q=0\); if \(x\in C^{\circ}\), then \(q=x\) and \(p=0\). If \(x\notin C\), then \(p\in\partial C\), while if \(x\notin C^{\circ}\), then \(q\in\partial C^{\circ}\). Hence when \(x\) lies outside both cones, both projection components are boundary points and satisfy \(x=p+q\) and \(\langle p,q\rangle=0\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside either cone, the corresponding metric projection lies on that cone's boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed Euclidean convex cone can have distance zero from an exterior point without containing any nearest point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \[C_0=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\] is a nonclosed convex cone. For \(z=(1,0)\), \(\operatorname{dist}(z,C_0)=0\), but \(z\notin C_0\); hence the distance is not attained and \(z\) has no metric projection onto \(C_0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Hilbert Projection Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the maximum norm, a closed subspace can contain infinitely many nearest points to one vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \((\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\), the distance from \((0,1)\) to \(L=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\) is \(1\), and every \((t,0)\in L\) with \(|t|\le1\) attains it. Thus the metric projection onto this closed convex cone is set-valued.
assumptions_latex: \(L=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\) is a closed linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nearest-point set in \(L\) to \((0,1)\) is \(\{(t,0):|t|\le1\}\), so projection is not single-valued.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of uniqueness in a non-Hilbert norm, even for a closed subspace.
Closedness failure for nearest-point existence, already in finite-dimensional Euclidean geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In Euclidean \(\mathbb R^2\), let \[C_0=\{(u,v):v>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \(C_0\) is a nonclosed convex cone and \[\operatorname{dist}((1,0),C_0)=0,\] but no point of \(C_0\) attains this distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex cone can have distance zero from an exterior point without containing any nearest point.

notation.meaning: The open upper half-plane together with the origin
