knowledge_statements.statement_title: Non-Hilbert Norm with Nonunique Nearest Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of single-valued projection in a non-strictly-convex norm, even for a closed linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \((\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\), let \(L=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\). For \(x=(0,1)\), every \((t,0)\in L\) with \(|t|\le1\) satisfies \[\|x-(t,0)\|_\infty=1=\operatorname{dist}(x,L).\] Hence the metric projection of \(x\) onto the closed convex cone \(L\) is not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside Hilbert geometry, a closed convex cone can have many nearest points.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R^2\) is equipped with the supremum norm.

notation.meaning: Horizontal-axis subspace, also a closed convex cone

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Hilbert Norm with Nonunique Nearest Points
Projection Boundaries beyond Closed Hilbert Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failures of projection existence and uniqueness when closedness or suitable norm geometry is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness cannot be omitted from a general projection-existence theorem: the convex cone \(C=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v>0\}\cup\{0\}\) is not closed, and \(x=(1,0)\) satisfies \(\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|_2=0\) without attaining the infimum. Uniqueness can fail outside Hilbert geometry: in \((\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\), the projection of \(x=(0,1)\) onto the closed convex cone \(L=\{(t,0):t\in\mathbb R\}\) is nonunique, because every \((t,0)\) with \(|t|\leq1\) has distance \(1\) from \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed Euclidean cone can lack nearest points, while a closed cone under a non-Hilbert norm can have multiple nearest points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing closedness can destroy projection existence, and replacing Hilbert geometry by a general norm can destroy projection uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-valued projection outside the closed Hilbert regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty. Define \(d_C(x)=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary definition distinguishing existence and uniqueness of best approximations when closed convex Hilbert-space hypotheses are not imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The metric projection correspondence is \[\operatorname{Proj}_C(x):=\{p\in C:\|x-p\|=d_C(x)\}.\] Projection existence holds at \(x\) when \(\operatorname{Proj}_C(x)\neq\varnothing\), and projection uniqueness holds when \(|\operatorname{Proj}_C(x)|=1\). The canonical projector \(P_C:X\to C\) is defined only when every \(x\in X\) has exactly one best approximation. Failure of closedness may produce \(\operatorname{Proj}_C(x)=\varnothing\); failure of convexity or strict norm geometry may produce multiple best approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Beyond nonempty closed convex subsets of Hilbert space, projection is first a set-valued best-approximation correspondence. A point may have no nearest point or more than one nearest point. A canonical single-valued projection operator exists only when every point has exactly one best approximation; thus existence and uniqueness must be stated separately outside the standard regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Proj}_C(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in C}\|x-p\|\), and a canonical \(P_C\) exists exactly when every such set is a singleton.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\) is proximinal if \(\operatorname{Proj}_C(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in X\).
\(C\) is Chebyshev if \(|\operatorname{Proj}_C(x)|=1\) for every \(x\in X\).
special_cases_latex: Every nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space is Chebyshev.
A nonclosed set can fail to contain a point realizing its distance infimum.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(C\) is not proximinal, no everywhere-defined selection \(P_C\) can be a metric projector.
If \(C\) is proximinal but not Chebyshev, any single-valued selection requires an additional choice rule.
boundary_notes: This record does not claim that closedness or convexity alone characterizes Chebyshev sets in arbitrary Banach spaces.
The Hilbert-space variational inequality and primal-polar decomposition cannot be transferred unchanged to a general normed space.

notation.meaning: set of all best approximations to x from C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection onto a Set with Respect to a Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conditional definition: for an arbitrary nonempty set, neither existence nor uniqueness of such a point is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathbb E,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space, let \(\varnothing\ne Q\subseteq\mathbb E\), and let \(x\in\mathbb E\). A point \(p\in Q\) is a projection of \(x\) onto \(Q\) with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\) if \[\|x-p\|=\inf_{y\in Q}\|x-y\|.\] One may denote such a point by \(p=\pi_{Q,\|\cdot\|}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a nonempty subset of a normed space, a point in the subset is a projection of x when it attains the smallest possible norm-distance from x. The definition does not guarantee that a projection exists or is unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is a projection of }x\text{ onto }Q\iff \|x-p\|=\inf_{y\in Q}\|x-y\|

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau decomposition relative to a cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle u,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the canonical orthogonal decomposition supplied by metric projections onto mutually polar cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Moreau cone decomposition of \(x\in\mathcal H\) relative to \(K\) is the ordered pair \[(x_K,x_{K^\circ}):=(P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x),\] characterized by \[x=x_K+x_{K^\circ},\qquad x_K\in K,\qquad x_{K^\circ}\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle x_K,x_{K^\circ}\rangle=0.\] These four conditions determine the pair uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau cone decomposition of a Hilbert-space vector is its unique expression as the sum of orthogonal components lying in a nonempty closed convex cone and its negative polar. The two components are exactly the metric projections of the vector onto those cones.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_{K^\circ}=\operatorname{Id}-P_K\).
A pair \((p,q)\) is the Moreau pair of \(x\) if and only if \(p\in K\), \(q\in K^\circ\), \(p+q=x\), and \(p\perp q\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed subspace \(V\), this is \(x=P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}x\).
For the nonnegative orthant, it is the coordinatewise positive-negative decomposition.
boundary_notes: The sign differs when the positive dual \(K^*=-K^\circ\) is used: then \(x=P_Kx-P_{K^*}(-x)\).
The defining uniqueness is for orthogonal primal-polar decompositions, not arbitrary sums from \(K+K^\circ\).

notation.meaning: component projected onto the polar cone

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Polar Decomposition Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Hilbert-space vector splits uniquely into orthogonal projections onto a closed convex cone and its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), there exists a unique pair \((p,q)\in C\times C^{\circ}\) such that \[x=p+q,\qquad \langle p,q\rangle=0.\] This pair is given by \(p=P_Cx\) and \(q=P_{C^{\circ}}x\). Equivalently, \(P_C+P_{C^{\circ}}=\operatorname{Id}\) and the two components satisfy \(\|x\|^2=\|P_Cx\|^2+\|P_{C^{\circ}}x\|^2\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in H\) has a unique orthogonal decomposition \(x=P_Cx+P_{C^{\circ}}x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau decomposition for a closed convex cone and its negative-polar convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness boundary for the metric decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t>0\}\). Then \(C\) is a nonempty convex cone but is not closed. For \(x=(1,0)\), \(d_C(x)=0\) while \(x\notin C\), so the distance is not attained and \(P_Cx\) does not exist. Consequently, the Moreau projection decomposition cannot be asserted for arbitrary nonclosed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex cone can have an unattained zero distance, so its metric projection and Moreau decomposition may fail to exist.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each Moreau component's norm is the distance to the opposite cone, and the squared distances sum to the squared norm.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), with polar \(K^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric relation formed by all Moreau component pairs, not merely a decomposition of one fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal-polar decomposition geometry of \(K\) is the orthogonality locus \[\mathcal G_K:=\{(p,q)\in K\times K^\circ:\langle p,q\rangle=0\}.\] Its synthesis map is \(\Sigma_K:\mathcal G_K\to\mathcal H\), \(\Sigma_K(p,q)=p+q\). For every \(x\in\mathcal H\), the unique pair in \(\Sigma_K^{-1}(x)\) is \[(p,q)=(P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x).\] Hence \(\Sigma_K\) is a bijection between the complementarity locus \(\mathcal G_K\) and \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-polar decomposition geometry is the set of all orthogonal pairs drawn from a cone and its polar. Adding the two components maps this locus bijectively onto the Hilbert space, and the inverse map sends a point to its two Moreau projection components.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathcal G_K\) is the graph, in component coordinates, of all Moreau decompositions.
For \((p,q)\in\mathcal G_K\), \(p=P_K(p+q)\) and \(q=P_{K^\circ}(p+q)\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed subspace \(V\), \(\mathcal G_V=V\times V^\perp\).
For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), componentwise complementarity is \(p_iq_i=0\), with \(p_i\geq0\) and \(q_i\leq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every fiber of \(\Sigma_K\) contains exactly one point.
The component norms satisfy \(\|p+q\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|q\|^2\) on \(\mathcal G_K\).
boundary_notes: The locus \(\mathcal G_K\) need not be convex.
Orthogonality is essential; the full product \(K\times K^\circ\) does not parametrize projections bijectively.

children.title: Self-Dual Specializations
children.top_down_role: Specialized decompositions for canonical self-dual cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz-Cone Positive-Part Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a Lorentz cone has a three-case closed form, giving its positive and negative Moreau components explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L_{n+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n:t\geq\|u\|_2\}\). For \(z=(t,u)\), put \(r=\|u\|_2\). Then \[P_{\mathcal L_{n+1}}(z)=\begin{cases}z,&r\leq t,\\0,&r\leq-t,\\\dfrac{t+r}{2}\left(1,\dfrac{u}{r}\right),&|t|<r.\end{cases}\] The self-dual Moreau decomposition is \(z=P_{\mathcal L_{n+1}}(z)-P_{\mathcal L_{n+1}}(-z)\), and the two cone components are orthogonal.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal L_{n+1}=\{(t,u):t\geq\|u\|_2\}\) carries the standard Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed three-case expression equals \(P_{\mathcal L_{n+1}}(z)\), and \(z=P_{\mathcal L_{n+1}}(z)-P_{\mathcal L_{n+1}}(-z)\) with orthogonal cone components.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form Moreau components for the canonical self-dual Lorentz cone.

notation.meaning: Euclidean norm of the vector component u.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Self-Dual Projection Costs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthant and Lorentz projections are linear-time direct formulas, while dense PSD projection is dominated by a cubic-time eigendecomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathbb R_+^n\), coordinatewise thresholding evaluates the projection in \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations. For \(\mathcal L_{n+1}\), evaluating one Euclidean norm and the three-case formula also costs \(O(n)\). For \(\mathbb S_+^n\), dense spectral thresholding is dominated by a symmetric eigendecomposition and costs \(O(n^3)\) arithmetic operations with \(O(n^2)\) storage.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic-operation counts use the standard dense real-arithmetic model.
The positive-semidefinite projection uses a dense symmetric eigendecomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Orthant and Lorentz projections cost \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations, while dense projection onto \(\mathbb S_+^n\) costs \(O(n^3)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(n^2)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard dense arithmetic costs for the three canonical self-dual projection specializations.

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order n.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Specializations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a self-dual cone, every vector is the difference of two orthogonal cone-valued projection components; this specializes to coordinatewise and spectral positive-negative decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Self-duality gives \(K^{\circ}=-K\). Therefore every \(x\in H\) admits the unique decomposition \[x=x_+-x_-,\qquad x_+,x_-\in K,\qquad \langle x_+,x_-\rangle=0,\] where \(x_+=P_Kx\) and \(x_-=P_K(-x)\). For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), these are the coordinatewise positive and negative parts. In \(H=\mathbb S^n\), for the positive-semidefinite cone \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), they are obtained by retaining respectively the positive and the absolute values of the negative eigenvalues in a spectral decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone self-dual under \(K^*:=\{y:\langle y,k\rangle\ge0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau decomposition specialized to self-dual cones using the positive-dual convention.

notation.meaning: Real symmetric matrices with the Frobenius inner product

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard dense arithmetic costs for the orthant, Lorentz, and positive-semidefinite projection formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In standard dense numerical implementations, projection onto \(\mathbb R_+^n\) by coordinatewise thresholding costs \(\Theta(n)\) arithmetic operations, projection onto \(L_{d+1}\) by the three-case formula costs \(\Theta(d)\), and projection onto \(\mathbb S_+^n\) by a symmetric eigendecomposition and eigenvalue thresholding costs \(O(n^3)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(n^2)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthant and Lorentz projections are linear-time closed-form computations, while a standard dense PSD projection is dominated by cubic-time eigendecomposition.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\). Its positive dual is \(K^*=\{u:\langle u,k\rangle\geq0\ \forall k\in K\}\), and its negative polar is \(K^\circ=-K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization to cones self-dual under the fixed Hilbert inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=K^*\), the self-dual Moreau components of \(x\in\mathcal H\) are \[x_+:=P_Kx,\qquad x_-:=P_K(-x).\] They satisfy \[x=x_+-x_-,\qquad x_+,x_-\in K,\qquad \langle x_+,x_-\rangle=0.\] Equivalently, the primal-polar pair is \((P_Kx,-P_K(-x))\in K\times(-K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a self-dual cone, both Moreau components can be represented using the same cone projector. Every vector is the difference of two orthogonal cone elements: the projection of the vector and the projection of its negative. In the negative-polar convention, the second primal-polar component is the negative of the latter.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_{K^\circ}x=-P_K(-x)\) when \(K^\circ=-K\).
The pair \((u,v)\in K\times K\) is the self-dual decomposition of \(x\) exactly when \(x=u-v\) and \(u\perp v\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), this is \(x=x_+-x_-\) with coordinatewise positive and negative parts.
For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), it is the positive-negative spectral decomposition of a symmetric matrix.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(x\in K\) if and only if \(P_K(-x)=0\).
boundary_notes: Self-duality depends on the selected inner product.
A cone satisfying \(K=K^\circ\) under the negative-polar convention is generally impossible except in the zero space; self-duality means \(K=K^*\).

children.title: Complementarity Geometry
children.top_down_role: Orthogonality structures reused by cone complementarity and optimality theory.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Face Incidence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary cone-feasible vectors lie in mutually incident exposed faces determined by their zero pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in K\) and \(v\in K^*\). Then \[\langle u,v\rangle=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in K\cap v^\perp\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v\in K^*\cap u^\perp.\] For fixed \(v\in K^*\), the set \(K\cap v^\perp\) is an exposed face of \(K\); symmetrically, \(K^*\cap u^\perp\) is an exposed face of \(K^*\). Thus a complementary pair occupies mutually incident primal and dual exposed faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\iff u\in K\cap v^\perp\iff v\in K^*\cap u^\perp\), and the displayed intersections are exposed faces of the respective cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed-face interpretation of conic complementarity, independent of optimization-specific KKT structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual cone components are complementary exactly when they are cone-feasible, orthogonal, and their signed difference equals the vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in H\), the pair \(u=P_Kx\) and \(v=P_{K^*}(-x)\) satisfies \[x=u-v,\qquad u\in K,\qquad v\in K^*,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=0.\] Conversely, any pair \((u,v)\) satisfying these four relations equals the displayed projection pair. Thus conic complementarity is the orthogonality condition linking the primal and dual components.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=u-v\), \(u\in K\), \(v\in K^*\), and \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\) characterize the paired projections.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection geometry expressed in the positive-dual convention used by complementarity theory.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial geometry of a complementary primal-dual cone pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset H\) be a convex cone in a real Hilbert space, with \(u\in K\) and \(v\in K^*\). Then \[\langle u,v\rangle=0\iff u\in K\cap v^\perp\iff v\in K^*\cap u^\perp.\] Thus a complementary pair lies in the exposed faces \(F_v:=K\cap v^\perp\) and \(G_u:=K^*\cap u^\perp\), which contain the respective primal and dual elements and are orthogonal to the exposing elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary cone elements lie in paired exposed faces of the primal and dual cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\iff u\in K\cap v^\perp\iff v\in K^*\cap u^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity as Paired Exposed-Face Incidence

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(K^*=\{v:\langle v,k\rangle\geq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonality geometry for primal and positive-dual cone elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The complementarity geometry of \(K\) is the set \[\operatorname{Comp}(K):=\{(u,v)\in K\times K^*:\langle u,v\rangle=0\}.\] A pair in this set is called complementary. In negative-polar coordinates, \((u,v)\in\operatorname{Comp}(K)\) exactly when \((u,-v)\in K\times K^\circ\) is orthogonal. Consequently, for every \(x\in\mathcal H\), \[\bigl(P_Kx,P_{K^*}(-x)\bigr)\in\operatorname{Comp}(K),\qquad x=P_Kx-P_{K^*}(-x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complementarity geometry of a cone is the locus of orthogonal pairs consisting of a primal cone element and a positive-dual cone element. Switching the dual component's sign identifies this locus with the orthogonal primal-polar pairs in Moreau decomposition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((u,v)\) is complementary if and only if \(u\in K\), \(-v\in K^\circ\), and \(u\perp v\).
Complementarity is the zero level set of the nonnegative pairing on \(K\times K^*\).

For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), \(U,V\succeq0\) are complementary when \(\operatorname{tr}(UV)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak, strict, and strong conic separation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A,B\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty sets, with at least one set a convex cone in the intended applications.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taxonomy of linear separation relations used for cones, points, subspaces, and affine sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonzero \(u\in\mathcal H\) separates \(A\) and \(B\) when \[\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\leq\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle.\] The separation is strict when the inequality is strict. It has margin \(\delta>0\) on normalized sets when \[\sup_{a\in A_0}\langle u,a\rangle+\delta\leq\inf_{b\in B_0}\langle u,b\rangle,\] where \(A_0,B_0\) are the specified bounded or normalized cross-sections. For a cone, homogeneity forces any finite separating level against the cone to be zero, so separating normals belong to a polar or dual cone according to orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic separation is linear separation specialized to homogeneous sets. Weak separation permits equality of the support levels, strict separation requires a gap, and quantitative strong separation records a positive margin on bounded or normalized cross-sections. Because a cone is invariant under nonnegative scaling, any finite supporting level through its vertex is zero, making polar-cone membership the natural certificate condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\neq0\) separates \(A,B\iff \sup\langle u,A\rangle\leq\inf\langle u,B\rangle\), with strict or positive-margin variants as stated.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A point \(x\) is separated from \(K\) when \(\{x\}\) and \(K\) satisfy the separation inequality.
For the orientation \(\sup_{k\in K}\langle u,k\rangle\leq\langle u,x\rangle\), finiteness on a cone requires \(u\in K^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: A point outside a nonempty closed convex set in Hilbert space is strongly separated from that set.
Two disjoint closed convex sets in finite dimensions admit weak separation.
immediate_consequences_latex: A separating vector defines two closed half-spaces containing the respective sets.
Changing \(u\) to \(-u\) reverses the orientation and interchanges polar and positive-dual conventions.
boundary_notes: Strict separation of unbounded sets need not provide a uniform Euclidean distance margin without normalization.
In infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, disjoint closed convex sets need not always be separated unless additional hypotheses hold.

notation.meaning: bounded or normalized cross-sections used to define a margin

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Margin Polar Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a closed convex cone equals the largest normalized polar separation margin, attained outside the cone by the normalized projection residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), \[d(x,C)=\max_{\substack{y\in C^{\circ}\\\|y\|\le1}}\langle y,x\rangle.\] If \(x\notin C\) and \(r=x-P_Cx\), the maximum is positive and is attained by \(y=r/\|r\|\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,C)=\max\{\langle y,x\rangle:y\in C^{\circ},\ \|y\|\le1\}\), with maximizer \((x-P_Cx)/\|x-P_Cx\|\) when \(x\notin C\).

notation.meaning: Metric projection of x onto C.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone–Point Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point outside a closed convex cone is strictly separated from it by a vector in the polar cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The vector \(y=x-P_Cx\) is nonzero and satisfies \(y\in C^{\circ}\). Moreover, \[\sup_{c\in C}\langle y,c\rangle=0<\langle y,x\rangle=\|y\|^2.\] Hence the hyperplane \(\{z:\langle y,z\rangle=0\}\) contains the cone on its nonpositive side and places \(x\) strictly on its positive side.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(y\in C^{\circ}\) such that \(\langle y,x\rangle>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong point separation with the separator supplied by the projection residual.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar certificate separating a point from a cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), let \(x\in\mathcal H\), and let \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle u,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation of an exterior point from a closed convex cone, oriented using the negative polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone-point separation certificate for \(x\) from \(K\) is a vector \[u\in K^\circ\setminus\{0\}\quad\text{such that}\quad \langle u,x\rangle>0.\] Equivalently, \[\sup_{k\in K}\langle u,k\rangle=0<\langle u,x\rangle.\] The certificate therefore places \(K\) in the half-space \(\{z:\langle u,z\rangle\leq0\}\) and \(x\) in its open complement. For \(x\notin K\), the canonical metric certificate is \(u=x-P_Kx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is strictly separated from a closed convex cone by a nonzero polar vector whose pairing with the point is positive. Homogeneity makes zero the cone's support level. For an exterior point, the projection residual is the canonical certificate and has positive value equal to its squared norm at the point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) separates \(x\) from \(K\iff u\in K^\circ\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\langle u,x\rangle>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(y=-u\in K^*\), the certificate is \(\langle y,k\rangle\geq0\) for all \(k\in K\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle<0\).
For the projection residual \(u=x-P_Kx\), \(\langle u,x\rangle=\|u\|^2>0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), a certificate can be chosen from \(\mathbb R_-^n\).
If \(K\) is a closed subspace, the certificate lies in \(K^\perp\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Such a certificate exists for every \(x\notin K\).
No such certificate exists when \(x\in K\), because polar pairings with cone elements are nonpositive.
boundary_notes: Closedness is needed for separation of every exterior point by the projection residual.
If weak separation replaces the strict inequality, points of \(K\) may satisfy the relation and membership is no longer excluded.

notation.meaning: positive dual cone, equal to minus the negative polar

knowledge_statements.title: Cone–Affine-Subspace Separation Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone's relative interior misses an affine subspace exactly when a polar functional constant on that affine subspace properly separates the two sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=a+L\) be a nonempty affine subspace. Then \[\operatorname{ri}C\cap A=\varnothing\] if and only if there exists \(y\in C^{\circ}\cap L^{\perp}\) such that \(\langle y,a\rangle\ge0\) and either \[\langle y,a\rangle>0\quad\text{or}\quad\langle y,c_0\rangle<0\text{ for some }c_0\in C.\] Thus y is nonpositive on C, constant and nonnegative on A, and the two sets are properly separated.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subset X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
\(A=a+L\), where \(L\subset X\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap(a+L)=\varnothing\) exactly under the displayed proper-separation certificate in \(C^{\circ}\cap L^{\perp}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-section variant of finite-dimensional cone–subspace separation.

notation.meaning: Affine subspace with direction space L.
Functionals constant on every translate a+L.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Cone–Subspace Separation Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone's relative interior misses a subspace exactly when a polar vector annihilates the subspace and is strictly negative somewhere on the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex cone \(C\subset X\) and a linear subspace \(L\subset X\), \[\operatorname{ri}C\cap L=\varnothing\] if and only if there exists \(y\in C^{\circ}\cap L^{\perp}\) such that \[\langle y,c_0\rangle<0\quad\text{for some }c_0\in C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subset X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap L=\varnothing\iff\exists y\in C^{\circ}\cap L^{\perp}\text{ with }\langle y,c_0\rangle<0\text{ for some }c_0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact homogeneous finite-dimensional equivalence with the strictness required for proper separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone–Subspace Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a cone's relative interior misses a subspace, a nonzero polar vector annihilates the subspace and weakly separates it from the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a nonzero \(y\in X\) such that \[\langle y,c\rangle\le0=\langle y,\ell\rangle\qquad\text{for every }c\in C\text{ and }\ell\in L.\] Equivalently, \(y\in C^{\circ}\cap L^{\perp}\), so a hyperplane containing \(L\) weakly separates it from \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subset X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
\(L\subset X\) is a linear subspace with \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap L=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional weak separation of a cone from a linear subspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separation of a convex cone from an affine section; the immutable linear-subspace theorem is the zero-offset case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=a+L\). If \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap A=\varnothing\), then there exists \(0\ne y\in C^{\circ}\cap L^{\perp}\) such that \(\langle y,a\rangle\ge0\). Thus \[\langle y,c\rangle\le0\le\langle y,a+\ell\rangle=\langle y,a\rangle\qquad(c\in C,\ \ell\in L).\] A positive uniform functional gap exists exactly when such a separator can be chosen with \(\langle y,a\rangle>0\). For \(a=0\), a positive gap is impossible because both sets contain the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior disjointness from an affine subspace yields a polar separator that annihilates its direction space. Its offset value determines whether the gap is positive.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subset X\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists y\in(C^{\circ}\cap L^{\perp})\setminus\{0\}\) with \(\langle y,a\rangle\ge0\); strict uniform separation is equivalent to the existence of such a \(y\) with \(\langle y,a\rangle>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation of a cone from a linear subspace
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone and let \(L\) be a closed linear subspace of a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\). Write \(L^\perp=\{u:\langle u,\ell\rangle=0\ \forall\ell\in L\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous separation of a cone and a subspace; quantitative strength is measured on the unit cross-section of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(u\neq0\) separates \(K\) from \(L\) in the polar orientation when \[u\in K^\circ\cap L^\perp,\] equivalently \(\langle u,k\rangle\leq0=\langle u,\ell\rangle\) for every \(k\in K\) and \(\ell\in L\). It strongly separates the nonzero directions of \(K\) from \(L\) when there is \(\delta>0\) such that \[\langle u,k\rangle\leq-\delta\|k\|\qquad\forall k\in K.\] In finite dimensions this strong condition is equivalent to \(-u\in L^\perp\cap\operatorname{int}K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone and a linear subspace are separated by a nonzero vector orthogonal to the subspace and lying in the cone's negative polar. Strong separation requires a uniform negative margin on unit cone directions. In finite dimensions, this means that the oppositely oriented normal lies in the intersection of the subspace orthogonal complement and the interior of the positive dual cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) separates \(K,L\iff u\in K^\circ\cap L^\perp\setminus\{0\}\); strong separation requires \(\langle u,k\rangle\leq-\delta\|k\|\) for some \(\delta>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(y=-u\), weak separation is \(y\in K^*\cap L^\perp\setminus\{0\}\).
In finite dimensions, strong separation is \(L^\perp\cap\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: If \(L=\{0\}\), weak certificates are simply nonzero dual or polar vectors.
For an affine space \(a+L\), the same normal lies in \(L^\perp\), while the separating level is shifted by \(\langle u,a\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strong certificate implies \(K\cap L=\{0\}\).
In the standard finite-dimensional closed-cone alternative, \(K\cap L=\{0\}\) is paired with the existence of an interior-dual vector in \(L^\perp\).
boundary_notes: A nonzero weak certificate does not by itself imply that \(K\cap L\) is trivial; it may vanish on a nonzero face of \(K\).
The interior-dual characterization requires the finite-dimensional regularity stated in the scope; infinite-dimensional cones may have empty dual interior.

notation.meaning: uniform separation margin on cone directions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak, proper, strict, and strong separation of convex sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,C_2\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets. For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), write \(H(u,\alpha)=\{z:\langle u,z\rangle=\alpha\}\), \(a_u=\sup_{x\in C_1}\langle u,x\rangle\), and \(b_u=\inf_{y\in C_2}\langle u,y\rangle\), allowing extended-real extrema when appropriate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean separation. Strict separation is pointwise and need not have a uniform margin; strong separation requires a positive uniform gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sets are weakly separated if there exist \(u\ne0\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\leq\langle u,y\rangle\) for every \(x\in C_1\) and \(y\in C_2\). Such a separation is proper if the two sets are not both contained in \(H(u,\alpha)\). It is strict if \(\langle u,x\rangle<\alpha<\langle u,y\rangle\) for every \(x\in C_1\) and \(y\in C_2\). It is strong if \(a_u<b_u\), equivalently if some \(\delta>0\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha-\delta\) and \(\langle u,y\rangle\geq\alpha+\delta\) for all \(x\in C_1\), \(y\in C_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak separation places the two nonempty convex sets in opposing closed half-spaces of one hyperplane. It is proper when the hyperplane does not contain both sets, strict when every point lies in the corresponding open half-space, and strong when the scalar projections have a positive uniform gap. In formulas, strong separation means \(\sup_{C_1}\langle u,\cdot\rangle<\inf_{C_2}\langle u,\cdot\rangle\) for some \(u\ne0\). Proper separation is governed by relative-interior disjointness, while strong separation is governed by positive distance, or equivalently by exclusion of zero from \(\operatorname{cl}(C_1-C_2)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are nonempty convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Proper separation exists if and only if \(\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2=\varnothing\).
Strong separation exists if and only if \(\inf\{\|x-y\|:x\in C_1,y\in C_2\}>0\), equivalently \(0\notin\operatorname{cl}(C_1-C_2)\).

For fixed \(u\), strong separation is equivalent to the existence of \(\alpha\) and \(\delta>0\) with \(C_1\subset\{z:\langle u,z\rangle\leq\alpha-\delta\}\) and \(C_2\subset\{z:\langle u,z\rangle\geq\alpha+\delta\}\).
special_cases_latex: If one set is a singleton \(\{p\}\) and the other is a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) with \(p\notin C\), they are strongly separated.
If \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are disjoint polyhedral convex sets, strong separation is available because \(C_1-C_2\) is closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strong separation implies strict, proper, and weak separation.
Strict separation need not imply strong separation when the projection extrema approach the separating level without attaining it.
Intersecting relative interiors precludes proper separation, even though a nonproper weak separation may exist.
boundary_notes: Disjoint closed convex sets can have zero distance and therefore fail to be strongly separated.
Ambient interiors may be empty for lower-dimensional sets; proper separation uses relative interiors to avoid this degeneracy.
The orientation of \(u\) is conventional: replacing \(u\) by \(-u\) interchanges the two half-spaces.

notation.meaning: Hyperplane with nonzero normal \(u\) and level \(\alpha\).
Relative interior of the convex set \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Distance Characterization of Strict Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex sets have a positive uniform separating gap exactly when their distance is positive; each functional gap gives a distance lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\) be nonempty convex subsets of a real normed space. They admit strict separation by a continuous linear functional with a positive uniform gap if and only if \[\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf_{a\in A,\,b\in B}\|a-b\|>0.\] Every separator \(x^*\ne0\) with gap \[\gamma:=\inf_{b\in B}\langle x^*,b\rangle-\sup_{a\in A}\langle x^*,a\rangle>0\] satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)\ge\gamma/\|x^*\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform-gap strict separation is equivalent to \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0\), and every functional gap satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)\ge\gamma/\|x^*\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization under the seed's uniform-gap convention.

notation.meaning: Infimum of distances between points of A and B.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the uniform-gap convention, strict separation means that a nonzero continuous linear functional orders two sets with a positive uniform gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the uniform-gap convention, the sets \(A\) and \(B\) are strictly separated if there exist \(x^*\in X^*\setminus\{0\}\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), and \(\delta>0\) such that \[\langle x^*,a\rangle\le\alpha-\delta<\alpha+\delta\le\langle x^*,b\rangle\] for every \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\). Equivalently, \[\sup_{a\in A}\langle x^*,a\rangle<\inf_{b\in B}\langle x^*,b\rangle.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the uniform-gap convention, strict separation holds exactly when a nonzero continuous linear functional has a positive uniform gap between the two sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition using the uniform-gap convention for strict separation; some sources call this strong separation.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between positive set distance, positive functional gap, and an optimal normalized separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex sets \(A,B\subset X\), let \(d(A,B)=\inf\{\|b-a\|:a\in A,b\in B\}\). Then, with extended-real support levels, \[d(A,B)=\sup_{\|u\|\le1}\left(\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle-\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\right).\] Consequently, \(A\) and \(B\) are strictly separated in the uniform-gap sense if and only if \(d(A,B)>0\). If a closest pair \((a_*,b_*)\) exists and \(d(A,B)>0\), then \(u_*=(b_*-a_*)/\|b_*-a_*\|\) attains the supremum and \[\sup_{a\in A}\langle u_*,a\rangle=\langle u_*,a_*\rangle<\langle u_*,b_*\rangle=\inf_{b\in B}\langle u_*,b\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty convex sets admit a positive uniform-gap separator exactly when their distance is positive. The largest gap over unit normals equals that distance, and an attained closest pair supplies an optimal normal.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict uniform-gap separation holds if and only if \(d(A,B)>0\), and the optimal unit-normal gap equals \(d(A,B)\).

notation.meaning: Infimal Euclidean distance between A and B
Unit normal obtained from an attained closest pair

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Characterization of Strict Separation
Finite-Dimensional Weak Separation Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two nonempty disjoint convex sets in finite dimensions are weakly separated, but their separating margin may be zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty, convex, and disjoint, then there exist \(u\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \[\langle u,a\rangle\le\alpha\le\langle u,b\rangle\qquad(a\in A,\ b\in B).\] The supporting levels may coincide, even when both sets are closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists u\ne0,\alpha:\langle u,a\rangle\le\alpha\le\langle u,b\rangle\) for all \(a\in A,b\in B\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Controlled Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous hyperplanes cannot distinguish a convex cone from its closure; only points outside the closure admit a strict functional gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Continuity gives \[\sup_{c\in C}\langle x^*,c\rangle=\sup_{c\in\overline C}\langle x^*,c\rangle,\qquad C^{\circ}=(\overline C)^{\circ}.\] Consequently, if \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\), no continuous linear functional can place \(x\) strictly above its supremum on \(C\). Conversely, when \(C\) is convex and \(x\notin\overline C\), standard point-versus-closed-convex-set separation yields a continuous functional with a strict gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Continuous linear inequalities describe \(C\) and \(\overline C\) identically, so strict separation detects only points outside \(\overline C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How closure determines what continuous hyperplane separation can distinguish.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Sum Criterion for Subspace Transversality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed Hilbert subspaces have a positive transverse angle exactly when their algebraic sum is closed; trivial intersection alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be closed subspaces of a Hilbert space and define their Friedrichs cosine by \[c(M,N):=\sup\{|\langle m,n\rangle|:m\in M\cap(M\cap N)^{\perp},\ n\in N\cap(M\cap N)^{\perp},\ \|m\|=\|n\|=1\},\] with value \(0\) if one of the reduced subspaces is \(\{0\}\). Then \[c(M,N)<1\iff M+N\text{ is closed}.\] In particular, when \(M\cap N=\{0\}\), a positive angular separation between their unit directions exists exactly when \(M+N\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real or complex Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(M,N)<1\iff M+N\text{ is closed}\); for \(M\cap N=\{0\}\), this is equivalent to positive unit-direction separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Trivial-Intersection Margin
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonzero closed cones in finite dimensions, trivial intersection forces positive separation between their unit directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) and \(D\) be nonzero closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional normed space. If \(C\cap D=\{0\}\), then \[\inf\{\|c-d\|:c\in C,\ d\in D,\ \|c\|=\|d\|=1\}>0.\] Thus trivial intersection forces a positive normalized directional margin in finite dimensions, unlike in the infinite-dimensional graph-subspace example.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonzero closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness boundary for the zero-angle pathology.
Closed-subspace example showing that trivial intersection need not yield a positive angular margin in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(H=\ell^2\oplus\ell^2\), let \(Te_n=n^{-1}e_n\), \(C=\ell^2\oplus\{0\}\), and \(D=\{(u,Tu):u\in\ell^2\}\). Then \(C\) and \(D\) are closed linear subspaces and \(C\cap D=\{0\}\). Nevertheless, for \[c_n=(e_n,0),\qquad d_n=\frac{(e_n,n^{-1}e_n)}{\sqrt{1+n^{-2}}},\] one has \(\|c_n\|=\|d_n\|=1\) and \(\|c_n-d_n\|\to0\). Hence \(\tau(C,D)=0\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subset X\) be a nonempty convex cone, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and define \(K^*=\{s\in X:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\). For each right-hand side \(b\in Y\), set \(P_b:\ b\in A(K)\) and \(D_b:\ \exists y\in Y\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous conic feasibility. The definition separates logical exclusivity from certificate completeness; completeness may require closedness or another regularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((P_b,D_b)\) is the conic alternative associated with \((A,K,b)\). It is exclusive when \(P_b\) and \(D_b\) cannot both hold, complete when at least one holds, and exact when exactly one holds. The family generated by \((A,K)\) is exact if \(P_b\mathbin{\veebar}D_b\) for every \(b\in Y\), where \(\veebar\) denotes exclusive disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general conic theorem of the alternative pairs primal membership \(b\in A(K)\) with a dual separating certificate. The certificate is a vector \(y\) whose adjoint image belongs to the dual cone and whose pairing with \(b\) is negative. These assertions are always incompatible: a feasible representation \(b=Ax\), \(x\in K\), would make \(\langle b,y\rangle=\langle x,A^*y\rangle\geq0\). The pair is called exact only when it is also complete, meaning that every infeasible right-hand side admits such a certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subset X\) is a nonempty convex cone and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(b\in Y\), and duality uses \(K^*=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_b:\ \exists x\in K,\ Ax=b;\qquad D_b:\ \exists y,\ A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0;\qquad \text{exactness}:\ P_b\mathbin{\veebar}D_b.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The primal assertion is the cone-membership statement \(b\in A(K)\).
The dual assertion says that the homogeneous half-space \(\{z\in Y:\langle z,y\rangle\geq0\}\) contains \(A(K)\), while \(b\) lies in its opposite open half-space.
Family-wide exactness means \(b\notin A(K)\Rightarrow\exists y\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\), for every \(b\in Y\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(A\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a^i\), the pair becomes the classical Farkas alternative: either \(b\) is a nonnegative combination of the \(a^i\), or some \(y\) satisfies \(\langle a^i,y\rangle\geq0\) for all \(i\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).
For \(K=X\), the dual cone is \(K^*=\{0\}\), so the certificate condition reduces to \(A^*y=0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\), the usual range-versus-nullspace alternative.
immediate_consequences_latex: The assertions \(P_b\) and \(D_b\) are mutually exclusive for every convex cone \(K\), independently of closedness.
Failure of exactness can occur only through failure of certificate completeness.
Scaling a certificate by any \(t>0\) preserves \(A^*(ty)\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,ty\rangle<0\).
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert that every cone image \(A(K)\) is closed.
The sign convention for \(K^*\) determines the displayed inequalities; using the polar cone reverses the signs.
Affine conic systems can be homogenized, but that construction is outside this slot.

notation.meaning: Primal feasibility and dual certificate assertions.
Exclusive disjunction: exactly one assertion holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Cone Alternative Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the linear image plus the closed cone is closed, either the conic system is feasible or a strict dual certificate exists, but never both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and suppose \(Q=A(\mathbb{R}^n)+K\) is closed. For every \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[b=Ax+k\quad\text{for some }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ and }k\in K;\] \[y\in K^*,\qquad A^*y=0,
\qquad \langle y,b\rangle<0.\] Thus failure of conic feasibility has a strict linear certificate whenever the relevant sum cone is closed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(b\in A(\mathbb{R}^n)+K\) and \(\exists y\in K^*:A^*y=0,\ \langle y,b\rangle<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic Farkas alternative under closedness of the feasible image cone.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subset X\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear. Denote its conic image by \(C=A(K)\) and use the dual cone \(K^*=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic systems in the closed-image regime. Closedness of \(K\) alone does not guarantee closedness of \(A(K)\); the image-closedness condition is explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A closed-cone alternative family is in the closed-image regime when \(K\) is closed and \(A(K)\) is closed in \(Y\). Its canonical alternative at \(b\in Y\) is \[\exists x\in K:\ Ax=b\qquad\mathbin{\veebar}\qquad\exists y\in Y:\ A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0.\] Equivalently, every point outside \(A(K)\) admits a homogeneous strict separating functional from \(A(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-cone alternative family is a conic feasibility family whose underlying cone \(K\) and conic image \(A(K)\) are both closed. For every right-hand side \(b\), the associated alternatives are primal representability as \(b=Ax\) with \(x\in K\), and existence of a dual vector \(y\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\). In this regime the image is a closed convex cone, so membership and strict homogeneous separation form an exact feasibility-certificate pair.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subset X\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(A(K)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall b\in Y:\quad b\in A(K)\quad\mathbin{\veebar}\quad\exists y\in Y\ \bigl(A^*y\in K^*\ \wedge\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The closed-image condition is \(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))=A(K)\).
Certificate completeness is equivalent to \(b\notin A(K)\Rightarrow b\notin\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\), followed by strong homogeneous separation of the point \(b\) from the cone.
The dual certificate can be normalized, when nonzero, by imposing \(\|y\|=1\) and retaining \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is polyhedral, then \(A(K)\) is polyhedral and hence closed, so the family lies in this regime.
If \(A\) is injective on all recession directions of \(K\), specifically \(K\cap\ker A=\{0\}\), a standard finite-dimensional closedness criterion ensures that \(A(K)\) is closed.
For \(A=I\), the alternative reduces to membership in a closed convex cone versus strict separation by an element of its dual cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every infeasible right-hand side has an elementary dual separating certificate.
No vector in \(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\) exists in this regime.
The family-wide conic alternative is exact, not merely exclusive.

When \(A(K)\) is not closed, points in \(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\) are infeasible but cannot satisfy the strict certificate inequality.
Infinite-dimensional images require additional topological qualifications and are excluded.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, homogeneous, full-dimensional strict feasibility. Strictness means membership in the ambient interior of the cone, not merely nonzero membership or relative-interior membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strict conic alternative associated with \((A,K)\) is the pair \[P_{\mathrm{str}}:\ \exists x\in X\text{ such that }Ax\in\operatorname{int}K,\qquad D_{\mathrm{str}}:\ \exists y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\text{ such that }A^*y=0.\] The data are in an exact strict-alternative regime when \(P_{\mathrm{str}}\mathbin{\veebar}D_{\mathrm{str}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict alternative compares a strictly conic primal point with a nonzero dual obstruction. Strict primal feasibility requires the range of \(A\) to meet the interior of \(K\). The dual assertion requires a nonzero vector in the dual cone that annihilates the entire range of \(A\), equivalently an element of \(K^*\cap\ker A^*\) other than zero. In the exact strict regime, precisely one assertion holds. For the nonnegative orthant, strict cone membership is coordinatewise strict positivity.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subset Y\) is a nonempty closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The strict primal assertion is \(\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\).
The dual assertion is the existence of a nonzero supporting functional for \(K\) that vanishes on \(\operatorname{ran}A\).
When \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^m\), the pair is \(\exists x:\ Ax>0\) componentwise versus \(\exists y\geq0\), \(y\ne0\), with \(A^*y=0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^m\), this is the homogeneous Gordan-type strict-positivity alternative.
If \(A\) is surjective, then \(P_{\mathrm{str}}\) holds because \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), while \(\ker A^*=\{0\}\).
If \(A=0\) and \(K\ne Y\), then strict feasibility fails and any nonzero element of \(K^*\) is a dual obstruction.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero \(y\in K^*\cap\ker A^*\) rules out every \(x\) with \(Ax\in\operatorname{int}K\).
The strict regime detects robust cone membership rather than mere boundary feasibility.
Positive scaling of a dual obstruction does not change the obstruction.
boundary_notes: If \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\), ambient strict feasibility is impossible; a relative-interior formulation must be stated separately.
Replacing \(\operatorname{int}K\) by \(K\setminus\{0\}\) produces a different and generally nonequivalent alternative.
This slot does not cover affine shifts \(Ax-b\in\operatorname{int}K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Interior Alternative Can Fail for a Lower-Dimensional Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-dimensional ray and the identity map, neither ambient strict feasibility nor a nonzero annihilating dual certificate holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(K=\{(t,0):t\geq0\}\) and let \(A=I\). Since \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^2}K=\varnothing\), no \(x\) satisfies \(Ax\in\operatorname{int}K\). On the other hand, \(A^*y=0\) implies \(y=0\), so there is no \(y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\) with \(A^*y=0\). Thus both alternatives in the ambient-interior statement fail when its nonempty-interior hypothesis is omitted.
assumptions_latex: Interior is taken in the ambient space \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete missing-interior boundary for the ordinary ambient-interior formulation of the strict conic alternative.

notation.meaning: Identity linear map on the plane.
Ambient Euclidean interior of the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Criterion for Strict Conic Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict dual separator exists exactly outside the closure; missing boundary points of a nonclosed cone are infeasible without such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subset\mathbb R^m\) be a convex cone and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). Then \[\exists y\in Q^*:\ \langle y,b\rangle<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\notin\overline Q.\] Consequently, if \(b\in\overline Q\setminus Q\), membership in \(Q\) is infeasible but no strict dual-cone certificate exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists y\in Q^*:\langle y,b\rangle<0\iff b\notin\overline Q\); hence \(b\in\overline Q\setminus Q\) admits no strict certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp closure boundary describing exactly when cone nonmembership admits a strict dual certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empty-Interior Failure of the Ambient Strict Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal finite-dimensional counterexample showing that the ambient-interior hypothesis cannot simply be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\) and let \(A=\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb R}\). Then \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\), so no \(x\) satisfies \(Ax\in\operatorname{int}K\). Moreover, \(K^*=\mathbb R\) and \(A^*=\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb R}\), so no nonzero \(y\in K^*\) satisfies \(A^*y=0\). Thus both systems in the ambient-interior strict alternative are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the cone has empty ambient interior, both sides of the ambient-interior strict alternative can fail simultaneously.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonclosed conic image with neither feasibility nor a strict separating certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:u\geq0,\ w\geq0,\ 2uw\geq v^2\},
\qquad A(u,v,w)=(u,v).
\]
Then \(C\) is a closed convex cone but
\[
A(C)=\bigl((0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\bigr)\cup\{(0,0)\}
\]
is not closed. For \(b=(0,1)\), one has \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(C)\setminus A(C)\). Hence \(Ax=b\) has no solution in \(C\), while no \(y\) satisfies \(A^*y\in C^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed rotated second-order cone can have a nonclosed projection, producing an infeasible limit point with no strict dual separation certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(A\) are defined by the displayed formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin A(C)\) and \(\nexists y:\ A^*y\in C^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\), although \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(C)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subset\mathbb R^m\) be a convex cone and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). A vector \(y\in Q^*\) satisfying \(\langle y,b\rangle<0\) exists if and only if \(b\notin\overline Q\). Hence every \(b\in\overline Q\setminus Q\) is infeasible for membership in \(Q\) but admits no strict dual-cone certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict separation detects points outside the closure, not missing boundary points of a nonclosed cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-alternative boundary of a conic image
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subset X\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and set \(C=A(K)\). Define the strong-alternative boundary \(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{str}}(A,K)=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus\operatorname{int}C\) and the escaped-image boundary \(\mathcal{E}(A,K)=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional ambient topology. The definition records both unattained closure points caused by nonclosed images and the loss of robust strict feasibility when the image has empty or deficient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The failure boundary for strong alternatives is \[\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{str}}(A,K)=\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus\operatorname{int}(A(K))=\bigl(A(K)\setminus\operatorname{int}(A(K))\bigr)\cup\bigl(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\bigr).\] Its escaped component \(\mathcal{E}(A,K)\) consists precisely of right-hand sides that are conically infeasible but cannot be strictly separated from \(A(K)\) by a homogeneous functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong-alternative failure boundary is the closure of the conic image with its ambient interior removed. It has an attained component, containing feasible right-hand sides on the boundary of \(A(K)\), and an escaped component \(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\), containing limits of feasible right-hand sides that are themselves infeasible. At an escaped point, the primal membership assertion fails, but a strict dual certificate also fails because every functional nonnegative on \(A(K)\) remains nonnegative on its closure. If the image has empty ambient interior, its entire closure lies on this strong-alternative boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subset X\) is a nonempty closed convex cone and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
All closures and interiors are taken in the ambient space \(Y\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(b\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{str}}(A,K)\) if and only if \(b\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\) but no neighborhood of \(b\) is contained in \(A(K)\).
\(b\in\mathcal{E}(A,K)\) if and only if there exists a sequence \(x_j\in K\) with \(Ax_j\to b\), while no \(x\in K\) satisfies \(Ax=b\).
The escaped component is empty exactly when \(A(K)\) is closed.
special_cases_latex: If \(A(K)\) is a proper closed full-dimensional cone, then \(\mathcal{E}(A,K)=\varnothing\) and \(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{str}}(A,K)=A(K)\setminus\operatorname{int}(A(K))\).
If \(\operatorname{int}(A(K))=\varnothing\), then \(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{str}}(A,K)=\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\).
For polyhedral \(K\), linear images are polyhedral and closed, so only the attained boundary component remains.
immediate_consequences_latex: An escaped-image point is a simultaneous failure of primal feasibility and elementary strict separation.
Closedness of \(A(K)\) removes the certificate gap \(\mathcal{E}(A,K)\).
Using relative interior instead of ambient interior can remove degeneracy caused solely by a lower-dimensional affine hull, but it does not repair nonclosedness.
boundary_notes: A boundary point already belonging to \(A(K)\) is primal feasible; its failure concerns strict or robust feasibility, not ordinary feasibility.
The definition does not identify all possible extended or facial-reduction certificates for escaped points.
Closedness of \(K\) does not by itself make \(\mathcal{E}(A,K)\) empty.
